title: Sweet Squash and Seaweed Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1 butternut squash (or other winter squash) 1 small onion or bunch of scallions
body:
1 stalk celery, diced

1 butternut squash (or other winter squash) 1 small onion or bunch of scallions

Few chopped leaves of Chinese cabbage

1 small piece of wakame seaweed, cut in small pieces 2 T. tamari or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos

3 T. garbanzo miso (or other light miso)

Begin with 2 quarts water. Peel and dice the butternut squash and simmer in water, adding the wakame. Add the onion, celery and cabbage. When the vegetables are tender, add the tamari or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos and garbanzo miso, which has been dissolved in a small amount of broth. Garnish with a sprig of cilantro. Serves 4.

title: Summer Vegetable Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1 c. tomato sauce Herb salt to season
body:
1 onion

2 carrots

1 clove garlic

1 zucchini

2 tomatoes

1 handful green beans

1 c. fresh corn

1 c. tomato sauce Herb salt to season

Tamari or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos

Chop vegetables into small pieces; add to 2 quarts water. Cook until tender then add 1 c. tomato sauce, heat until warm. Season to taste with herb salt, tamari, or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos and garnish with finely chopped cilantro and chives. Serves 4.

title: Soup Stock
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 4 six- to eight- inch pieces kombu seaweed
body:
4 six- to eight- inch pieces kombu seaweed

6 Chinese mushrooms

1 carrot

1 stalk celery

1 onion

Add all the above ingredients to 2 quarts water and bring to a boil. Then simmer for 1 hour. Strain and use the liquid for making soups or grains. It will store well in the refrigerator for about a week. Use the vegetables in some dish, perhaps a soup.

title: Black Bean Soup or Sauce
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 c. black beans

1 four-inch piece kombu

1 small onion, finely chopped

2 garlic cloves

3 T. tamari

1 t. ginger juice

½ red bell pepper 2 T. cilantro

Soak beans overnight. Discard soak water, cover with fresh water and cook beans and kombu for about an hour. You may need to add more water. During the last 20 minutes of cooking, add garlic, onions, and red bell pepper. Mix tamari and ginger juice in at the end. Blend for a creamy sauce to pour over grains or steamed vegetables. Garnish with cilantro. Serves 4.

title: Beet Soup or Sauce
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
5-6 carrots

2-3 large beets

2 onions

2-4 stalks celery

3-4 cloves garlic

2 T. miso

2 T. olive oil

1 t. basil, chopped

1 t. oregano, chopped

1 t. umeboshi plum paste

Cook vegetables with 3-4 cups water until tender. Blend vegetables with the cooking liquid. Add the miso, olive oil, basil, oregano, and umeboshi plum paste. Return to flame and simmer for 20 minutes to mix flavors. To make into a sauce, add arrowroot dissolved in ¼ c. water to the mixture and heat until thick and smooth. Serve sauce over noodles or steamed vegetables. Serves 4-6.

title: Chinese Noodle Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 8 Chinese mushrooms, soaked with stems removed and sliced very thin
body:
8 Chinese mushrooms, soaked with stems removed and sliced very thin

6 white mushrooms, sliced very thin

1 red bell pepper, sliced very thin

1 small yellow squash, sliced

1 small piece wakame, sliced into small pieces

Put vegetables into 2 quarts water or vegetable broth and cook until tender. Then add the following:

3 T. cilantro, chopped

3 green onions, chopped

1 T. tamari

1 t. peanut oil or toasted sesame oil

1 small handful bean threads (mung bean noodles)

Remove from fire and let sit covered for 5 minutes. Serves 4.

title: Winter Melon Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 3 c. winter melon, peeled and chopped
body:
3 qt. vegetable broth

3 c. winter melon, peeled and chopped

2 carrots

2 celery stalks

1 onion

12 Chinese mushrooms, stems removed

6 oz. tofu noodles or finely sliced baked tofu

1 t. chives

1 t peanut oil

1 T. tamari

Cook together until tender, about 25 minutes. Season with chives, tamari, and peanut oil. Serves 4.

title: Creamy Split Pea Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 c. green split peas

3 c. water

1 six-inch piece kombu

1 carrot

1 celery stalk

1 small onion

1 t. tamari

½ c. soymilk (or almond milk)

1 T. cilantro

¼ t. paprika

½ t. curry powder

½ t. coriander seed

Pinch nutmeg

Cook peas and kombu until soft. Add the vegetables and cook another 15 minutes. When vegetables are done, put in blender with the tamari, soy milk, cilantro, paprika, curry powder, coriander seed powder, and nutmeg. Serves 4-6.

title: Fancy Rice
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 c. dry brown rice

2 c. water

1 carrot, chopped finely

3 scallions, chopped

¼ red bell pepper, chopped finely

Cook brown rice as usual with water. After about 25 minutes, add the carrot, scallions, and red bell pepper. Cook another 20 minutes or until water is all absorbed. Serves 2.

title: Nori Burritos
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
Sheets of nori seaweed

Cooked rice

Carrots, sliced and steamed

Pickled ginger

Sesame seeds, toasted and crushed

Toast sheets of nori seaweed briefly over stovetop flame until it changes color from brown to green (this take about 15 seconds) or use sushi nori that has already been toasted. On one end, lay out cooked rice, chopped green onion, steamed carrot slices, pickled ginger, and crushed, toasted sesame seeds. Roll up like a burrito, moistening the edge to make it stick. The edge can be moistened with tamari or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos for added flavor.

title: Vegetable Pie
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
Crust:

1 c. brown rice

2½ c. water

½ c. couscous

1 c. jicama root, grated

1 t. chives

½ t. basil

¼ t. curry powder

1 t. tamari or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos

Filling (finely chopped):

6 oz. tempeh

2 small carrots

1 leek

1 celery stalk

5 Chinese mushrooms, soaked with stems removed

Cook brown rice in water for 30 minutes, then add couscous and cook another 10-15 minutes or until water is absorbed. When done, stir in the jicama, chives, basil, curry powder and tamari. Press into a pie pan and add the filling ingredients.

Steam the pie for 30 minutes. Garnish the top with chopped cilantro. Serves 4-6.

title: Millet Patties
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 c. millet

2½ c. water

½ t. basil

3 scallions, finely chopped

¼ c. grated carrots

1 T. tamari

Cook millet in water for 30 minutes, or until water is absorbed. Add basil, scallions, carrots and tamari and mix well. Form 2- inch wide patties and put on an oiled cookie sheet. Bake at 325 degrees for 20-30 minutes. They should be crisp on the outside. Serves 4-6.

title: Stuffed Pumpkin
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Cut the top off a small pumpkin; clean out the seeds and strings; save the lid. Fill with the following mixture:
body:
Cut the top off a small pumpkin; clean out the seeds and strings; save the lid. Fill with the following mixture:

3 c. cooked rice or barley

1 T. toasted sesame seeds, crushed

2-3 stalks celery, chopped

1 onion, finely chopped

1 T. parsley

1 t. thyme

1 t. sage

½ t. rosemary

1 T. tamari

Cover with lid and bake at 350 degrees for 1¼-1½ hours (until fork easily goes into pumpkin).

Serves 4-6.

title: Simple Couscous Pie
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: ¼ c. amaranth or quinoa or millet (presoaked a few hours)
body:
1 c. couscous

¼ c. amaranth or quinoa or millet (presoaked a few hours)

1½ c. boiling water or broth

6 Chinese mushrooms, soaked and sliced

1 c. winter squash, grated or mashed

1 small leek

2 chard leaves

½ red bell pepper

Chopped walnuts

Soak grains in the water 15-30 minutes until soft. Mix with vegetables, all finely chopped. Press into a pie pan and top with chopped walnuts. Steam 40 minutes over medium flame. Serves 6.

Variations:

1. Substitute 1 c. fresh corn kernels for the red bell pepper.

2. Substitute 1 c. grated carrot for the squash.

3. Substitute 1 c. spinach for the chard.

This is an very portable dish and easy to pack for lunch.

title: Basic Protein Cereal
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1 c. brown rice (or ½ barley, ½ brown rice)
body:
1 c. brown rice (or ½ barley, ½ brown rice)

1/3 c. soybeans

1 T. sesame or sunflower seeds

Soak above in 3 c. water overnight or in hot water for a few hours. Pour into blender and blend well. Put into a bowl and steam for 1½-2 hours. Serves 4.

Variations:

1. Substitute black or azuki beans for the soybeans.

2. Substitute ½ c. millet for ½ c. brown rice.

3. Substitute walnuts or pecans for the sesame seeds.

4. Season with ginger or cinnamon, or honey or rice syrup, or nut butter.

5. Substitute raw peanuts for the soybeans.

title: Chestnut Rice
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1 c. brown rice or sweet rice
body:
½ c. dried chestnuts

1/3 c. raw peanuts

1 c. brown rice or sweet rice

Soak together the above with 3 ¾ c. water overnight or in hot water for several hours. Pour into a bowl and steam over low flame for 2 hours, stirring occasionally, until chestnuts are tender. Serves 4.

Variations:

1. Substitute walnuts for the chestnuts

2. Substitute ½ c. barley for ½ c. rice

title: Simple Grain Dish
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1 c. whole grains (brown rice, barley, millet, sweet rice, couscous, or a mixture of these)
body:
1 c. whole grains (brown rice, barley, millet, sweet rice, couscous, or a mixture of these)

2 c. water

Preparation:

1. Mix grains and water and steam for 1½-2 hours over a medium flame. Serves 2-4.

2. Use 1 c. grain to 2-2½ c. water to cook grains in pot with lid directly on stove (as opposed to steaming) for 45-50 minutes or until the water is absorbed.

Variations:

1. Add dates or raisins and cinnamon for seasoning.

2. Add steamed peanuts.

3. Add brown rice syrup or maple syrup.

title: The Fastest Cereal: Couscous
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Pour 1 c. boiling water over ¾ c. couscous. Let sit for 5 minutes, covered. Garnish with scallions and cilantro. Serves 2-4.
body:
Pour 1 c. boiling water over ¾ c. couscous. Let sit for 5 minutes, covered. Garnish with scallions and cilantro. Serves 2-4.

Variations:

1. Omit the scallions and cilantro and add a grated apple, ¼ c. raisins and a pinch of cinnamon.

2. Add steamed peanuts.

3. Add ½ c. grated carrots and a pinch of ginger.

title: Steamed Corn Bread
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1 c. grated apple (or chopped fresh pineapple)
body:
1 c. grated apple (or chopped fresh pineapple)

2 c. coconut milk (or soymilk, or almond milk, or pineapple- coconut juice)

1 medium banana

1/3 c. whole wheat flour

1 c. cornmeal

½ c. oatmeal (or millet flour or brown rice flour)

1/8 c. goji berries or raisins (optional)

Blend the liquid with the banana. Add the rest of the ingredients and mix well. Pour into a pie plate and steam 30 minutes over medium flame. It is done when a chopstick inserted in the center comes out clean. Serves 6.

Variations:

1. Substitute 1 c. grated carrot for the apple or use ½ carrot and ½ apple.

2. Add a pinch of each: cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg.

3. Add ¼ c. coconut.

title: Mochi
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1. Soak 2 c. brown or black sweet rice in 2 c. water. Then put in blender, a little at a time. Continue until all is blended.
body:
Preparation:

1. Soak 2 c. brown or black sweet rice in 2 c. water. Then put in blender, a little at a time. Continue until all is blended.

2. Combine 2 c. powdered brown or black sweet rice and 2 c. water. Mix together well.

Steam for 1½ hours on medium flame, covered. Open and stir well about ½ hour before it is done. Let the rice paste cool.

Use wet hands to handle the rice paste. Form a small ball, flatten between hands, and put a small amount of one of the following fillings in the center: a combination of chopped, cooked Chinese mushrooms, seaweed, baked tofu and seasoning; bean paste (azuki, black, or mung—good in summer); nut butter; or raisins. For a sweeter variety, fill with bean paste and honey or rice syrup. This makes an excellent dessert.

Next, close the patty and form a ball. Roll it over one of the following: sunflower, sesame, or cashew meal, coconut, carob powder, or toasted soybean flour. Serves 4-6.

title: Sweet Breakfast Porridge
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
¾ c. brown rice

¼ c. barley flakes

½ c. raw skinless peanuts

10 Chinese jujube dates

1 slice fresh ginger root

Cook all ingredients with 5 c. water in a crock-pot overnight, or on the stove for 2½-3 hours on low, stirring occasionally. Serves 4.

title: Tofu and Mushroom Casserole
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
2 lb. plain tofu, lightly steamed

12 large Chinese mushrooms, soaked until soft, thinly sliced

2 c. pea pods

1 bunch scallions

2 T. tamari or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos

3 T. kuzu (or arrowroot or cornstarch)

Slice tofu into 1/2 inch slices and put in bottom of rectangular baking dish. Lightly simmer mushrooms then add pea pods and scallions for last 5 minutes. Put these vegetables on top of the tofu. Use the vegetable cooking water plus enough water to make 3 c. liquid. Add tamari. Dissolve kuzu in a small amount of liquid; add to the rest of the liquid, simmer, stirring often, until the liquid thickens. Pour this gravy on top of the tofu and vegetable mixture. Garnish with crushed, toasted almonds and finely chopped cilantro. Serves 4.

title: Azuki Bean and Squash Casserole
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 c. azuki beans, soaked overnight

Two 6-8 inch pieces of kombu

1 small butternut squash or other winter squash

Cover beans and kombu with water and simmer about one hour, adding water if needed. Peel and cube the squash and add to the beans. Cook until tender, about ½ hour. Stir in a pinch of sea salt or 1-2 teaspoons tamari. Serves 4.

title: Clinton’s Savory Azuki Beans with Chestnuts
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 c. azuki beans, soaked overnight

¼ c. dried chestnuts, soaked 1 hour

4 six-inch strips kombu seaweed

1 t. tamari or pinch sea salt

1 t. goji berries (optional)

Soak azuki beans overnight; discard soak water. Place kombu in pot then add chestnuts and beans. Cover with 2 inches water and bring to a boil. Simmer 2–3 hours, adding enough water to keep beans covered. Add tamari and the goji berries 10-15 minutes before cooking is done. Serves 4.

title: Tofu Skins and Mushrooms
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 12 strips dried tofu skins (available at Asian grocery stores)
body:
12 strips dried tofu skins (available at Asian grocery stores)

6 Chinese mushrooms, thinly sliced, stems removed

8 white mushrooms, sliced Red bell pepper, sliced

4-6 c. water

2 T. tamari

1-2 T. kuzu (or arrowroot)

Soak the dried tofu skins and Chinese mushrooms in 4-6 cups water and tamari for at least 4 hours. Then tie each strip in a knot, and simmer for 20 minutes. Add the white mushrooms and the red bell pepper and continue to simmer another 10–15 minutes. Pour off the liquid and thicken it with kuzu (do this in a separate pan, heating until thick). Pour the sauce over the tofu and mushroom mixture and serve over steamed greens. Serves 4.

title: Steamed Peanuts
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Soak peanuts in water overnight or in hot water for a few hours. Steam using the soaking water for 1½-2 hours over medium flame. This makes a delicious, nutritious addition to cereals, vegetable dishes and grains.
body:
1 c. raw peanuts

2 c. water

Soak peanuts in water overnight or in hot water for a few hours. Steam using the soaking water for 1½-2 hours over medium flame. This makes a delicious, nutritious addition to cereals, vegetable dishes and grains.

title: Scrambled Tofu
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Chop vegetables finely. Sauté in ¼ c. water or 1 T. oil. When almost done, add crumbled tofu. Let heat 5-10 minutes. Season with tamari.
body:
½ lb. tofu

2 stalks celery

6 white mushrooms

1 tomato

1 t. tamari

Chop vegetables finely. Sauté in ¼ c. water or 1 T. oil. When almost done, add crumbled tofu. Let heat 5-10 minutes. Season with tamari.

Variations:

1. Substitute one beaten egg for ½ of the tofu.

2. Substitute one small zucchini squash for the mushrooms.

title: Tofu with Seaweed
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 1 package baked tofu, sliced or ½ lb. plain tofu, cubed
body:
1 package baked tofu, sliced or ½ lb. plain tofu, cubed

1 handful hiziki or arame seaweed, soaked in hot water 20-30 minutes

1 large carrot, diced

½ c. jicama, diced

1 small onion, chopped

4 Chinese mushrooms, presoaked and sliced

Stir-fry carrots, onions, mushrooms and lastly jicama in small amount of water (or mushroom soak water). When almost done, add the tofu and seaweed. Cover and let steam for 5-10 minutes. Season with tamari and toasted sesame oil.

Variations:

1. Substitute wakame or kombu for the hiziki. These need to be presoaked for 1-2 hours.

2. Add diced burdock root (gobo) at the beginning with the carrots.

3. Use white mushrooms instead of the Chinese ones.

title: Tofu Dressing
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
½ lb. plain tofu

¼ c. oil

1 T. lemon juice

1 t. honey or rice syrup

1 t. rice or apple cider vinegar

½ t. tamari

1 T. sesame tahini

Blend all the ingredients until creamy. Use on salads, vegetables or sandwiches.

Variations:

1. Add ¼ c. poppy seeds.

2. Add 1½ t. prepared mustard.

3. Add ½ t. basil and ¼ t. garlic powder.

4. Add two whole green onions.

title: Basic Herb Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1-3 oz. (30-90 grams) herb combination

½–1½ lb. meat or fish (optional)

½ c. grain

¼ c. beans, presoaked (optional)

1-3 c. chopped vegetables

6-8 c. water or broth

Cook herbs, meat, beans, grains and hard vegetables (like carrots, potatoes) about 1 hour, until done. Add soft or leafy vegetables and finish cooking for 15-30 minutes. Season to taste with miso, tamari, soy sauce, rice vinegar or sea salt. The soup could be prepared in a crockpot on high heat for 3-4 hours.

title: Dang Gui Cornish Hen Stew
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 Cornish hen (or 3 chicken legs)

10 grams Dang Gui (Angelica sinensis)

2 parsnips, chopped

2 carrots, chopped

1 onion, chopped

2 celery stalks, chopped

1 handful wakame or dulse seaweed

8 c. water

Put all ingredients together and simmer for 1 hour. Remove the Cornish hen (or chicken legs). Remove bones, chop meat, and return to the soup. Cook for an additional 15 minutes. Season to taste with miso or soy sauce and chopped cilantro (or parsley). This soup will nourish Chi and blood.

title: Shan Yao Longevity Stew
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
10 grams Chinese Yam (Shan Yao)

10 grams goji berries (Gou Qi Zi, also called lycii berries ) .

10 grams lotus seed (Lian Zi)–presoaked

5 shiitake mushrooms–presoaked

1 onion, chopped

1 carrot or sweet potato, chopped

½ c. white or brown rice

8 c. water (include the shiitake soaking water)

Put all ingredients together and simmer for 1 hour. Season to taste with coriander seed and sea salt. This stew strengthens Spleen and Kidney.

title: Goji Berry (Gou Qi Zi) Oats
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Add a small handful of goji berries (also called lycii berries) and a small handful of almonds (or walnuts) into Scotch oats and cook until soft. Usually 3 parts water to 1 part oats. This will tonify Chi and blood.
body: Add a small handful of goji berries (also called lycii berries) and a small handful of almonds (or walnuts) into Scotch oats and cook until soft. Usually 3 parts water to 1 part oats. This will tonify Chi and blood.

title: Black Bean Stew
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Simmer ½ c. black beans with 3 c. water for 1 hour. Then add 6-8 c. chicken broth and the following herbs and vegetables:
body:
Simmer ½ c. black beans with 3 c. water for 1 hour. Then add 6-8 c. chicken broth and the following herbs and vegetables:

1 oz. Shan Yao (Chinese yam)

1 oz. goji berries (Gou Qi Zi)

½ oz. Long Yan Rou (longan fruit)

1 fennel root, chopped

6-7 shiitake mushrooms, soaked and sliced

Simmer the whole dish for 1 hour. Season to taste with sea salt, cumin seeds and brown rice vinegar. This will tonify Chi and blood.

title: Butternut Mushroom Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 butternut squash, chopped

1 handful wakame seaweed

1 oz. lily bulbs (Bai He)

Enough water to cover vegetables

Cook the above ingredients together until the squash are soft. Remove the butternut squash peel, than blend all ingredients until smooth with the cooking water

In a separate pan sauté in olive oil :

1 purple onion, chopped

2 celery stalks, chopped

12 fresh shiitake mushrooms, sliced

Combine the sautéed ingredients and the blended ones together with the following seasonings :

1 t. basil

1 t. oregano

Sea salt, Bragg’s Liquid Aminos or soy sauce, to taste

title: Sweet and Spicy Pumpkin Soup
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 kabocha squash (Japanese pumpkin)

1 onion, chopped

1 fennel bulb, chopped

1 red bell pepper, chopped

Cook squash in enough water to cover until soft, then blend with the cooking water. Return to pan and add the chopped vegetables and the following presoaked herbs:

1 oz. Chinese yam (Shan Yao)

1 oz. lily bulb (Bai He)

1 oz. goji berries (Gou Qi Zi)

1 oz. longan fruit (Long Yan Rou)

Simmer for 45 minutes. Remove from flame and season with:

1 T. lemon juice

1 t. ginger juice

½ t. cinnamon

½ t. coriander powder

½ t. curry powder

Sea salt or soy sauce to taste

Garnish with chopped cilantro. This soup is both tonifying and calming.

title: Sesame Seed Garnish
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Wash 2 c. whole, brown sesame seeds. Toast in dry skillet, stirring often until seeds can be easily crushed between the fingers. Separately, heat ½ t. sea salt in dry skillet until the chlorine gas is removed (you will smell it). Then mix t
body: Wash 2 c. whole, brown sesame seeds. Toast in dry skillet, stirring often until seeds can be easily crushed between the fingers. Separately, heat ½ t. sea salt in dry skillet until the chlorine gas is removed (you will smell it). Then mix together sesame seeds and salt and grind in blender or in mortar and pestle. Store in the refrigerator. Use as a garnish for a strong nutty flavor. Salt can be omitted if desired; kelp powder may be substituted for salt.

title: Basic Vegetable Stir-Fry
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Use a variety of vegetables, diced or sliced. Stir-fry in a small amount of water or broth, covered, the slower cooking vegetables and presoaked seaweed first (i.e. carrots, green beans, cauliflower, nori, kombu, etc.), then add the faster
body:
Use a variety of vegetables, diced or sliced. Stir-fry in a small amount of water or broth, covered, the slower cooking vegetables and presoaked seaweed first (i.e. carrots, green beans, cauliflower, nori, kombu, etc.), then add the faster cooking vegetables (i.e. jicama, zucchini, broccoli, etc.) When the last vegetables go in, you can add tofu or gluten pieces.

When the vegetables and seaweed are cooked, season to taste with oil, soy sauce (or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos), herb salt, or your favorite cooking herbs. Basil and cilantro are particularly good with vegetables.

Variations:

1. Add steamed peanuts or almonds.

2. Add one garlic clove at the beginning.

3. Add finely grated ginger toward the end of the cooking.

4. Add chopped green onions at the end.

5. Add Chinese mushrooms (presoaked) at the beginning.

title: Almond Nut Stir-Fry
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 small yam

1 s mall head cauliflower

1 leek or onion

2 summer squash

1 handful green beans

¼ lb. white mushrooms

½–¾ c. almonds

½ t. toasted sesame oil

1 T. arrowroot (or cornstarch)

Chop vegetables into small pieces. Put in skillet with about ¼ inch water. Cover and steam until vegetables are tender. Pour out any remaining water into a bowl. Add arrowroot and stir until dissolved; pour back into vegetables and heat briefly until liquid thickens. Stir in almonds and toasted sesame oil. Garnish with toasted sesame seeds. Serves 2-4.

title: Stir-Fry Over Noodles
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 2 c. broccoli, chopped 1 red bell pepper, sliced 2 garlic cloves
body:
2 c. broccoli, chopped 1 red bell pepper, sliced 2 garlic cloves

1 zucchini, diced

2 leeks, chopped

1 carrot, diced

5 white mushrooms, sliced

1 T. peanut oil

¼ c. water or broth

Heat peanut oil and sauté the garlic and leeks. Add the mushrooms, carrots, broccoli, and water or broth. Cover and cook 5 minutes. Lastly, add the zucchini and red bell pepper and cook another 5 minutes. Season to taste with basil, cilantro, and tamari. Serve over whole wheat or tofu noodles. Serves 2-4.

title: Almond Milk
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: ½ t. vanilla or almond extract
body:
1 c. raw almonds

2 c. water

½ t. vanilla or almond extract

2 T. honey or maple syrup

Pinch cinnamon

Soak almonds for at least 4 hours. Grind in blender with water, strain and put the solids back in the blender and repeat the process two more times. Combining all of the strained milk there should be a total of 6 cups. Put some of the liquid back in the blender with the vanilla, honey and cinnamon. Blend and mix back into the other liquid. Store in the refrigerator and use within a few days. Almond milk can also be sweetened by grinding in 5-6 dates or a small handful of raisins. This same procedure can be used to make other nut milks like cashew or sesame milk.

title: Soybean Milk
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Soak soybeans at least 8 hours, or as long as three days in the refrigerator. Blend soaked beans with 3 c. water, then strain through a cloth, squeezing out the milk. Put the pulp back in the blender with more water and repeat the process u
body: Soak soybeans at least 8 hours, or as long as three days in the refrigerator. Blend soaked beans with 3 c. water, then strain through a cloth, squeezing out the milk. Put the pulp back in the blender with more water and repeat the process until you have 1½ quarts of soymilk. Bring to a boil and simmer for 15- 20 minutes, stirring often to prevent sticking and boiling over. Soymilk can be used plain, mixed with carob powder and rice syrup, or blended with fruits such as papaya or banana (cool soymilk before mixing with fruit).

title: Protein Pudding
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
3 c. soymilk

1/3 c. rice syrup (or maple syrup)

1 bar agar seaweed

Rinse agar, then mix with soymilk. Cook together until agar is dissolved. Stir in syrup. Pour into dishes and let firm.

Variations:

1. Add ½ c. raisins or chopped dates.

2. Add ½ c. pecans, sunflower seeds, walnuts, or cashews.

3. Flavor with ½ t. vanilla or 3 T. carob powder.

4. Substitute almond milk for the soymilk and garnish the top with ¼ c. almonds when almost firm.

title: Pecan Pudding
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: ¼–1/3 c. maple or brown rice syrup
body:
2 c. soymilk

½ c. pecans or walnuts

¼–1/3 c. maple or brown rice syrup

3 T. arrowroot (or kudzu or sweet rice flour) 2 T. carob powder

Blend all ingredients well. Heat over low flame until thickened, stirring constantly. Serve warm.

title: Wheat Gluten (Wheat Meat)
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 2½ lbs. gluten flour (or unbleached white flour or whole wheat flour)
body:
2½ lbs. gluten flour (or unbleached white flour or whole wheat flour)

1 qt. water Tamari to season

Mix flour and water until it forms a stiff dough. Let sit one hour. Then cover with water and knead with both hands. Pour off the starchy white water and repeat the process until the water is clear. This will take many washings and much kneading. For tender gluten, cover the finished gluten with water and let stand for 1-2 days before using. To cook, drop small pieces into boiling water for 30 minutes. Remove from water and season with tamari. Gluten can also be marinated before or after cooking. Tamari, ginger, garlic, and onions make a good marinade. Gluten can be used whenever a “meaty” textured food is desired.

title: Basic Tomato Sauce
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: 3 c. chopped tomatoes 1 bell pepper, chopped 1 garlic clove
body:
3 c. chopped tomatoes 1 bell pepper, chopped 1 garlic clove

1 small onion, chopped

2 T. fresh basil (or ½ t. dried)

½ t. oregano

1 t. onion powder 1½ T. tamari

2 T. arrowroot (or kudzu or cornstarch)

Cook the tomatoes, bell pepper, garlic and onion until tender. Then put in blender with the basil, oregano, onion powder and tamari. Return to pan when well blended. Mix arrowroot with a small amount of water. Add to the tomato mixture, and heat stirring often until thick.

Variations for Basic Tomato Sauce:

1. Add ½ c. sautéed white mushrooms.

2. Add ½ c. zucchini

3. Serve over noodles or steamed spaghetti squash.

title: Simple Oil and Vinegar Dressing
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: ½ c. vinegar, rice or apple cider
body:
½ c. oil

½ c. vinegar, rice or apple cider

Lemon juice (optional)

1 T. tamari or Bragg’s Liquid Aminos (optional)

¼ t. garlic or onion powder

Blend the oil and vinegar by whisk, shaker or blender. You may add the optional ingredients. For an Italian dressing, add ½ t. oregano and ½ t. basil to the oil and vinegar mixture.

title: Coriander Vinaigrette
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
2 T. coriander seeds

½ c. olive oil

¼ c. brown rice vinegar

½ bunch cilantro, roughly chopped

1 T. shallots or chives, chopped

Salt and pepper to taste

Blend together until smooth. Serve over mixed greens or grains.

title: Lemon Vinaigrette
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: ½ lemon, whole with seeds removed
body:
1 clove garlic

½ lemon, whole with seeds removed

½ c. chopped sweet onion

½ c. lemon juice

1½ t. Dijon mustard

½ c. red wine vinegar

½ t. honey

½ t. pepper

½ t. salt

2 c. olive oil

Blend together until smooth. Serve over dark leafy greens for a Liver benefiting effect.

title: Pecan Dressing
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
½ c. sesame oil

½ c. toasted pecans

½ c. coconut milk

3 T. lemon juice

2 T. honey Salt to taste

Blend the above ingredients together and serve over the following coleslaw:

½ c. each : finely shredded cabbage, fennel and carrots 1/3 c. chopped crystallized ginger

1 T. coriander or fennel seeds

¾ c. cilantro, chopped

title: Rainbow Mix
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: This is a blend of azuki beans, mung beans and lentils. Soak seeds (together or separately) overnight. Pour off the soak water and rinse twice daily. A jar with a screen on top is very handy for growing sprouts. Store in a warm, dark place
body: This is a blend of azuki beans, mung beans and lentils. Soak seeds (together or separately) overnight. Pour off the soak water and rinse twice daily. A jar with a screen on top is very handy for growing sprouts. Store in a warm, dark place for 3-5 days remembering to rinse twice daily. At the end of the growth period, put in sunlight for 30-60 minutes for the leaves to produce chlorophyll. These can be eaten raw or lightly sautéed. Whole peas or whole wheat may also be added to this mix.

title: Light Mix
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: This blend is alfalfa seeds, red clover seeds and daikon radish seeds (optional). Sprout these in the same fashion as above. These sprouts can be eaten raw as a garnish in salads and sandwiches.
body: This blend is alfalfa seeds, red clover seeds and daikon radish seeds (optional). Sprout these in the same fashion as above. These sprouts can be eaten raw as a garnish in salads and sandwiches.

title: Rainbow Sprouts
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Lightly sauté the following in water or oil: mung, azuki and lentil sprouts, grated carrots, shredded red cabbage, soaked hiziki seaweed and grated ginger.
body: Lightly sauté the following in water or oil: mung, azuki and lentil sprouts, grated carrots, shredded red cabbage, soaked hiziki seaweed and grated ginger.

title: Garbanzo Spread
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Cook garbanzo beans until soft. Mash and mix with sesame tahini, lemon juice, garlic powder and a pinch of salt. Garnish with alfalfa/clover sprouts and tomato slices.
body: Cook garbanzo beans until soft. Mash and mix with sesame tahini, lemon juice, garlic powder and a pinch of salt. Garnish with alfalfa/clover sprouts and tomato slices.

title: Nut Butter
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Blend almond butter, sesame butter, or cashew butter, grated carrots, green onions and cilantro.
body: Blend almond butter, sesame butter, or cashew butter, grated carrots, green onions and cilantro.

title: Soy Burger
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Combine cooked soy and garbanzo beans, grated carrots, sliced mushrooms, and enough cornstarch or arrowroot or flour to hold together. Steam for 15-20 minutes over medium flame.
body: Combine cooked soy and garbanzo beans, grated carrots, sliced mushrooms, and enough cornstarch or arrowroot or flour to hold together. Steam for 15-20 minutes over medium flame.

title: Sweet Treat
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Combine almond butter, rice syrup, grated apple and a pinch of ginger or cinnamon.
body: Combine almond butter, rice syrup, grated apple and a pinch of ginger or cinnamon.

title: Eggplant Spread
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Steam eggplant until soft. Mash and mix with sesame tahini, garlic and lemon juice.
body: Steam eggplant until soft. Mash and mix with sesame tahini, garlic and lemon juice.

title: Colorful Sandwich
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
desc: Steam beets and carrots. Mash and mix with sautéed, finely chopped tofu, cabbage, and celery.
body: Steam beets and carrots. Mash and mix with sautéed, finely chopped tofu, cabbage, and celery.

title: Basic Congee Recipe
author: Mao Shing Ni and Cathy McNease
body:
1 c. rice (white, brown, sweet, basmati)

5-10 c. water (depending on how thick or thin you want the dish to be)

Cook for about 4-6 hours on a low flame or overnight in a crock pot. The finished congee can be mildly seasoned with sea salt, miso or honey.

title: Stir-Fried Chinese Water Spinach with Fermented Tofu Tahini Sauce
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
腐乳麻酱空心菜

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral, Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Stomach, Liver, Large Intestine

Functions: Aids Digestion

This sauce will make any leafy green shine. It is creamy, savory, and funky in the best way possible. Fermented tofu is a magical condiment that can be found in shelf-stable jars at grocery stores or online. It’s filled with probiotics, and when combined with fiber and other ingredients that moisten the Large Intestine, such as tahini and hemp seeds, it can help with constipation and foster a healthier microbiome. If you cannot find it, you can use miso paste instead, but miso alone will not have the same umami; funky, mouthwatering taste; and smell of fermented tofu.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 15 minutes

1 bunch fresh Chinese water spinach

One 1-inch-square piece fermented tofu or 2 teaspoons miso paste, plus more as needed

2 tablespoons tahini

1 tablespoon hemp seed butter*

1 tablespoon warm water, plus more as needed

1 tablespoon extra virgin olive oil

⅛ teaspoon ground clove

Sea salt, to taste

1. Rinse the Chinese water spinach thoroughly. With a knife, cut off the bottoms of the larger, tougher stems and discard. Roughly chop the thinner stems with leaves into finger-length chunks.

2. In a small bowl, mix the fermented tofu, tahini, hemp seed butter, and water into a thick sauce. The consistency should resemble heavy cream. Adjust the amount of water as needed. Taste the sauce and add another square of fermented tofu if it is not savory enough.

3. In a big pan or wok, heat the olive oil over medium-high heat. When the oil is hot, add the Chinese water spinach and cook for 1 minute, or until the leaves are wilted and turn darker. Add the fermented tofu sauce and mix to coat the vegetables evenly. Add the ground clove. Continue stir-frying until the vegetables are cooked and the sauce has reduced a little, about 3 minutes. Taste and season with sea salt. Serve immediately.

title: Purslane Salad with Soy-Sesame Dressing
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
马齿苋色拉

Dairy-free ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Warm, Humid

Energetics: Cold, Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Liver, Large Intestine

Functions: Cooling, Liver Health

If you are experiencing a flaring skin rash or if you are in a very hot and humid environment, look no further than this refreshing salad. You might be wondering why I would include this recipe, as TCM seems to regard raw vegetables as the culprit for everything. Well, that’s not the case here. The purslane and other vegetables are kept raw to amplify their Cooling and detoxifying functions. They are also fairly soft and easy-to-digest produce that should not cause indigestion. That said, if you are not experiencing any Heat symptoms (see here) or inflammation and have a very weak Spleen and Stomach, you may want to skip this recipe or cook the purslane by blanching or stir-frying.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 15 minutes

Dressing

⅓ cup light rice vinegar

¼ cup sesame oil

2 tablespoons soy sauce

1 tablespoon finely minced ginger

2 teaspoons honey

Sea salt, to taste

Salad

1 bunch (200 grams) fresh purslane

1 cup thinly sliced cantaloupe

1 cup thinly sliced cucumber

Picked leaves of 1 sprig fresh dill, large stem discarded

1. Make the dressing. Whisk the rice vinegar, sesame oil, soy sauce, ginger, and honey in a small bowl to combine. Season with sea salt. This recipe makes about 1 cup of dressing. You can store it in the fridge in an airtight container for up to 1 month.

2. Assemble the salad. On a plate or in a large bowl, mix the purslane, cantaloupe, cucumber, and dill. A plating tip is to use a mandolin to slice long, thin ribbons of the cantaloupe and cucumber. Roll them up and place them among the purslane.

3. Drizzle the salad with the soy-sesame dressing and enjoy.

title: Pumpkin and Lotus Seed Hummus with Crudités
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
南瓜莲子鹰嘴豆泥配时蔬

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Aids Digestion, Calming

I’d never had hummus before I came to the United States! I love how easy it is to make and how versatile it is on a dining table. Lotus seeds are perfect for making hummus because they blend so well into a smooth paste. The addition of pumpkin further strengthens our Spleen, while providing an abundance of vitamin A and fiber. This is a great recipe for those who wish to have more lotus seeds in their diet to secure the Kidney, strengthen the Spleen, and calm the Spirit.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 35 minutes

Hummus

¾ cup (75 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed, soaked in water for at least 3 hours

¾ cup cooked chickpeas, plus more as needed

1 cup pumpkin puree or mashed roasted pumpkin

3 tablespoons tahini

2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil, plus more as needed

1 tablespoon lemon juice

1 teaspoon salt, or to taste

½ teaspoon (1 gram) ground nutmeg

½ teaspoon ground cumin, or to taste

Crudités

Raw seasonal vegetables of choice*

1. Place the lotus seeds in a small saucepan with enough water to cover them. Boil for 20 minutes, then strain. Reserve a few seeds for garnish.

2. In a blender or a food processor, add the cooked lotus seeds and the rest of the hummus ingredients, and blend until smooth. If it is difficult to blend or the mixture is too thick, add more olive oil, a tablespoon at a time. If your hummus is too thin, you can thicken it by adding more chickpeas. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

3. Serve with fresh vegetables, the reserved cooked lotus seeds, and a drizzle of olive oil.

title: Herbal Poached Artichoke Hearts
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
护肝枸杞菊花煮洋蓟

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral, slightly Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Liver, Kidney

Functions: Liver Health, Respiratory Health

I’d never seen a fresh artichoke until I went to college in New York City. I didn’t even know the Chinese name for it. But it was love at first sight when I spotted it at the Union Square farmers’ market. It’s such a beautiful vegetable and its tender heart captivated me so much that I later had it tattooed on my chest. Artichokes contain two phytonutrients called cynarin and silibinin, both of which are very beneficial to the liver. By poaching the artichokes with goji berries, chrysanthemum flowers, and dandelion, three potent herbs for liver detoxification, you are making a great appetizer that can prepare you for a night of drinking. I always make this dish during the holiday season when drinking is just hard to avoid.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 20 minutes

2½ cups canned or 14 fresh artichoke hearts

2 cups vegetable stock

1 lemon, cut in half, plus additional lemon juice for serving

⅓ cup extra virgin olive oil, plus more for finishing

¼ teaspoon coriander seeds

2 sprigs fresh thyme

2 sprigs fresh rosemary

2 fresh sage leaves

2 dried or fresh bay leaves

2 tablespoons (8 grams) dried chrysanthemum flowers

½ cup (5 grams) dried dandelion, loosely packed

1 tablespoon (10 grams) goji berries

Sea salt and freshly ground black peppercorn, to taste

1. If using canned artichoke hearts, drain and rinse them. If using fresh ones, proceed to Step 2.

2. In a small pot, combine the stock, the juice of the lemon as well as the lemon itself, the olive oil, coriander seeds, thyme, rosemary, sage, and bay leaves. Bring to a boil over high heat and then add the artichoke hearts. Reduce the heat to medium-low and cook, covered, for 10 minutes.

3. In a reusable or single-use tea bag, combine the chrysanthemum flowers and dandelion and tie the bag. Add the tea bag and goji berries to the pot and cook for another 10 minutes. If using fresh artichoke hearts, cook them for longer, until they are soft, about 20 minutes.

4. Strain and reserve the liquid to use as a vegetable stock in other recipes. Place the goji berries and artichokes on a plate or in a shallow bowl. Drizzle with olive oil and lemon juice. Sprinkle sea salt and black pepper on top.

title: Creamy Goji Cashew Dressing
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
顺滑枸杞酱

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Liver, Kidney

Functions: Liver Health, Tonifies Qi and Blood

Fifteen years ago in Shanghai, the most international city in China, salad was rare and difficult to find. The Chinese really didn’t care for salad, partly due to their belief that one should not consume large portions of raw foods, and partly due to a matter of taste. I used to hate salads. I thought the combination of raw lettuce, tart cherry tomatoes, pungent raw onions, bitter olive oil, and sour lemon juice was simply horrendous. Nowadays, salads have become a trendy health food in China under the influence of the West and they’ve started to grow on me while I’ve been living in the States. However, it’s still difficult to find tasty salad dressings that are dairy-free and heartier than a vinaigrette. So, here is my go-to salad dressing that I make at home. You can also use this versatile sauce to accompany cabbage rolls, vegetable stir-fries, and even protein like chicken breast. Goji blends so well with cashews and creates a beautiful orange color and nondairy creaminess for your plate. It is always a crowd favorite at friends’ gatherings!

YIELD: 1 cup

TIME: 15 minutes

½ cup raw cashews

2 tablespoons (20 grams) goji berries

½ cup warm water or vegetable stock, plus more as needed

3 tablespoons nutritional yeast

2 tablespoons lemon juice

1 tablespoon Dijon mustard

1 small clove garlic

1 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste

½ teaspoon white pepper

1. Soak the raw cashews and goji berries in warm water for 2 hours or overnight. Drain.

2. Combine all the ingredients in a blender and blend on high speed until smooth. If it is difficult to blend or the mixture is too thick, add some extra virgin olive oil or more water. Taste and add additional sea salt if needed. It should taste pretty savory since it is a dressing. You can store the dressing in an airtight container in the fridge for up to a week.

title: Herbal Steamed Egg Custard with Soy-Scallion Vinaigrette
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
药膳青葱酱油蒸蛋

Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood

I often ate steamed egg custard while I was growing up. I can still visualize the look of my mom’s egg custard so clearly in my mind. She always makes it in a big ramen bowl for the entire family to enjoy. The silky yellow egg custard is topped with a thin layer of savory sauce and bright green scallions. When I dig in with a spoon, it is so warm, soft, and inviting. It is a great kid-friendly and postpartum-friendly dish that is packed with flavor and good nutrition. It is also very gentle for our digestive system and helpful for patients who have trouble chewing or swallowing. In this recipe, rather than using water, I used herbal broth as the liquid base for additional therapeutic qualities. Feel free to change the combination of herbs based on your own preference or at your TCM practitioner’s suggestion.

YIELD: 3 servings

TIME: 20 minutes

Custard

1 cup hot water or broth

3 thin slices (6 grams) American ginseng

2 pieces (8 grams) astragalus root

3 tablespoons (20 grams) goji berries

5 jumbo eggs*

Vinaigrette

4 tablespoons soy sauce

4½ tablespoons minced ginger

3 tablespoons minced scallions

3 tablespoons minced chives

1 tablespoon sesame oil

1. Make the custard. In a small pot, combine the water, American ginseng, astragalus root, and 1 tablespoon of the goji berries and bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat to medium and let it simmer, covered, for 5 minutes. Strain the herbal liquid into a bowl and discard the solids.

2. Prepare your steamer. (See here for steaming methods.)

3. In a medium bowl, whisk the eggs until well combined. Reserve 1 tablespoon of the herbal liquid and add the rest to the eggs. Mix well. Strain the egg mixture through a fine-mesh sieve. Make sure not to create too many bubbles during the process. This ensures a smoother texture.

4. Pour the egg mixture evenly into 3 small heatproof bowls. If you want to achieve a smooth look for the egg custard, cover each bowl with plastic wrap. Make sure the plastic wrap does not touch the custard. Steam for 10 minutes, until the center of the egg custard is set.

5. Make the vinaigrette. Meanwhile, mix together the soy sauce, ginger, scallions, chives, sesame oil, the rest of the goji berries, and the reserved tablespoon of herbal liquid in a small bowl and set aside.

6. Remove the eggs from the heat, discard the plastic wrap if used, and serve topped with the sauce.

title: Crispy Baked Purple Sweet Potato Fries with Herbal Spice
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
烤紫薯条

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach, Large Intestine

Functions: Warming, Aids Digestion

Crispy, sweet, and aromatic, these fries always disappear in seconds when I make them for my friends and family. Baking fries uses a lot less oil than frying and maintains a gentler energetic. Besides fiber and natural sugar, purple sweet potatoes contain an abundance of antioxidants. The spices used in this recipe add a pleasantly aromatic surprise to the sweetness of the potatoes, while helping regulate the Spleen and Stomach Qi for better digestion and Blood circulation.

YIELD: 2 to 3 servings

TIME: 45 minutes

Sweet Potato Fries

1 pound purple sweet potatoes, washed

2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil

2 tablespoons sesame oil

1 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste

½ teaspoon garlic powder, or to taste

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black peppercorn, or to tatste

½ teaspoon ground star anise

½ teaspoon (1 gram) ground nutmeg, plus more for garnish

½ teaspoon ground cinnamon, plus more for garnish

½ teaspoon (1 gram) aged tangerine peel powder*

Tofu Sour Cream

¾ block (12 ounces) silken tofu

1 tablespoon lemon juice

1 tablespoon apple cider vinegar

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast

½ teaspoon sea salt, or to taste

1. Preheat the oven to 425°F.

2. Make the sweet potato fries. Cut off the ends of the potatoes. I like to keep the skin on, but you can peel them if you prefer. Cut the potatoes into ¼- to ½-inch wedges. Place them on a large baking sheet.

3. In a small bowl, whisk the olive oil, sesame oil, sea salt, and all the spices until well combined. Pour the mixture over the potatoes and toss until they are well coated, then arrange them in a single layer. Bake for 15 minutes. Flip each fry, then bake for an additional 10 minutes, until the fries are crispy on the ends and starting to turn golden brown around the edges.

4. Meanwhile, make the tofu sour cream. Combine all the ingredients in a blender and blend on high speed until smooth. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

5. Remove the fries from the oven. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Then transfer the fries to a plate and drizzle the tofu sour cream on top. Garnish with additional nutmeg and cinnamon (about ⅛ teaspoon each). Serve immediately.

title: Hemp Seed and Tahini Salad
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
火麻仁芝麻色拉

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Warm, Dry

Energetics: Neutral, slightly Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Liver, Large Intestine

Functions: Yin Nourishing, Liver Health, Aids Digestion

I’ve never been a fan of kale because of its tough texture. I find that baby kale is much softer, easier to digest, and packed with even more nutrients. It pairs really well with other soft leaves like baby spinach; add creamy avocado to make a refreshing and well-balanced salad. The star of the salad, though, is the dressing. From ophiopogon root to tahini to hemp seeds, these Yin-nourishing ingredients can help hydrate our body and moisten the Large Intestine to help with constipation caused by Dryness. What’s more, the dark leafy vegetables can also help to cool Liver Fire that may cause red eyes, agitation, and vertigo. If you are concerned with eating raw foods due to weak digestion, you can blanch or sauté the veggies and then pair them with the dressing.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 30 minutes

Dressing

½ cup water

3 to 4 pieces (10 grams) ophiopogon root

2 tablespoons tahini, plus more as needed

3 tablespoons hulled hemp seeds

Juice of ½ lemon

1 large handful fresh basil

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast, or to taste

1 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste

Olive oil as needed

Salad*

½ ripe avocado

4 tablespoons hulled hemp seeds

2 cups baby spinach

2 cups baby kale

⅓ cup carrots, julienned

1. Make the dressing. In a small saucepan, bring the water to a boil over high heat. Add the ophiopogon root, reduce the heat to medium, and cook for 20 minutes. Discard the root and keep the hot liquid.

2. In a blender, combine the tahini, the warm ophiopogon root water, hemp seeds, lemon juice, basil, nutritional yeast, and sea salt and blend until smooth and creamy. Taste and adjust the seasoning. If the dressing is too thick, add more liquid or olive oil. If it’s too thin, add more tahini.

3. Assemble the salad. Cut the avocado into thick slices, place the slices in a bowl, and cover each slice with hulled hemp seeds. Set aside. In a large bowl, toss together the baby spinach, baby kale, and carrots. Drizzle some of the dressing onto the veggies, making sure to cover them with a thin layer. Use your hands to massage the dressing into the salad greens.

4. Plate the salad. In a salad bowl, brush additional dressing along the bottom and sides. Place the salad in the bowl and top with the hemp-crusted avocado. Serve.

title: Stir-Fried Pea Shoots with Ginger and Goji
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
姜味枸杞清炒豆苗

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral, slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Liver

Functions: Liver Health, Respiratory Health

This is an extremely simple yet delicious way to consume leafy greens. Pea shoots are so tender and pleasant to eat. Like other leafy greens, they wilt and shrink a lot when cooked, so don’t be afraid to add a lot of them to the pan to make sure you’ve got enough for your plate. You can use other greens as a substitution for pea shoots, such as Chinese broccoli, asparagus, or bok choy.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 10 minutes

2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil

2 tablespoons finely minced ginger

2 to 3 large handfuls pea shoots, rinsed

1 tablespoon (10 grams) goji berries

½ teaspoon fine sea salt, or to taste

1. In a deep pan or wok, heat the oil and ginger over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes until the ginger is fragrant. Add the pea shoots and stir-fry until the leaves wilt and turn dark green, about 5 minutes. Do not overcook them to avoid losing their heat-sensitive vitamins.

2. Add the goji berries and stir-fry for 15 more seconds. Season with the sea salt. Serve immediately.

title: Rainbow Stir-Fry with Ginkgo Nuts
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
白果小炒

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Respiratory Health

I often make vegetable stir-fries at home because they are so fast and easy, and ensure my daily vegetable intake. This rainbow stir-fry contains many different textures and layers of flavor. Even though it is very simple, I never get tired of eating it! It is a very flexible recipe, as you can use any vegetables you prefer to substitute for the bell peppers and celery. Fresh Chinese yam is highly recommended, as it works with the ginkgo nuts to stabilize the Kidney Essence, tonify the Lung Qi, and strengthen the Spleen.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 20 minutes

4 medium jujube dates (20 grams)

1 tablespoon extra virgin olive oil

2 teaspoons minced ginger

1 cup chopped bell peppers

1 cup sliced fresh shiitake mushrooms

1 cup chopped celery

1 cup chopped fresh Chinese yam (see here for tips on preparation)

10 ginkgo nuts*

Sea salt and freshly ground black peppercorn, to taste

1. Remove the pit of each jujube date. Discard the pits and cut the dates into slices.

2. In a medium pan, heat the oil over medium heat with the minced ginger. Once the oil is hot, add the bell peppers, shiitake, celery, Chinese yam, ginkgo nuts, and the sliced jujube dates. Stir-fry for about 5 minutes, until everything is cooked. You may add a splash of water to the pan to facilitate cooking. Season with sea salt and black pepper.

title: Chinese Chive Scrambled Eggs with Sichuan Peppercorn
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
花椒韭菜炒蛋

Dairy-free ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold

Energetics: Hot

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Warming, Aids Digestion

This is one of the few vegetarian dishes that my dad actually likes because it is so full of inviting aroma. Chinese chives have a unique and aromatic flavor that is quite different from scallions and Western chives. You can find them easily in Manhattan’s Chinatown and many other Asian markets across the United States. I love to make this in the mornings on winter days because it actually wakes me up with its pungent flavors and warms my Spleen and Stomach to get me prepared for the cold outside. The combo of Chinese chives and eggs was first mentioned in The Classic of Poetry (circa 1100–600 BCE). It always fascinates me that we are still cooking certain things the same way our ancestors did thousands of years ago.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 15 minutes

5 large eggs

1 teaspoon Shaoxing wine or sake (optional)

2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil

2 tablespoons sesame oil

2 teaspoons (10 grams) Sichuan peppercorns

2 cups chopped Chinese chives*

½ teaspoon sea salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black peppercorn

1. Crack the eggs into a large bowl and add the Shaoxing wine, if using. Beat for 30 seconds and set aside.

2. In a small nonstick pan, heat the olive oil, sesame oil, and Sichuan peppercorns over medium-high heat, until the oil just starts to bubble. Add the chives and sauté for 30 seconds, until they are slightly wilted. Pour in the beaten eggs and stir-fry, using a spatula to prevent the eggs from sticking to the pan. Once the eggs are cooked and have turned firm, about 3 minutes, season with the sea salt and black pepper. Serve immediately.

title: Four Gods Clarifying Yuba Soup
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
四神清体腐竹汤

Dairy-free ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Humid, Warm

Energetics: Neutral, slightly Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Aids Digestion, Calming

This is one of the most classic and recognizable soups in TCM food therapy. “Four gods” is pronounced si shen in Chinese, which is derived from si chen, meaning “four ministers.” In TCM herbology, herbs used in a formula are assigned one of four roles—monarch, minister, assistant, or envoy—to illustrate their function and purpose. The four herbs used in this soup—lotus seed, poria, fox nut or coix seed, and Chinese yam—often serve as “ministers” in a formula because they excel in supporting a stronger herb (the monarch). This soup is historically used to strengthen the Spleen, reduce Dampness, clarify the skin, and support our overall energy level. It is quite pleasant and mild, and is suitable for children and pregnant women as well.

Yuba, also called tofu skin, is the membrane that forms on the surface of boiled and cooled soy milk. Dried yuba is thin, brittle, yellow, and semitransparent. When rehydrated in cold water for a couple of minutes, it turns into a delicate, soft, off-white piece that can be used as a wrap or added to soups. When a flat yuba sheet is gathered together into a bundle before the drying process, it becomes what we are using in this recipe—thick yuba (fu zhu 腐竹). Fu zhu is sold as dried sticks about the length of a forearm. I love its slightly chewy but soft texture and unique look.

This dish is traditionally made with pork, but I’m offering a vegan alternative using fresh mushrooms.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 1.5 hours

1½ pounds pork ribs or 1 pound assorted fresh mushrooms

½ cup (50 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed

½ cup (80 grams) fox nuts

½ cup (90 grams) coix seeds

⅓ cup (50 grams) poria

8 pieces (60 grams) dried Chinese yam

12 pinky-length pieces dried thick yuba*

1 cup chopped fresh Chinese yam

1 teaspoon ground white pepper

Sea salt, to taste

1. If using pork ribs, bring a large pot of water to a boil over high heat. Blanch the pork ribs in the boiling water for 1 minute and drain. Set aside. If using fresh mushrooms, clean and cut them into chunks or slices. Set aside.

2. In a medium mixing bowl, combine the lotus seeds, fox nuts, coix seeds, poria, dried Chinese yam, and dried thick yuba, then add enough water to cover. Soak for 15 minutes. Strain, reserving the clean soaking water.

3. In a large soup pot or clay pot, combine the blanched pork rib or fresh mushrooms, soaked herbs with the soaking water, fresh Chinese yam, and water to cover. Bring everything to a boil over high heat. Skim the foam on the surface with a mesh skimmer. Lower the heat to medium-low and simmer, covered, for 1 hour. Season with the white pepper and sea salt. Serve warm.

title: Reishi Mushroom Miso Soup
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
灵芝味增汤

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Aids Digestion, Calming

Whether it’s made by a Michelin-star restaurant or your local takeout joint, miso soup is always so comforting for both our Heart and digestive system. This miso soup recipe incorporates many different kinds of mushrooms to add extra umami flavor and adaptogenic qualities. The addition of reishi, depending on the variety and form you use, may give this soup a slightly bitter aftertaste. If that bothers you, you can skip it and still make a healing bowl of miso soup.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 2 hours

10 dried or fresh black wood ear mushrooms

3 dried shiitake mushrooms

1 hand-size piece kombu

3 pieces (6 grams) reishi or 2 teaspoons reishi extract

3 teaspoons gluten-free soy sauce

2 teaspoons mirin

2 tablespoons sake

3 medium jujube dates (15 grams), pitted and halved

8 cups bone broth or vegetable stock

2 teaspoons sesame oil

1 teaspoon finely minced ginger

½ pound assorted fresh mushrooms, thinly sliced

3 tablespoons white or red miso paste

½ block (8 ounces) silken tofu, cubed

Sea salt, to taste

2 tablespoons chopped scallions, for garnish

1. Carefully wash the dried wood ear mushrooms and soak in warm water for 1 hour in a medium mixing bowl. Drain. The wood ear mushrooms expand significantly after soaking. If using fresh black wood ear mushrooms, you do not need to soak them.

2. In a large soup pot, add the soaked wood ear mushrooms, dried shiitake mushrooms, kombu, reishi, soy sauce, mirin, sake, jujube dates, and broth. Bring to a boil over medium heat. Reduce the heat to low and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes. Strain the base broth through a fine-mesh sieve into a large mixing bowl.

3. Cut the cooked kombu into strips and set aside. Reserve the jujube dates and discard the rest of the solids.

4. In the empty soup pot, heat the sesame oil over medium-high heat and cook the ginger until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the sliced fresh mushrooms and cook for 1 minute. Pour in the prepared base broth and bring to a boil. Ladle ½ cup of the broth into a small bowl and add the miso paste. Stir and let the miso paste completely dissolve in the broth. Pour the miso mixture back into the soup pot. Add the cubed silken tofu and cooked kombu. Simmer for another 5 minutes. Season with sea salt.

5. Ladle the soup into 6 bowls and serve warm, garnished with the chopped scallions.

title: The Ultimate TCM Silkie Chicken Bone Broth
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
补气血乌骨鸡汤

Dairy-free ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach, Liver, Kidney

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Warming, Yin Nourishing

In China, this soup is traditionally given to new moms or patients recovering from trauma. Usually sold in Chinese grocery stores or by online Chinese grocery delivery services, Silkie chickens may look a little daunting with their gray-black skin, but they are considered a fantastic medicinal ingredient in TCM food therapy that nourishes the Kidney, Blood, and Yin. When paired with tonifying herbs like jujube dates, goji berries, astragalus root, and angelica root, it makes the ultimate herbal bone broth for longevity and overall wellness. The meat of a Silkie chicken is edible but doesn’t have the best texture, so I usually only drink the broth. Make a big pot and freeze the broth, so you can have access to a nourishing bone broth at any time.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 4 hours

2 tablespoons dried black wood ear mushrooms

1 whole (2 to 3 pounds) Silkie chicken, cleaned*

¼ cup Shaoxing wine, sake, or soju (optional)

4 scallions, chopped (both green and white parts with root ends removed)

1 yellow onion, roughly chopped

8 thick slices fresh ginger

4 dried or fresh bay leaves

8 dried shiitake mushrooms

10 medium jujube dates (50 grams)

¼ cup (40 grams) goji berries

5 pieces (15 grams) sliced astragalus root

6 pieces (25 grams) sliced angelica root

Sea salt, to taste

1. Carefully wash the dried wood ear mushrooms and soak in warm water for 1 hour in a small bowl. Reserve the clean soaking water.

2. Meanwhile, in a large mixing bowl, rub the Silkie chicken with the Shaoxing wine, if using. Place the scallions inside the cavity of the chicken and set aside.

3. In the bottom of a large pot, place the chopped onion and ginger slices. Put the Silkie chicken on top of them. Add the bay leaves, dried shiitake mushrooms, and the soaked wood ear mushrooms, along with the soaking water. Add more water to cover the chicken and bring it to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat to medium-low and cook, covered, for 2.5 hours.

4. Skim the foam off the surface with a mesh skimmer. Add the jujube dates, goji berries, astragalus root, and angelica root into the soup pot and stir to make sure they are submerged. Cook for an additional 30 minutes.

5. Season with sea salt and serve warm. I recommend straining the solids and only drinking the bone broth.

title: Tonifying Beef Bone Broth
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
牛骨汤

Gluten-free ◦ Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Dry

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach, Liver, Kidney

Functions: Warming, Tonifies Qi and Blood

Rich and comforting, this bone broth will bring you back to life on a freezing winter day. It has all the goodness of a traditional bone broth but is strengthened with an array of tonifying herbs. Several aromatic spices and powerful roots are used to promote the flow of Qi and warm our body from within. Blood-tonifying herbs are also included to facilitate these Qi-tonifying herbs. I recommend having this broth in colder weather or when you are feeling chills or other Yang Deficiency symptoms (see here).

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 4.5 hours

8 to 10 dried or fresh black wood ear mushrooms

3 pounds beef bones*

2 cups peeled, seeded, and chopped pumpkin or butternut squash

1 cup chopped carrot

1 cup chopped celery

1 medium yellow onion, chopped

5 thick slices fresh ginger

2 sprigs fresh rosemary

1 small bunch fresh thyme

1 hand-size piece kombu

8 dried shiitake mushrooms

2 whole red cardamom pods (5 grams)

6 whole star anise

1 tablespoon whole black peppercorns

Pinch of saffron

5 pieces (50 grams) dried Chinese yam

2 tablespoons (20 grams) goji berries

8 dried longan fruit (25 grams)

6 medium jujube dates (30 grams)

5 pieces (20 grams) sliced astragalus root

Sea salt, to taste

1. Carefully wash the dried wood ear mushrooms and soak in a medium bowl with enough warm water to cover for at least 1 hour. They should expand significantly. Skip this step if using fresh wood ear mushrooms.

2. Bring a large pot of water to a boil over high heat. Blanch the beef bones in the boiling water for 2 to 3 minutes. Strain and set aside.

3. In a large soup pot, add the blanched beef bones, pumpkin, carrot, celery, onion, ginger, rosemary, thyme, kombu, dried shiitake mushrooms, red cardamom, star anise, whole black peppercorns, and soaked wood ear mushrooms. Add enough water to cover everything. Bring to a boil and then simmer on medium-low heat, covered, for 3 to 4 hours.

4. Add the saffron, Chinese yam, goji berries, longan fruit, jujube dates, and astragalus root. Return to a boil and cook for another 30 minutes.

5. Season with sea salt right before serving. All the herbs used in this recipe are edible. No straining required.

title: Yin-Nourishing Pork Bone Broth
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
西洋参玉竹滋阴降火猪骨汤

Dairy-free ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Warm, Dry

Energetics: Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Yin Nourishing, Cooling, Calming

Pork bone broth is difficult to come by in the United States unless you are having a bowl of tonkotsu ramen. In China, when bone broth is mentioned, it implies that it is pork-bone based. Pork bone has a Neutral to Cooling energetic, and thus is suitable to nourish Yin and cool excessive Heat in our body. Beef and chicken bone broth are great too, but they don’t have the same Cooling quality as pork bone broth. To pair with pork bones, I chose a blend of Yin-nourishing, Cooling herbs that are functional for the respiratory, digestive, and reproductive organs. Without the common aromatics you often see in a bone broth, this clear, light soup is perfect to help you calm down and unwind.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 3.5 hours

2 pounds pork ribs or pork leg bones

½ cup (35 grams) dried or fresh lily bulb

½ cup (20 grams) Solomon’s seal

⅓ cup (25 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed

⅓ cup (25 grams) glehnia root

⅓ cup (25 grams) ophiopogon root

2 tablespoons (8 grams) sliced American ginseng

2 tablespoons (20 grams) goji berries

1 hand-size piece kombu

1 medium carrot, peeled and chopped

1 medium parsnip, peeled and chopped

2 celery ribs, chopped

Sea salt, to taste

Chopped fresh chives, for garnish

1. Bring a large pot of water to a boil over high heat and blanch the pork ribs for about 5 minutes. Drain and set aside.

2. Rinse and drain the lily bulb, Solomon’s seal, lotus seeds, glehnia root, ophiopogon root, American ginseng, and goji berries. Add enough clean water to cover and set aside to soak for 30 minutes.

3. In a large soup pot, combine the blanched pork bones, kombu, carrot, parsnip, celery, and water to cover. Bring everything to a boil over high heat, then reduce the heat to medium-low to simmer the broth, covered, for 2 hours. Skim the foam off the surface with a mesh skimmer. Add the soaked ingredients to a filter or cheesecloth bag, tie, add to the pot, and cook for 1 hour.

4. Fish out the bag of herbs and discard. Season the broth with sea salt and serve warm, garnished with the fresh chives.

title: Chestnut and Mushroom Cream Soup
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
滋阴补肾栗子浓汤

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Yin Nourishing, Tonifies Qi and Blood, Aids Digestion

Chestnuts tonify Qi, circulate Blood, and restore Kidney Essence. Roasted chestnuts are a popular street snack in China during the winter—I love watching the chestnuts roast in front of me and then holding a brown kraft bag of freshly roasted, warm chestnuts in my hands. This recipe was adapted from a traditional British chestnut soup, which is buttery, velvety, and nutty. The addition of lotus seeds, fox nuts, goji berries, shiitake mushrooms, reishi, and sesame makes this soup an excellent tonic for the Kidney. Drinking this silky-smooth soup in the winter can help warm and replenish the Kidney and improve immunity.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 45 minutes

1 cup (100 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed

⅓ cup (50 grams) fox nuts

2 tablespoons (20 grams) goji berries

6 to 8 cups vegetable stock

1 tablespoon extra virgin olive oil

2 shallots, diced

1 large leek, chopped

1 cup fresh shiitake mushrooms, sliced

1 celery rib, diced

1 pound ready-to-eat chestnuts, plus more as needed

2 teaspoons reishi powder or 4 drops reishi tincture

2 tablespoons tahini

¼ teaspoon ground clove

½ block (8 ounces) silken tofu

Sea salt and freshly ground black peppercorn, to taste

Toasted sesame oil and black sesame seeds, for garnish

Seared shiitake mushrooms, for garnish

1. The night before making this dish, rinse and soak the lotus seeds, fox nuts, and goji berries in 6 cups of vegetable stock for at least 3 hours, preferably overnight. If you don’t have time, you can boil the herbs instead, for about 30 minutes, until they are soft.

2. In a medium pan, heat the olive oil over medium-high heat. Cook the shallots, leek, shiitake mushrooms, celery, and chestnuts for about 5 minutes.

3. In a large soup pot, add the cooked vegetables, reishi, tahini, ground clove, silken tofu, and the soaked herbs and their soaking stock. Bring everything to a boil over high heat and then simmer, covered, for 30 minutes.

4. In a blender, carefully add the soup and puree to a smooth consistency. If it’s too thick, you can add more vegetable stock. If it is too thin, you can add more chestnuts. Season with sea salt and black pepper and blend again for a couple of seconds to evenly distribute the seasonings.

5. Garnish with sesame oil, black sesame seeds, and seared shiitake mushrooms. Serve warm.

title: Clam and Winter Melon Soup
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
蛤蜊冬瓜汤

Gluten-free ◦ Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Humid

Energetics: Neutral, slightly Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Kidney, Bladder

Functions: Cooling, Aids Digestion

A classic TCM food therapy recipe, this umami-filled soup is everything you need on a day when you feel bloated, swollen, and “stuck.” Clams are Heat-clearing and Phlegm-removing. They pair exceptionally well with the softness of winter melon, the chewiness of coix seeds, and the juiciness of corn. Most ingredients used in this recipe can help you to reduce Dampness and Phlegm, while promoting urination to get that excessive water out of your body efficiently. Some of the items, such as winter melon, corn silk, and dried scallops, may not be the easiest to find, but it is best not to use any substitutions here because each ingredient serves a distinct function and complements the others very well. If you live near a Chinese community, where most of these ingredients can easily be found, it’s worth the effort to make a shopping trip there!

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 1 hour

1 pound fresh clams

2 thick slices fresh ginger

1 tablespoon rice cooking wine

1 pound winter melon, peeled and seeds removed, cut into chunks*

2 ears of corn, cut into disks

2 tablespoons (30 grams) coix seeds, soaked in water for 1 hour

1 tablespoon dried scallops, soaked in water overnight

½ cup fresh or dried corn silk

Sea salt, to taste

2 tablespoons chopped scallions, for garnish

1. Clean the clams thoroughly by rinsing them under running water and scrubbing them with a brush. In a large pot, combine the ginger slices, cooking wine, winter melon, corn disks, coix seeds, dried scallops, corn silk, and water to cover. Bring to a boil over high heat, then lower the heat to medium-low and continue to cook for 30 minutes.

2. Add the clams and bring to a boil again over high heat. Continue boiling for 10 minutes, covered. All the clams should be open (if not, discard them) and the coix seeds should be soft. Season with sea salt and garnish with the scallions. Serve warm.

title: Warming Lamb Noodle Soup
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
暖体当归羊肉汤面

Dairy-free ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Liver, Kidney

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Warming

This comforting and aromatic recipe is originally an herbal prescription mentioned in many Traditional Chinese Medicine books, as far back as the Qing Dynasty (1636–1912 CE) and Han Dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE). It was used to treat bloating due to Cold invading the digestive system, Yang Deficiency, and postpartum abdominal pain and discharge. Nowadays in China, this food therapy prescription is a classic dish, especially for families living in Northern and Northwestern China, where the climate is cold and red meat is a dominant part of the regional diet. In this version, I incorporated more spices and vegetables for a stronger flavor. It’s better to consume this soup in cold weather rather than on a hot and humid day. If you have a strong Damp Heat constitution, do not have this noodle soup frequently.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 4 hours

Broth

3½ pounds lamb bones with meat (such as ribs, neck, and spine), cut into chunks

5 thick slices fresh ginger, skin removed

½ cup roughly chopped scallions

1 medium carrot, roughly chopped

1 large yellow onion, roughly chopped

2 tablespoons rice cooking wine

3 dried or fresh bay leaves

3 whole star anise

1 tablespoon fennel seed

1 tablespoon whole black peppercorns or ½ teaspoon freshly ground black peppercorn

2 slices (25 grams) angelica root

4 slices (15 grams) astragalus root

Sea salt, to taste

For Serving

6 ounces noodle of choice*

Cooked vegetables of choice

Fresh sliced scallions or cilantro (optional)

Sesame oil (optional)

Chili sauce (optional)

1. Make the broth. Bring a large pot of water to a boil over high heat. Blanch the lamb for 2 to 3 minutes. Strain and discard the water and foam.

2. In a large soup pot, combine the blanched lamb, ginger, scallions, carrot, onion, cooking wine, bay leaves, star anise, fennel seeds, and black peppercorns. Add enough water to cover. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, covered, for at least 3 hours.

3. In the last 30 minutes of cooking, add the angelica root and astragalus root. Once done cooking, strain out all the solids, reserving the broth and meat. Season with sea salt.

4. Serve the soup. Prepare the noodles according to the instructions on the package.

5. Divide the cooked noodles among 4 bowls. Pour the broth over the noodles and add the lamb and any preferred toppings.

title: Steamed Thirteen-Spice Vegetable Dumplings
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
十三香素饺

Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Humid

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Warming, Tonifies Qi and Blood

Folding dumplings with my family during Lunar New Year (and frankly any major holiday) is among the best memories of my childhood. I would wake up to the rhythmic sound of my grandma’s cleaver hitting the chopping board, mincing every filling ingredient by hand. The food processor has no place in her kitchen! I would watch her mix the meat, vegetables, and seasonings together. In different seasons, she would use different ingredients. This recipe is for the cold-weather months, filled with Warming ingredients for the Lung, Spleen, and Kidney.

The star ingredient here is the thirteen-spice powder, a proprietary blend of herbs that is believed to have originated in the Song Dynasty (960–1279 CE). It can be purchased at any Asian grocery store or online. It includes aged tangerine peel, cinnamon, cumin, ginger, angelica root, Sichuan peppercorn, star anise, nutmeg, galangal, white pepper, cloves, Chinese licorice, and cardamom. The blend adds plenty of medicinal value, as well as an aromatic, peppery flavor to these dumplings. Make some with your family and friends for your next dinner party! Besides steaming, you can also pan-fry or boil them.

YIELD: 20 to 30 dumplings

TIME: 40 minutes

Filling

8 ounces ground beef or lamb*

1 large egg, beaten

1 cup chopped Chinese chives or scallions

1 tablespoon minced ginger

½ cup finely chopped yellow onion

¾ cup chopped mixed fresh mushrooms

2 tablespoons soy sauce, or to taste

1 teaspoon fine sea salt, or to taste

1 tablespoon thirteen-spice powder, or to taste

1 teaspoon freshly ground black peppercorn, or to taste

Splash of rice cooking wine

2 tablespoons sesame oil

Assembly

1 pack (usually around 50 pieces) round white dumpling skins*

Dipping Sauce

¼ cup soy sauce

1 tablespoon maple syrup

1 tablespoon warm broth of choice

1 tablespoon hot sauce or chili sauce

1 tablespoon sesame oil

1 tablespoon minced cilantro

1 tablespoon minced scallions

1. Make the filling. In a large mixing bowl, combine all the filling ingredients, stirring in one direction only for better texture. Cook a little bit of it in a pan so you can taste and adjust the seasoning.

2. Prepare your steamer. (See here for steaming methods.)
