3. Assemble the dumplings. Fill a small side dish with water to use as the dumpling “glue.” Make the dumplings using whichever folding method you prefer. I like to first dip one finger in the water and moisten the edge of the dumpling skin. Then place about 2 tablespoons of the filling in the center. If your dumpling skin is small, reduce the amount of filling to 1 tablespoon. Use three fingers to close the edges tightly to form a triangular-shaped dumpling with three points. Place each shaped dumpling in your steamer basket and cover with a damp towel. They should be placed in one layer with some space in between each to prevent sticking.

4. Steam the dumplings for about 10 minutes, until the skin and center are both completely cooked.

5. Make the dipping sauce. In a small bowl, whisk all the dipping sauce ingredients together. Dip the cooked dumplings in the sauce to enjoy.

title: Lotus Leaf Steamed Sticky Rice with Chicken and Ginkgo Nuts
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
荷叶杂粮糯米鸡

Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Aids Digestion, Calming

This is my rendition of a traditional Chinese dim sum dish: chicken sticky rice wrapped in lotus leaf, or zhen zhu nuo mi ji (珍珠糯米鸡). It is usually made with white sticky rice, Chinese sausages, shredded chicken, and dried shiitake mushrooms, wrapped in a small piece of lotus leaf. You can find these smartphone-size lotus leaf wraps in Chinatown bakeries, on dim sum carts, and in the freezer section of a Chinese grocery store. For this recipe, I used an entire lotus leaf for a family-size dish and added herbs and whole grains to make it more medicinal. When you unwrap the lotus leaf, its subtle fragrance is inviting and refreshing. The mixture of herbs—lotus seeds, coix seeds, adzuki beans, fox nuts, and ginkgo nuts—and three different kinds of sticky grains help eliminate Dampness from the Lung, Spleen, and Kidney. The rice mixture inside has a sticky, chewy texture that is truly addicting and it carries over the fresh fragrance of the lotus leaf. It is definitely a dish to impress your guests with at the dinner table! Remember to start soaking the grains and herbs the night before.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 13 hours

Rice and Chicken

⅓ cup (35 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed

⅓ cup (75 grams) coix seeds

2 tablespoons adzuki beans

2 tablespoons (30 grams) fox nuts

1 cup glutinous millet*

1 cup white sticky rice

½ cup purple sticky rice

1 piece whole dried lotus leaf

8 frozen ginkgo nuts

½ pound chicken thighs

Marinade

2 tablespoons soy sauce

2 tablespoons sesame oil

1 tablespoon minced ginger

2 tablespoons minced scallions

1 tablespoon rice cooking wine

⅓ cup finely chopped carrot

⅓ cup finely chopped fresh mushrooms

1. Prepare the rice and chicken. The night before serving this dish, rinse the lotus seeds, coix seeds, adzuki beans, fox nuts, glutinous millet, white sticky rice, and purple sticky rice. Place them together in a large bowl with enough water to cover, and soak overnight. In another large, shallow bowl or tray, cover the lotus leaf with water, and soak overnight to soften.

2. Thaw the ginkgo nuts. You don’t need to soak them.

3. With a knife, score the chicken thighs, then set aside.

4. Make the marinade. In a small bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, sesame oil, minced ginger, minced scallions, and cooking wine. Pour the marinade over the scored chicken thighs and let the chicken marinate in the refrigerator overnight in a covered container.

5. The next day, prepare your steamer. (See here for steaming methods.)

6. Unfold and lay the soaked lotus leaf flat in your steamer basket. Drain the soaking herb and rice mixture. Mix in the carrot and mushrooms. Place half of the mixture on the lotus leaf. Remove the chicken from its marinade. Add the marinated chicken on top. Cover the chicken with the rest of the herb and rice mixture. Drizzle the marinade on top. Fold in the sides of the lotus leaf to cover all the ingredients. Steam for 40 minutes over high heat, until all the grains are soft.

7. Serve warm. The lotus leaf is not edible.

title: Shiso Rice Rolls with Shiso Pesto
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
紫苏生姜饭卷

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen

Functions: Respiratory Health, Aids Digestion

When I was a child, I felt nauseous frequently and always had stomach issues (until I figured out that dairy was the culprit). Whenever nausea hit, my grandma would give me a cup of warm ginger tea, a piece of fresh shiso, and a little cooked rice. This tremendously alleviated the suffering. After I came to the United States, I grew to love pesto. It is such a great way to consume fresh green herbs like basil, parsley, and shiso! So, I created this fusion recipe to make shiso into a pesto that can be paired with rice, pasta, bread, and more!

Although these rolls are delicious anytime, you may find them comforting if you’re experiencing nausea or an upset stomach. They are also great for pregnant people who experience morning sickness.

YIELD: 12 rolls

TIME: 1.5 hours

Shiso Pesto

30 fresh shiso leaves

3 tablespoons pine nuts

2 tablespoons minced ginger

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast

½ teaspoon sea salt

⅛ teaspoon ground amomum fruit

¼ cup extra virgin olive oil

Rice Rolls

2½ cups water

1 cup short-grain brown rice

¼ cup short-grain white rice

1 teaspoon sea salt

2 teaspoons clear rice wine vinegar

3 sheets roasted nori seaweed, cut into 12 shiso-leaf-size pieces

12 fresh shiso leaves

Assorted steamed vegetables, cut into thin strips (optional)

2 tablespoons toasted sesame seeds

1. Make the shiso pesto. Add all the pesto ingredients to a food processor and blend until a pesto consistency is reached, about 30 seconds. Set aside.

2. Make the rice rolls. Rinse the brown and white rice and drain. In a medium pot, combine the water, brown rice, white rice, and salt. Cover with a lid, set over high heat, and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat to low and simmer until the water is absorbed and the rice is very tender, about 40 minutes. Remove from the heat and set aside with the lid still on, about 10 minutes. (You can also use a rice cooker to make the rice.) Stir in the vinegar, then spread the rice on a large baking sheet until just cool enough to handle, about 5 minutes.

3. On a flat surface, like a clean chopping board, place a piece of nori seaweed on top of a piece of fresh shiso leaf. Add about ½ cup of the cooked rice in the center with some assorted steamed vegetables, if using; a sprinkle of the sesame seeds; and some of the shiso pesto. Roll up and repeat with the remaining ingredients. Serve with additional pesto on top.

title: Spiced Lily Bulb and Apricot Kernel Pho
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
百合南杏越南粉

Dairy-free ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Dry

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung

Functions: Respiratory Health

Whenever I have Vietnamese pho, it feels like I am getting a big and warm hug from the person who cooked it. The key to a Heart-Warming bowl of pho is the bone broth. A variety of aromatics, bones, and meat is used to create the broth. The spices help regulate and move Qi, while the marrow bones and tendons contribute collagen and a wide range of nutrients to improve our skin and overall health. For this recipe, I also added a blend of Chinese herbs that benefit the Lung to alleviate Dryness, Phlegm, and coughing. Lily bulb, aged tangerine peel, and apricot kernels contribute a mild, fruity flavor to the broth, while cloves, ginger, star anise, coriander seeds, and cinnamon add an incredible layer of aroma. I like to make a big batch of the broth and freeze it so I can have quick access to a bowl of homemade pho at any time.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 4 hours

2 large white onions, halved

6 thick slices fresh ginger

10 whole star anise

3 whole cloves

1½ tablespoons coriander seeds

1 cinnamon stick

3 pounds beef brisket

2 pounds meaty beef bones

2 pounds marrow bones (such as knuckle), cut to reveal the marrow

1 hand-size piece kombu

1 cup shimeji mushrooms or another fresh mushroom of choice, such as enoki or shiitake

4 quarts water

1 tablespoon light brown sugar

1 tablespoon sea salt, or to taste

3 tablespoons (30 grams) apricot kernels

1 cup (75 grams) lily bulb

½ cup (25 grams) aged tangerine peel

10 ounces dried rice noodles

1 bunch fresh Thai basil, regular basil, or mint, for garnish

1 lime, cut into 6 wedges, for garnish

Blanched Chinese broccoli or vegetable of choice, for garnish

1. In a small skillet over medium-high heat, dry-toast the onions, ginger, star anise, cloves, coriander seeds, and cinnamon for about 3 minutes, or until the onions are translucent and the spices turn fragrant.

2. Bring a large pot of water to a boil over high heat and then blanch the beef brisket and bones for 5 minutes. Drain the liquid and set the meat and bones aside.

3. In a large stockpot, combine the toasted aromatics, blanched meat and bones, kombu, shimeji mushrooms, water, brown sugar, and sea salt. The water should just cover everything. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, covered, for 3 hours. Remove the brisket, slice, and set aside.

4. Add the apricot kernels, lily bulb, and aged tangerine peel. Simmer, uncovered, for an additional 40 minutes.

5. Strain the broth and discard the solids, if desired. You can eat the apricot kernels and lily bulb. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

6. Just prior to serving, prepare the rice noodles according to the instructions on the package.

7. In each serving bowl, place about 2 cups of the cooked noodles. Add some of the brisket and ladle over about 2 cups of hot broth. Garnish each bowl with Thai basil, a lime wedge, and blanched Chinese broccoli.

title: Longan Chicken Stew with Red Koji Fermented Tofu
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
龙眼南乳炖鸡

Gluten-free ◦ Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Spleen

Functions: Calming, Tonifies Qi and Blood, Aids Digestion

This dish has a unique glistening red color from red koji fermented tofu (hong fu ru 红腐乳), a nutrient-packed condiment that you can find in many Chinese grocery stores. Sold in jars, it is made by fermenting tofu cubes with salt, red rice yeast, and gut-friendly bacteria. The stew is savory, saucy, and subtly fruity because of the longan fruit. Traditionally, this sauce is used to cook pork, especially pig trotters and pork belly, but I find it suitable for chicken as well. The fermented tofu, packed with probiotics to benefit our gut microbiome, tenderizes the chicken and makes it easier to digest. Longan fruit, reishi, and lotus seeds work together to calm the mind, making this a perfect dish to cook for postpartum moms, those who could use some calming energy, or to treat yourself after a hectic week. Don’t forget to mix the extra meat sauce with rice to get all the goodness from this recipe!

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 35 minutes

2 cubes red koji fermented tofu, along with 2 tablespoons of its juice

2 cups chicken broth

2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon minced ginger

2 pounds bone-in chicken legs (drumsticks and thighs)

2 cups roughly chopped fresh Chinese yam*

4 drops reishi extract

⅓ cup (30 grams) dried longan fruit

½ cup (50 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed

Sea salt and freshly ground black peppercorn, to taste

1 tablespoon finely chopped scallions, for garnish

1. In a blender, combine the red koji fermented tofu cubes and the juice with the chicken broth and blend on high speed until smooth. Set aside.

2. In a large, deep pan over medium-high heat, heat the olive oil and ginger until fragrant. Add the chicken, skin side down, and sear for about 4 minutes until the skin is slightly browned and the fat has released. Add the fresh Chinese yam, reishi extract, longan fruit, and lotus seeds. Add the reserved fermented tofu sauce and bring everything to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered, for 20 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce is reduced by 2 cups. Taste and season with sea salt and black pepper.

3. Ladle into bowls and serve warm, topped with the chopped scallions.

title: Steamed Whole Fish with Herbal Soy Sauce
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
药膳酱油清蒸鱼

Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Liver

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood

Steamed fish is one of the easiest and healthiest things you can make. In my family, we always steam whole fish or make fish soup with a giant fish head. Eating the meat off the bones brings me so much joy. Most Chinese households have this dish on their dinner table often. With this recipe, I added a special herbal soy sauce component that I came up with to bring more medicinal benefits to the dish.

Make sure to choose fresh, high-quality fish, which will make a big difference in terms of the taste and texture.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 30 minutes

Herbal Soy Sauce

1 to 2 cups stock or broth of choice

2 pieces (10 grams) angelica root

3 pieces (10 grams) astragalus root

3 thick slices fresh ginger

1 hand-size piece kombu

2 dried shiitake mushrooms

¼ cup soy sauce

2 tablespoons (15 grams) goji berries

Steamed Fish

1 whole (1½ to 2 pounds), cleaned and gutted fish of choice, such as sea bass, trout, or red snapper

2 scallions, roots discarded and roughly chopped, plus more for garnish

1 tablespoon minced ginger

1 bunch fresh thyme

1 tablespoon sesame oil

1. Make the herbal soy sauce. In a small pot, combine the stock, angelica root, astragalus root, ginger, kombu, and mushrooms. Make sure there’s enough stock to cover all the ingredients. Bring to a boil over high heat, and then reduce the heat to low and simmer until the liquid has reduced to about half, 15 to 20 minutes. Strain the solids and reserve the liquid. Stir in the soy sauce and goji berries and mix until well combined. Set aside.

2. Prepare your steamer. (See here for steaming methods.)

3. Make the steamed fish. Rinse the surface and cavity of the fish and pat dry with a paper towel. Place the fish on a heatproof plate and stuff the belly with the scallions, ginger, and thyme. Drizzle the sesame oil on the surface of the fish.

4. Steam the fish for 7 to 9 minutes, depending on the size of the fish, or until the center is completely cooked. The flesh should look opaque and white rather than transparent.

5. Remove the fish to a serving platter and drizzle with the herbal soy sauce, including the goji berries. Garnish with chopped scallions. Serve immediately.

title: Shanghainese Sweet and Sour Pork Rib with Hawthorn Berries
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
山楂红枣排骨

Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Aids Digestion

Every Shanghainese grew up eating sweet and sour pork ribs (tang cu pai gu 糖醋排骨). The dish has the perfect combination of bold flavors and textures—savory, sweet, tart, sticky, and saucy—which truly represent Shanghainese cuisine. Whenever I eat these ribs at Chinese restaurants, it brings up so much nostalgia that I had to include this recipe in my book. I modified the original ingredients to use less oil and added TCM herbs like hawthorn, jujube, and goji. Hawthorn berries contribute a lovely tart flavor in addition to the aged vinegar. Since this is a heavier and very addictive dish, hawthorn berries can help with indigestion and balancing blood cholesterol. Besides the medical benefits, I love the pops of red that these herbs contribute, making the dish eye-catching as well as delicious.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 45 minutes

3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon minced ginger

2 whole star anise

1 whole red cardamom pod (3 grams)

2 pounds pork ribs, chopped into small chunks

2 cups vegetable stock

2 tablespoons Shaoxing wine, sake, or soju

2 tablespoons honey, or to taste

1 tablespoon soy sauce, or to taste

1 tablespoon Chinese aged black rice vinegar, or to taste

1 tablespoon (10 grams) goji berries

2 teaspoons dark soy sauce

8 whole dried hawthorn berries (40 grams)*

6 medium jujube dates (30 grams)

1 tablespoon finely chopped scallions, for garnish

1. In a large, deep skillet, heat the olive oil, ginger, star anise, and red cardamom over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Stir the spices to prevent burning. Add the ribs and sear until they are slightly brown on all sides, about 2 minutes for each side.

2. In the same deep skillet, add the rest of the ingredients except for the scallions. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Reduce the heat to low, and simmer, covered, for about 30 minutes. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking. After 30 minutes, uncover, turn up the heat to high, and reduce the liquid until the sauce has thickened and the ribs are coated and sticky, 5 to 10 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed.

3. Top with the chopped scallions and serve warm.

title: Basic Multigrain Porridge
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
杂粮粥

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Aids Digestion

If you want to memorize just one recipe from this book, this is it. Knowing how to cook a perfect bowl of multigrain porridge is a foundation of TCM food therapy. It is easy to digest, filling, versatile, and so good for the Spleen and Stomach. Anyone can benefit from this recipe, no matter if you are a bodybuilder, an elementary school kid, or a retired older person. Feel free to add your own spin to this basic recipe by changing the varieties of grains and the condiments used. In place of water, you can use nut milk, bone broth, or vegetable stock for additional flavor and nutrients. Make this porridge your own and have a small bowl daily for breakfast to help build up strong digestion.

YIELD: 8 servings

TIME: 13.5 hours

½ cup foxtail millet

⅓ cup black rice

¼ cup (60 grams) coix seeds

½ cup glutinous rice

⅓ cup brown rice

⅓ cup rolled oats

¼ cup quinoa

¼ cup adzuki beans

10 cups water (see headnote)

1. In a large bowl, mix the millet, black rice, coix seeds, glutinous rice, brown rice, oats, and quinoa together. Thoroughly wash and drain them under running water until the water runs clear, then add enough water to cover and soak them overnight.

2. The next day, drain the soaked grains and add them to a large pot with the water. Bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, partially covered, about 1.5 hours, until it reaches a porridge consistency. Stir occasionally during the cooking process to prevent the grains from sticking to the bottom of the pot. Add more liquid if the porridge is too thick or still not cooked; cook for longer or add more oats if the porridge is too thin.

3. Serve as the main starch of your meal, with soft-boiled eggs, pickles, kimchi, baked chicken, or anything else you prefer. You can even serve it with honey or fruit compote to make a sweet dish. Store leftovers in your fridge in an airtight container for up to 7 days or freeze for up to 6 months.

title: Spiced Pumpkin Multigrain Porridge with Tahini
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
麻酱香料南瓜杂粮粥

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Heart, Spleen

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Warming, Aids Digestion

This porridge is so creamy that it may remind you of a pumpkin risotto made with cream and butter. With ten different kinds of aromatic spices added, this recipe can warm your body and stimulate digestion. At the same time, it is not going to cause Yin Deficiency or excess Heat because it is cooked with Neutral or Cooling ingredients and a water-based cooking method. I love to pair it with some green leafy vegetables and good-quality protein, such as roasted sea bass or a soft-boiled egg. Remember to soak your brown rice overnight for this recipe!

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 13 hours

Porridge

½ cup brown rice

½ cup gluten-free rolled oats, plus more as needed

⅓ cup millet, rinsed

1 cup pumpkin puree

1 tablespoon minced ginger

6½ cups plant-based milk, plus more as needed*

4 tablespoons tahini

4 tablespoons nutritional yeast

Pinch of saffron

⅓ teaspoon freshly ground black peppercorn

½ teaspoon ground turmeric

¼ teaspoon ground amomum fruit

¼ teaspoon (0.5 gram) ground nutmeg

¼ teaspoon five-spice powder

Sea salt, to taste

1 large handful spinach

Topping

4 tablespoons tahini

1 to 2 tablespoons warm water

1 teaspoon gluten-free soy sauce

1 tablespoon honey, or to taste

4 tablespoons pumpkin seeds or mixed nuts, for serving

1. Rinse the brown rice, place in a medium bowl with enough water to cover, and soak overnight.

2. Make the porridge. Drain the soaked brown rice. In a large pot, add the brown rice, oats, millet, pumpkin puree, minced ginger, plant-based milk, tahini, nutritional yeast, saffron, black pepper, turmeric, amomum fruit, nutmeg, and five-spice powder. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered, for 45 minutes, until it reaches a porridge consistency. Keep stirring to prevent the grains from sticking to the bottom of the pot. Add more liquid if the porridge is too thick or still not cooked; cook for longer or add more oats if the porridge is too thin. Season with sea salt. Right before serving, add in the spinach and cook for 1 more minute until the spinach wilts.

3. Make the topping. In a small bowl, whisk the tahini with the warm water, soy sauce, and honey to combine.

4. Divide the porridge into 4 bowls and top with the tahini mixture and the pumpkin seeds. Serve warm. Store extra porridge in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to a week or in a freezer-safe container in the freezer for up to 3 months.

title: Sour Jujube Seed Mushroom Porridge
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
助眠酸枣仁蘑菇粥

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Calming, Yin Nourishing

This recipe is inspired by one of the most famous formulas in TCM herbology: suan zao ren tang 酸枣仁汤 (sour jujube seed decoction), developed by Chinese pharmacologist and physician Zhang Zhongjing of the Eastern Han Dynasty (25–220 CE). Modern randomized control trials have supported the effectiveness of suan zao ren tang for insomnia. I modified the formula for this recipe to enhance the taste while respecting the intended functionalities of treating insomnia caused by a hectic work schedule, Heart Blood Deficiency, and irritability caused by Yin Deficiency. Cooking this classic formula for a creamy bowl of porridge is a sustainable and delicious way to give you a restful night of sleep. Eat a serving every day in the afternoon or evening for at least two weeks for the best results.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 13 hours

⅔ cup short-grain white rice

⅓ cup foxtail millet

2 dried shiitake mushrooms

½ cup (60 grams) crushed sour jujube seeds

¼ cup (25 grams) longan fruit

3 medium jujube dates (15 grams)

½ cup (25 grams) Chinese licorice root

¼ cup (40 grams) poria

1 teaspoon saffron

6 cups unsweetened soy milk, plus more as needed*

½ cup diced carrots

½ cup diced celery

½ cup diced fresh mushrooms

3 tablespoons almond butter or cashew butter

2 tablespoons nutritional yeast

Gluten-free soy sauce, to taste

1. The night before serving this dish, rinse the rice and millet under cold running water. Drain and put in an airtight bag or container. Freeze overnight. This step shortens the cooking time significantly. (You can skip this step, but you will need to cook the rice and millet in step 3 for at least 1 hour rather than 15 minutes.)

2. The next day, in a large pot, add the dried mushrooms, crushed sour jujube seeds, longan fruit, jujube dates, Chinese licorice root, poria, saffron, and soy milk. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to low and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes. Strain and discard the solids and return the liquid to the pot.

3. Add the rice and millet, carrots, celery, and mushrooms. Bring to a boil again; reduce the heat to low; and simmer, covered, for 15 minutes. Stir midway to prevent the grains from sticking to the bottom of the pot. You may need to add extra liquid if your porridge is too thick. The porridge is done when the grains are very soft.

4. Add the nut butter, nutritional yeast, and soy sauce. Stir to make sure everything is well incorporated. Serve warm with cooked leafy greens, such as Chinese broccoli.

title: Brown Rice Chicken Porridge with Toasted Radish Seeds
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
助消化莱菔子糙米鸡粥

Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Aids Digestion, Respiratory Health

Radish seed porridge is another classic food therapy recipe mentioned in many ancient Chinese medical texts. Cheng You, a famous TCM physician of the Qing Dynasty (1636–1912 CE), wrote in his health and wellness book Shou Shi Qing Bian that radish seeds should be toasted and ground up and then cooked in porridge to treat shortness of breath and wheezing. Later, wellness expert and author Tingdong Cao of the Qing Dynasty added in his book Yang Sheng Sui Bi that radish seed porridge is also effective in treating indigestion, bloating, and constipation. I include amomum fruit and aged tangerine peel in this recipe to strengthen the toasted radish seeds in aiding digestion. The aromatic flavors match with chicken perfectly. I always make this dish to help my digestive system recover from all the overeating during the holiday season.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 14 hours

¾ cup brown rice

¼ cup foxtail millet

2 tablespoons (15 grams) toasted radish seeds*

6 cups chicken broth

4 thick slices fresh ginger

1 pound bone-in chicken legs or thighs, skin on

1 teaspoon sea salt

3 tablespoons chopped scallions, both green and white parts

½ cup (25 grams) aged tangerine peel

4 whole amomum fruit

Gluten-free soy sauce, to taste

1 tablespoon sesame oil, or to taste

Chopped scallions, sesame seeds, hulled hemp seeds, or cilantro, for garnish

1. The night before serving this dish, rinse the brown rice and millet under cold running water and drain. Add to a large bowl with enough water to cover and soak overnight.

2. The next day, use a grinder to finely crush the toasted radish seeds into a powder. Set aside.

3. Drain the soaked grains. In a large pot, add the soaked grains, chicken broth, ginger, chicken legs, and sea salt. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to low; and simmer for 1.5 hours, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. Remove the chicken legs and set aside.

4. Add the reserved radish seed powder, scallions, and aged tangerine peel to the porridge. Cook for an additional 30 minutes. Add the amomum fruit and the chicken legs. Cook for an additional 15 minutes. The porridge is done when the grains are very soft and the consistency is smooth. Season with soy sauce and sesame oil.

5. Remove the aged tangerine peel and amomum fruit and discard. Ladle the porridge into bowls and serve warm with toppings of choice, such as scallions, sesame seeds, hemp seeds, or cilantro. Store leftover porridge in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to a week.

title: Lily Bulb Oatmeal
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
安神百合燕麦粥

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Heart, Spleen

Functions: Calming, Respiratory Health

I adore a bowl of warm oatmeal in the morning. It is essentially a Western version of Chinese congee! Through consultations with my patients, I came to realize that oatmeal is a common choice of breakfast for many people. Seven out of ten patients who come to see me tell me that they eat oatmeal for breakfast. That’s why I included this recipe, a small upgrade of regular morning oats with TCM herbs and sweet potato for even more nutrients and Heart-nourishing qualities. Jujube dates, Chinese licorice root, and lily bulb add a gentle and slightly sweet layer of flavor to the oatmeal. Feel free to top it with your favorite fruits, nuts, and seeds!

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 50 minutes

½ cup (30 grams) Chinese licorice root

½ cup (45 grams) dried lily bulb*

3½ cups soy milk or oat milk

6 medium jujube dates (30 grams), pitted and chopped

½ cup diced purple sweet potato

½ cup diced sweet potato

1 cup rolled oats

¼ teaspoon sea salt

Light brown sugar or honey, to taste

1. In a medium pot, add the Chinese licorice root, lily bulb, and soy milk. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to low and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes. Strain and discard the herbs and keep the liquid in the pot.

2. Add the chopped jujube dates, both diced sweet potatoes, rolled oats, and sea salt to the pot. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for about 20 minutes, until the oatmeal has thickened. Add a sweetener and serve warm. You can store the leftover oatmeal in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days.

title: Adzuki and Coix Seed Porridge with Snow Fungus
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
祛湿红豆薏米银耳粥

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free ◦ Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Humid

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Aids Digestion

If you mention to any Chinese grandma that you are suffering from Dampness in your body, like acne or eczema, it is very likely that she will cook this dish for you. Filled with potent Spleen-strengthening herbs and ingredients, this porridge is a lifesaver for me on humid days, when I feel sticky and sluggish. It is also suitable for those looking to manage weight in a healthy way. One of the star ingredients in this recipe is snow fungus, which is also called tremella mushroom or silver ear mushroom. In its dried form, it almost resembles off-white marigolds. In its fresh state or when soaked thoroughly, it becomes transparent but retains a slightly milky hue. In recent years, snow fungus has become one of the trendiest skin care ingredients. It is known for its hydrating, hyaluronic-acid-like effect, being able to hold five hundred times its weight in water. At the same time, it can also hydrate our body from within. In TCM food therapy, it is known as a beauty food, used very often as a Yin-nourishing ingredient to foster healthy skin, delay aging, relieve dryness in the throat and skin, boost immunity, and benefit the Stomach.

The consistency of this porridge is very loose and soupy compared to a regular rice porridge. Although a big spoonful of cane sugar can make it very palatable, I recommend using a natural sugar substitute like monk fruit extract, or even keeping it bland to avoid introducing Dampness into your body. All herbs used in this recipe are edible except for the poria. Therefore, I recommend putting the poria in a reusable or single-use tea bag or a small muslin bag while cooking so that you can remove and discard it easily.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 13.5 hours

⅔ cup (150 grams) coix seeds

⅔ cup adzuki beans

1 fist-size dried snow fungus*

¼ cup (40 grams) poria

7 cups rice milk or other nondairy milk

Monk fruit extract or other natural sugar substitute, like honey, to taste

1. The night before serving this dish, dry-toast the coix seeds and adzuki beans in a medium pan over medium heat for 3 minutes. Let them cool in the pan for 5 minutes.

2. Rinse the coix seeds, adzuki beans, and snow fungus under cool running water. Add to a large bowl with enough water to cover and soak overnight.

3. The next day, drain the soaking water. Break the snow fungus into small pieces with your hands and remove and discard the hard, yellow parts if there are any.

4. Put the poria in a reusable or single-use tea bag and add it to a medium pot with the soaked ingredients and rice milk. Bring everything to a boil over high heat; reduce heat to medium; and cook, covered, for 1 hour, until the adzuki beans and coix seeds are completely soft. Take out the poria tea bag and discard. This is meant to be a soupy, thin type of porridge. Add monk fruit extract.

5. Serve warm or at room temperature. Make sure to drink all the liquid for optimal benefits.

title: Fox Nut Millet Porridge
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
莲子芡实山药小米粥

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Spleen, Stomach, Kidney

Functions: Aids Digestion, Calming

My mom always makes millet porridge for my dad for breakfast to help with his blood sugar issues. The night before, she sets up the rice cooker with the grains and broth in it, and the next morning she simply scoops the porridge out and tops it with a salted duck egg, sautéed leafy greens, and some homemade pork floss.

This recipe is inspired by the care and love my mom gives to our family. The ingredients are focused on both Spleen and Kidney health, restoring Essence while strengthening digestion to help with diabetes, diarrhea, chronic fatigue, and sluggish digestion. I recommend having this in the morning, along with some healthy fats and protein like eggs and roasted fish, to nourish your digestive system and provide sustained energy. Note: It’s important that you use bright yellow Chinese foxtail millet to achieve a creamy consistency for the porridge. Other millet, in my experience, tends to result in a loose, quinoa-like texture that is not particularly suitable.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 4 hours

⅓ cup (35 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed

¼ cup (50 grams) fox nuts

1 cup foxtail millet, rinsed

5 cups mushroom broth or soy milk, plus more as needed*

1 tablespoon minced ginger

1 teaspoon (2 grams) ground nutmeg

1 cup diced fresh Chinese yam*

1 tablespoon sesame oil

Sea salt, to taste

1. Rinse and soak the lotus seeds and fox nuts in water to cover for at least 3 hours. Drain and discard the soaking water.

2. In a medium pot, add the soaked lotus seeds and fox nuts, foxtail millet, broth, ginger, nutmeg, and Chinese yam. Bring everything to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to low; and simmer, covered, for about 30 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The porridge is done when the millet is completely soft. Season with the sesame oil and sea salt. You can add more broth if your porridge is too thick.

3. Ladle into bowls and serve warm.

title: Sugar-Free Sweet Cooling Tea
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
罗汉果金银花凉茶

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Warm, Humid

Energetics: Cold

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Liver, Gallbladder

Functions: Cooling, Liver Health

Cooling tea, or liang cha (凉茶) in Chinese, was selected as one of the intangible cultural heritages of China in 2006, which shows how important it is to Chinese culture and how effective it can be in terms of preventing Heat-induced illnesses, like indigestion and skin inflammation. Liang cha originated in Guangdong, China, a southern province with hot and humid weather. People there cannot live without a daily cup of Cooling tea. There are streetside booths and stores that sell only Cooling teas, usually with a menu of teas with the symptoms of different Heat and Damp conditions that they address, so the customer can choose which is the most suitable for them.

This recipe is a very general and classic one to cool Summer Heat and Liver Fire. The monk fruit adds natural sweetness to balance the bitter flavors from the other herbs. If you are in a hot and humid environment while reading this recipe, make a big jug of it and sip some every day!

Besides the honeysuckle and chrysanthemum that I introduced in Part II, prunella (xia ku cao 夏枯草) is also a TCM food therapy herb. It is used almost exclusively in beverages for Cooling. You can find it easily at a Chinese grocery store or herbal pharmacy. If you can’t find any, you can substitute mint or simply skip it.

YIELD: 10 servings

TIME: 35 minutes

1 whole monk fruit or monk fruit extract, to taste*

1 cup (20 grams) honeysuckle

3 cups (25 grams) dried prunella or 3 cups (90 grams) fresh mint

2 cups (36 grams) dried chrysanthemum flowers

1. In a large pot, add all the ingredients and 10 cups of water. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to low; and simmer, covered, for 35 minutes. Make sure to stir and submerge all the herbs.

2. Discard all solids. Serve warm or at room temperature. Feel free to dilute the tea with additional water or to add additional sweetener if preferred.

title: Wu Zhi Yin
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
五汁饮

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Warm, Humid

Energetics: Cold

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach, Bladder

Functions: Cooling, Yin Nourishing, Aids Digestion, Calming, Respiratory Health

Wu zhi yin means “beverage made from five types of juices” in Chinese. Wu Jutong (1758–1836), a Qing Dynasty TCM physician, mentioned the recipe in detail in his book Wen Bing Tiao Bian, which I’ve adapted here. Wu wrote that this recipe is for those with Tai Yin Warm Disease (severe indigestion, nausea, vomiting, foaming at mouth) and Heat caused by excessive Yang energy in the body. In modern life, this recipe is great for Cooling our body, reducing inflammation in our respiratory and digestive systems, and providing optimal hydration. I recommend having a glass of this daily on the hottest days of summer. The ingredients in this recipe may be difficult to source, but I strongly recommend finding them online or taking a trip to Chinatown.

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 10 minutes

2 tablespoons (30 grams) cooked coix seeds*

1 Asian pear, peeled and chopped

⅓ cup chopped fresh lotus root

4 whole water chestnuts

1 tablespoon (25 grams) fresh ophiopogon root (optional)

Honey, to taste

1. Using a blender or juicer, combine all the ingredients except the honey and blend until smooth. Strain using a cheesecloth and pour into a glass; discard the solids. If the consistency is too thick, add some of the liquid from the boiled coix seeds or just plain water.

2. Taste and add honey as needed. Serve cooled. If you have a Cold constitution, you can warm it before drinking.

title: Calming Papaya Smoothie
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
安神木瓜果昔

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Warm

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Aids Digestion, Calming

Papaya is my favorite fruit. When I was doing volunteer work in Costa Rica, I had some minor illnesses, like constipation, indigestion, skin rashes, sore throat, and a little bit of homesickness. No matter what my problem was, my host mom would always give me papaya and say, “¡Come un poco de papaya y te recuperarás!” (“Eat a little papaya and you will be fine!”)

Papaya is loaded with antioxidants, enzymes like papain, vitamin C, lycopene, and more. This smoothie adds to the healing benefits of papaya with Spirit-calming herbs like jujube dates, longan fruit, lotus seeds, and lily bulb. These sweet and mild herbs fit perfectly in a smoothie and provide additional fiber, protein, and natural sweetness. I love having this smoothie on a summer afternoon!

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 35 minutes

⅓ cup (30 grams) lotus seeds, hearts removed

1 cup roughly chopped ripe papaya

1 cup nondairy yogurt

1 cup nut milk of choice, plus more as needed

2 medium jujube dates (10 grams), pitted

3 fresh longan fruit (20 grams), pitted, or dried (6 grams)

1 tablespoon (15 grams) fresh lily bulb*

Ice (optional)

1. In a small pot, add 2 cups of water and bring to a boil over medium heat. Add the lotus seeds and cook, covered, until they are very soft, about 20 minutes. Strain and reserve the lotus seeds. Discard the liquid.

2. In a blender, add the cooked lotus seeds and the rest of the ingredients and blend at high speed until smooth. Adjust the consistency by adding nut milk. Enjoy at room temperature or iced.

title: Hawthorn Berry Sparkling Mocktail
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
山楂气泡水

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral, slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Aids Digestion, Tonifies Qi and Blood

I always serve a hawthorn berry–based welcome beverage at the pop-up dinners I host in New York City because it can stimulate the appetite while preventing post-meal indigestion. This recipe is great to serve at gatherings, where the guests may tend to overindulge in food and drink. In addition, if you know someone with high cholesterol and high blood pressure, serve this mocktail, as it does wonders for the blood vessels. It is best to use fresh hawthorn berries if you can find them, although the dried ones also work well.

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 20 minutes

3 whole fresh hawthorn berries (50 grams)*

2 teaspoons cane sugar or a natural alternative sweetener, or to taste

½ cup fresh or frozen berries, such as raspberry, blueberry, or blackberry

⅛ teaspoon ground amomum fruit

½ teaspoon dried osmanthus flowers (optional)*

1 cup kombucha or any kind of sparkling water

Ice (optional)

1. Combine the hawthorn berries, cane sugar, other berries, amomum fruit, and osmanthus flowers in a small pot, and cover with ⅔ cup of water. Cook over medium heat for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until everything softens and reaches a compote-like consistency. Remove from the heat and let cool.

2. In a cocktail shaker, mix 2 tablespoons of the compote with the kombucha. Add ice, if using. Taste and adjust the sweetness, adding more compote if necessary.

3. To serve, place a tablespoon of the remaining compote in a tall glass, top off with the mocktail mix, add more ice if necessary and if using, and enjoy.

title: Hawthorn Berry and Lotus Leaf Tea
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
降脂山楂荷叶茶

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Aids Digestion

Meant for healthy weight management, this is not the green “ballerina” diet tea you may have seen on the shelves of an Asian market. While that one contains only senna leaves, which can give you diarrhea, this recipe can truly help facilitate weight loss by removing stagnated Phlegm and stimulating digestion, especially in individuals with high cholesterol, high blood pressure, high body fat, and water retention. It tastes tart and slightly bitter. You can dilute it with water or add monk fruit extract or another natural zero-calorie sweetener to sweeten it up. Drink it throughout the day for one month at least and you are likely to feel lighter and refreshed!

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 30 minutes

3 whole dried hawthorn berries (15 grams)*

⅓ cup (8 grams) lotus leaf, broken up by hand

1 piece (10 grams) aged tangerine peel

2 cups water

1. In a small pot, add all the ingredients. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to medium; and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes.

2. Strain and pour the tea into a cup; discard the solids. Drink while the tea is warm.

title: Saffron Mulled Wine
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
活血化瘀藏红花水果酒

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Dry

Energetics: Hot

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Spleen, Liver

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Warming

This is a perfect recipe for the holiday season. When the weather is cold and dry, drinking this mulled wine can warm our body, promote healthy Blood circulation, and lift our mood. The taste of this herbal mulled wine is fruity, slightly sweet, and mildly spicy. Saffron or safflower wine has a long history in TCM food therapy to treat Blood stagnation. While this recipe is great for postpartum care (you can replace the wine with grape, cranberry, or pomegranate juice), it is not suitable for pregnancy as it moves Blood very strongly.

YIELD: 8 servings

TIME: 35 minutes

One 750 milliliter bottle dry red wine (such as merlot, cabernet sauvignon, syrah, pinot noir, or malbec)

2 cups cranberry juice or pomegranate juice

3 cinnamon sticks

1 tablespoon whole cloves

4 whole star anise

12 medium jujube dates (60 grams)

⅓ cup (40 grams) goji berries

Zest of 1 orange

4 slices (40 grams) whole angelica root

1 teaspoon saffron (or ⅔ cup loosely packed safflower petals)

4 sprigs fresh thyme

2 sprigs fresh rosemary

Dark brown sugar or honey, to taste (optional)

1. In a large pot, combine all the ingredients except the brown sugar. Place over medium-high heat and cook until it reaches a boil. Reduce the heat to low and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes. Taste and add more brown sugar as needed.

2. Strain and pour the mulled wine into a serving container; discard the solids. Serve warm.

Note: This recipe is not suitable for pregnant women.

title: Warming Jujube Date and Longan Fruit Tea
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
暖体红枣桂圆茶

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Dry

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Spleen

Functions: Warming, Tonifies Qi and Blood, Calming

If you’re someone who grew up with a Chinese mom or grandma, you may have had this tea made for you with lots of love and care. If not, this recipe is delicious and so easy to make for yourself. It has a sweet, deep, and mildly spicy taste that reminds me of a Middle Eastern medjool date dessert soaked in spiced syrup. This is a very popular folk recipe that has been used in Chinese families for hundreds of years to treat menstrual cramps, add some rosy color to dull and pale cheeks, and replenish Qi and Blood for women. However, anyone can drink and benefit from this tea!

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 20 minutes

6 medium jujube dates (30 grams)

6 dried longan fruit (15 grams)

4 thin slices fresh ginger

1 teaspoon molasses or dark brown sugar (optional)

1. In a small pot, combine all the ingredients except the molasses with 3 cups of water. Place over medium heat and let it come to a boil; reduce the heat to low and simmer, covered, for 20 minutes. Taste and add molasses as needed.

2. Serve warm. To get the most out of these herbs, you can eat the longan fruit and jujube dates.

title: Warm Black Sesame Smoothie
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
黑芝麻护发奶昔

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Liver, Kidney, Large Intestine

Functions: Yin Nourishing, Aids Digestion

A warm smoothie may sound like a bad idea, but allow this recipe to change your mind. Growing up, I always had this kind of warm smoothie made from seeds, nuts, and whole grains when I was with my grandparents. It is nutty, incredibly creamy, and smooth, with the perfect amount of sweetness. Soaking, blending, and cooking makes these grains very easy to digest and their nutrients more available for absorption. This recipe focuses on our Liver and Kidney health, particularly helping with hair loss, fatigue, and soreness in the lower back and knees. It is also filled with fiber and healthy fats. If you drink this on an empty stomach in the morning, it can also help with constipation by moistening the Large Intestine. The best thing for me, though, is that it doesn’t give me brain freeze like an iced, raw smoothie does.

YIELD: 2 servings

TIME: 13 hours

1 tablespoon black rice, rinsed

¼ cup gluten-free oats

¼ cup toasted black sesame seeds

¼ cup walnuts

3 cups soy milk, plus more as needed

2 ripe bananas

1 teaspoon honey, or to taste

2 teaspoons (5 grams) mulberry powder or ¼ cup (40 grams) fresh mulberries

1. The night before serving this dish, combine the black rice, oats, black sesame seeds, walnuts, and soy milk in a medium bowl, and let it soak in the refrigerator overnight.

2. The next day, transfer the grain and nut mix to a blender and blend at high speed until smooth. This may take a couple of minutes. Strain the liquid through a fine mesh and reserve; discard the solids.

3. Pour the liquid into a medium saucepan. Place over medium-high heat until it reaches a boil; reduce the heat to low; and simmer, covered, for 20 minutes. Let it cool for 15 minutes.

4. Return the cooked liquid to the blender. Add the bananas, honey, and mulberry powder. Blend until smooth. If your blender has a soup setting, use it here. Add more soy milk if your smoothie is too thick. Taste and add more honey as needed.

5. Pour into 2 glasses. Serve warm.

title: Reishi Hot Chocolate
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
灵芝热巧克力

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free ◦ Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Heart, Liver, Spleen

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Warming, Yin Nourishing, Calming

This is a perfect treat to cozy up with during the cold months. Reishi is a powerful ingredient that not only boosts immunity but also balances the mood and Spirit. Its slightly bitter flavor and brown color pairs perfectly with cacao, another superfood filled with antioxidants. In comparison, store-bought hot chocolate mix often contains plenty of dairy powder and sugar. Make this recipe at home and you will not be disappointed. I love to keep the longan fruit and jujube dates in the hot chocolate, so that when I get to the bottom of the cup, I can have them like a sweet surprise!

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 15 minutes

1½ cups soy milk or another nondairy milk of choice

Pinch of saffron

4 dried longan fruit (10 grams)

1 medium jujube date (5 grams)

1 ounce vegan dark chocolate bar, broken into pieces, or 2 tablespoons dark chocolate chips

2 tablespoons cacao powder, plus more for garnish

1 teaspoon reishi powder*

1 tablespoon honey, or to taste

⅛ teaspoon ground cinnamon

⅛ teaspoon ground star anise

1. In a milk pan, combine the soy milk, saffron, longan fruit, and jujube date. Place over medium heat until it reaches a boil; reduce the heat to low; and simmer, covered, for 10 minutes.

2. Turn off the heat and add the chocolate to the warm milk. Whisk until the chocolate dissolves completely. Add the remaining ingredients. Whisk until well combined, with no lumps. Taste and adjust the sweetness, adding more honey if necessary.

3. Top with more cacao powder and serve warm.

title: Rose Latte
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
疏肝玫瑰拿铁

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free ◦ Dairy-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Liver

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Liver Health, Calming

Once, I had a rose matcha latte at a very “Instagrammable” café in SoHo, New York City. Despite its exorbitant price, I loved it. The distinct aroma of rose matched so well with the smooth nut milk that I was inspired to make my own version of it at home. With dried rose, rose water, and a touch of pink from beets, this cup can win anyone over. It gently regulates Liver Qi, calms the Spirit, and removes Blood stagnation to make more room for us to find love.

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 15 minutes

1½ cups hemp milk or other nondairy milk of choice

2 tablespoons (6 grams) dried rose buds

Monk fruit extract or another preferred sweetener, to taste

½ teaspoon beet powder or 1 tablespoon beet juice

1 tablespoon rose water

1. In a milk pan, bring the hemp milk to a boil over medium heat. Once boiled, turn off the heat. Add the dried rose buds and steep for 10 minutes. Strain and discard the solids.

2. Return the rose milk to the milk pan and add the monk fruit extract. Taste and adjust the sweetness. Add the beet powder and the rose water. Use a milk frother to mix the beet thoroughly in the latte and create froth. You can adjust the amount of beet to create different hues of pink.

3. Pour into a glass and serve warm.

title: Shiso Ginger Tea
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
生姜紫苏茶

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Humid

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Stomach, Liver

Functions: Respiratory Health, Liver Health

This is a very effective and delicious recipe to treat nausea, morning sickness, and early flu symptoms, like coughing, nasal congestion, and headaches. It can also be used to help with Liver Fire if you take out the ginger. If your symptoms are mild, you can drink this tea once a day. If you are suffering from more severe symptoms, you can double the recipe and consume it all in one day. It is safe for adults, pregnant women, and children (dilute to 50 percent).

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 10 minutes

1 tablespoon minced ginger, skin peeled

4 whole dried or fresh shiso leaves

10 fresh mint leaves (15 grams)

½ cup (9 grams) dried chrysanthemum flowers

In a small saucepan, combine all the herbs with enough water to cover (about 2 cups). Place over medium heat until it reaches a boil, then turn off the heat immediately. Let it steep for 5 minutes and then strain into a cup; discard the solids. Serve warm.

title: Mochi-Stuffed Jujube Dates
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
心太软

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Humid, Dry

Energetics: Neutral

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen

Functions: Aids Digestion, Tonifies Qi and Blood

This is a traditional Shanghainese dessert that I grew up eating. It has a beautiful name in Chinese: xin tai ruan 心太软 (“heart that is too soft”), because the dark red color of jujube dates resembles that of a heart and the mochi in the center is very soft. I made a modification to the original recipe by including Chinese licorice root, honey, and Chinese yam to increase the Spleen-strengthening quality without changing too much of its signature taste. One bite into this dessert will make you smile! If you don’t have jujube dates, medjool dates are a good substitution.

YIELD: 6 pieces

TIME: 30 minutes

6 jumbo jujube dates

2 tablespoons rice flour

3 tablespoons glutinous rice flour

1 tablespoon (15 grams) ground dried Chinese yam*

2 teaspoons (8 grams) ground Chinese licorice root*

2 teaspoons honey

2 tablespoons soy milk, plus more as needed

1 teaspoon dried osmanthus flowers or another dried edible flower, for garnish (optional)

1. Cut the dates open and remove the pits.

2. Prepare your steamer. (See here for steaming methods.)

3. In a small mixing bowl, combine the rice flour, glutinous rice flour, ground Chinese yam, ground Chinese licorice root, and honey. Using a fork, slowly drizzle in the soy milk and mix for 2 to 3 minutes, until a smooth dough forms that is neither too dry nor too wet. Shape 2 teaspoons of dough with your fingers into a small strip that is of similar length to the jujube dates and stuff it into a cut date. Repeat with the remaining dough and dates.

4. Steam the dates for 5 to 8 minutes, until the centers are soft.

5. Remove the dates from the steamer and place them on a serving dish. Garnish with the osmanthus flowers, if desired. Serve warm. The dates can be kept frozen for up to 6 months in an airtight container; reheat by steaming before serving.

title: Apricot Kernel Pear Jelly
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
止咳杏仁冻

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Warm, Dry

Energetics: Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Stomach

Functions: Respiratory Health, Cooling, Yin Nourishing

Traditionally, this dessert is called “apricot kernel tofu” in modern Chinese and “apricot kernel cheese” in ancient literature. It truly has nothing to do with tofu or cheese other than its resemblance to their smooth, white, inviting appearance. And because it is so beautiful, this recipe is frequently mentioned in many ancient cookbooks and novels. Song Dynasty poet Yuan Mei, in his book Recipes from the Garden of Contentment (1792 CE), recorded how he made this dessert with rice flour instead of agar-agar. Qing Dynasty author Zhu Yizun, in his cookbook Shi Xian Hong Mi (1731 CE), described how he used the ash from the firepit of his kitchen to make the jelly set. All of the ancient recipes simply used water or milk as the liquid base. Here, I substituted the liquid with an herbal decoction and pear juice that make this recipe more effective for Yin nourishing. It is great for coughing, chronic thirst, and dry throat.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 45 minutes + setting time

⅔ cup (50 grams) glehnia root

1 cup (30 grams) Solomon’s seal

½ cup (60 grams) apricot kernels, soaked in water overnight in fridge

1 tablespoon agar-agar powder*

2 cups pear juice*

1 tablespoon honey, or to taste

2 teaspoons dried osmanthus flowers or chopped pear, for garnish (optional)

1. In a medium pot, combine the glehnia root and Solomon’s seal in 3 cups of water and bring to a boil over medium heat. Cook, covered, for 20 minutes. Strain and discard the solids, then keep cooking, uncovered, to reduce the liquid to about 2½ cups.

2. In a blender, combine the soaked apricot kernels with the 2½ cups of herbal water and blend at high speed for 1 minute. Strain the pulp and reserve the liquid. You can save the pulp and use it in baked goods or pancakes.

3. In a small bowl, dissolve the agar-agar powder in 1 cup of the pear juice. Whisk together until there are no lumps.

4. In a clean medium pot, add the apricot herbal milk, honey, and the cup of pear juice containing the agar-agar powder. Mix well and bring to a boil over medium heat. Turn the heat down to low and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring constantly. Turn off the heat and pour in the remaining cup of pear juice. Stir well to combine. Taste and adjust the sweetness, adding more honey as needed.

5. Strain the mixture again, through a fine-mesh strainer, while it is still hot. Then pour it into 6 small containers, such as ceramic dessert dishes, and let it cool at room temperature or in the fridge. Once the jelly is completely set, top with the osmanthus flowers, if using. Serve at room temperature or chilled.

title: Mulberry Honey Compote
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
桑葚蜜

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Warm, Dry

Energetics: Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Liver, Kidney

Functions: Yin Nourishing, Tonifies Qi and Blood, Liver Health

Mulberry paste in Chinese has historically been called wen wu gao (文武膏). Wen means “literature and penmanship”; wu means “combat and military”; and gao means “herbal jam or paste.” Even after searching through many resources, I still couldn’t figure out why it was named this. I imagine that is because this paste is versatile and suitable for everyone, from a sedentary scholar to a soldier on a battlefield. There is a recipe for it in Su Wen Bing Ji Qi Yi Bao Ming Ji (1601 CE), written by Liu Wansu from the Jin Dynasty, which I adapted for the modern home cook and to which I added honey, to further its Yin-nourishing, tonifying quality. This compote is fantastic for tonifying the Blood, moistening Dryness, and supplementing the Liver and Kidney, and it is especially beneficial for older people who suffer from constipation and menopausal women who experience Yin Deficiency, Heat, and Dryness. You can use it like jam to put on toast or dissolve it in warm water to drink.

YIELD: About 2 cups

TIME: 45 minutes

1½ pounds (680 grams) fresh, ripe mulberries, rinsed and stems removed

⅓ cup honey, or to taste

Zest and juice of 1 orange

1. Place the mulberries in a small pot and gently muddle them with the back of a spoon. Add the honey and the orange zest and juice and turn the heat to low. Simmer for 20 minutes or until the berries have really broken down. Stir constantly to prevent the berries from burning and to dissolve the honey. When the mixture acquires a loose jam consistency, it is ready. Taste and adjust the sweetness, adding more honey if necessary.

2. You can use the compote as is or puree it in a blender for a smoother texture. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 6 months.

title: Fermented Brown Sugar Rice Cake
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
天然发酵红糖糕

Vegan ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Dry

Energetics: slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Heart, Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Aids Digestion, Calming, Warming

Sweet and slightly alcoholic, the smell of this rice cake is extremely inviting. I grew up eating this kind of fluffy steamed rice cake for breakfast or as a snack (note that this is not nian gao, the sticky, chewy, dense rice cake). This recipe is quite time-consuming because we are using natural fermentation rather than commercial bread yeast and baking powder. The active agent here is homemade rice wine (jiu niang 酒酿), a lightly alcoholic and sweet Chinese specialty that you should try in order to understand its unique flavor and texture. We are using both the rice grains and the liquid from jiu niang in this recipe, as they can help promote Blood circulation, Warm up our bodies, and supply probiotics to our digestive system. The essential ingredient in making rice wine is rice wine yeast or Shanghai rice wine yeast ball. You can find them in small packets in most Chinese grocery stores.

The cake itself is very light and refreshing, without any added oil or large amounts of sugar. This is an unconventional way of making steamed rice cake, but this is how my grandma does it and she nails it every time. I can eat the whole six servings in one day—that’s how good and loving this recipe is. For this book, I changed the plain water in her recipe to an herbal decoction inspired by Shi Quan Da Bu Tang (“All-Inclusive Great Tonifying Decoction”—doesn’t that sound wonderful?), which adds a pleasant herbal aroma to the cake.

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 5 days

Jiu Niang (Fermented Rice Wine)*

2 cups white sticky rice

1 packet rice wine yeast or 1 Shanghai rice wine yeast ball

2 cups distilled water

Brown Sugar Rice Cake

3 whole slices (20 grams) angelica root

6 long pieces (20 grams) astragalus root

⅓ cup (30 grams) longan fruit

⅓ cup (20 grams) Chinese licorice root

2 tablespoons (20 grams) poria

5 slices (20 grams) reishi

1 cup raw white short-grain rice, soaked in water overnight

½ cup cooked white rice

2 tablespoons dark brown sugar

Vanilla Silken Tofu Cream Sauce

½ block (8 ounces) silken tofu

1 teaspoon maple syrup, or to taste

½ teaspoon vanilla extract

Pinch of fine sea salt

1 teaspoon lemon juice

Pinch of dried osmanthus flowers, for garnish (optional)

1. Make the jiu niang. Rinse the sticky rice 3 to 4 times and then soak in water overnight in the fridge. After soaking, the grains should be soft enough to be easily crushed by hand.

2. The next day, drain the water and steam the rice (see here for steaming methods). Let it cool. (You can also cook sticky rice in a rice cooker on the setting for sticky rice, in which case, you should skip soaking it.)

3. Sanitize all your tools and cookware from this point on by boiling them in a pot of water for 10 minutes.

4. Dissolve the packet of rice wine yeast in the distilled water. If you are using the rice wine yeast ball, break it up before dissolving.

5. In a sanitized large mixing bowl, combine the steamed rice with the yeast water and mix thoroughly. Make sure the rice grains are not sticking to one another by breaking them apart using a spoon or gloved hands. Transfer the mixture to a sanitized container of choice. Usually I use a 2-quart (64-ounce) glass jar with a wide mouth. Gently press the rice down in the container and dig a hole in the center. This is so we can check if the rice wine is ready, as the liquid will rise and be visible in the hole.

6. Use a piece of thin cotton cloth or plastic film with holes to cover the container. Do not use a lid. Store in a shady, warm environment (72°F/22°C to 95°F/35°C) and let it ferment for 3 to 5 days (the higher the temperature, the faster the fermentation process), until the center hole is filled with rice wine and some bubbles appear. Now the rice wine is ready to be used as an active fermentation agent for our brown sugar rice cake.

7. Store any leftover rice wine and rice mixture in the fridge to slow down the fermentation for an additional week or so. Your rice wine will taste sweeter, and the alcohol content will increase. The fermented rice can also be eaten directly or added to sweet beverages, such as juice, lemonade, or sweet tea.

8. Make the vanilla silken tofu cream sauce. In a blender, add all the ingredients and blend until smooth. Taste and adjust the sweetness, adding more maple syrup if necessary. The sauce should be thin and mild.

9. Make the brown sugar rice cake. In a medium pot, combine the angelica root, astragalus root, longan fruit, Chinese licorice, poria, and reishi with enough water to cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat; reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer for 30 minutes. Strain and reserve the liquid and the longan fruit. Let it cool. Discard the other herbs.

10. Strain the raw rice, then combine in a blender with the cooked rice, 1 cup of the jiu niang (both liquid and rice), brown sugar, and the reserved cooled herbal liquid and longan fruit. Blend at high speed until you have a smooth batter. The batter should be quite thin, similar to a runny pancake batter.

11. Pour the batter into a large mixing bowl. Cover with a piece of cloth or plastic film and let it rise in a warm place for 1.5 to 2 hours. Once the batter has at least doubled in size and bubbles have appeared, it is done. Use a spatula to gently stir the batter to let out any excess air.

12. Meanwhile, prepare your steamer (see here for steaming methods) and line a 6-inch square cake pan or small individual cupcake molds with parchment paper or cupcake liners. Pour the batter into the prepared molds and fill only about three-quarters of the way full, as the batter will rise during the steaming process.

13. Steam on high heat for 30 minutes, until the center is completely solid and cooked through. Serve with the vanilla silken tofu cream sauce and garnish with the osmanthus flowers, if using. Enjoy warm!

14. The rice cake can be stored in the freezer, wrapped in plastic wrap or foil, for up to 6 months. Reheat it by steaming.

title: Purple Rice–Stuffed Lotus Root with Herbal Brown Sugar Glaze
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
药膳紫米糖藕

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Dry, Cold

Energetics: Neutral, slightly Warming

Meridian Affinity: Spleen, Liver

Functions: Tonifies Qi and Blood, Calming

Lotus ponds and rice fields are a signature landscape of my hometown. I grew up eating this dessert as an appetizer at family banquets. To further help tonify Qi and Blood, I added herbal components to the syrup of the original recipe that my mom taught me when I was a little girl. The lotus root is soft and starchy, while the sticky rice is chewy and satisfying. Paired with a decadent brown sugar herbal syrup made from saffron, rose, goji berries, and jujube dates, this recipe is simply delicious as an appetizer or dessert! When you pull the cooked sliced lotus root apart, you will see a lot of thin “strings” between the slices. These are the delicate lotus stem fibers that are also used to make textiles!

YIELD: 6 servings

TIME: 7 hours

⅔ cup white sticky rice

⅔ cup purple sticky rice

1 forearm-length (10- to 12-inch) fresh lotus root

2 tablespoons osmanthus flower loose leaf tea (optional)

½ cup dark brown sugar

1 tablespoon gluten-free soy sauce

½ teaspoon saffron

½ cup (20 grams) dried rose buds

3 tablespoons (20 grams) goji berries

10 medium jujube dates (50 grams)

1. Rinse the white and purple rice under cool running water, drain, and add to a large bowl with enough water to cover. Soak for at least 3 hours, or preferably overnight. Drain and set aside.

2. Peel the brown skin off the lotus root with a peeler. Cleanly cut off each end of the root so the holes inside are exposed, and reserve the cut ends.

3. In a large mixing bowl, combine 1 tablespoon of the osmanthus flower tea, if using, and the white and purple sticky rice. Use a chopstick to poke the rice mixture into the lotus root holes. Make sure they are stuffed all the way through but do not overstuff. Once the lotus root is fully stuffed, use toothpicks to securely reattach the ends that you originally cut off, so that the rice doesn’t come out when the lotus root is boiled.

4. Place the stuffed and capped lotus root in a large pot. Add enough water to cover. Add the brown sugar and soy sauce. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, covered, for 2 hours. Add the saffron, rose buds, goji berries, and jujube dates directly to the pot and cook for another hour, until the lotus root is soft. You may need to add additional water during the process to make sure most of the lotus root is still submerged. (You can also use a pressure cooker instead of the stovetop: Cook the lotus root with enough water to cover, along with the brown sugar, soy sauce, saffron, rose buds, goji berries, and jujube dates, for 40 minutes, then let sit for 1 to 2 hours before opening the pressure cooker lid.)

5. When the root is soft, remove it from the pot and let cool on a baking sheet. Strain and discard the solids from the liquid. Return the liquid to the pot and continue letting the liquid reduce over low heat, until it reaches a syrupy consistency, about 10 minutes.

6. Cut the lotus root into ⅓-inch-thick slices and place each slice on a plate. Discard the two ends. Top the plated slices with the herbal syrup and the remaining osmanthus flower tea, if using. Enjoy warm or at room temperature.

title: Adzuki Bean and Aged Tangerine Peel Sweet Soup with Rice Mochi
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
陈皮红豆沙配紫糯米汤圆

Vegan ◦ Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Humid, Cold

Energetics: Neutral, Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Respiratory Health, Aids Digestion

Tang yuan 汤圆, the inspiration for this recipe, was my absolute favorite dessert when I was growing up. Tang means “soup” and yuan means “round.” Essentially, it is sweet mochi balls in a sweet soup. It is so warm, soft, and chewy that I always overeat when my grandma makes it. In this recipe, purple sticky rice flour is used to add a whole-grain component to the mochi. Purple sticky rice flour might be a difficult ingredient to find. You can either grind your own from whole purple sticky rice grains or use regular white sticky rice flour (mochi flour). The creamy and aromatic sweet soup base can also be served on its own as a dessert. It has some of the best Dampness-reducing properties in it. From the aged tangerine peel to the nutmeg and adzuki beans, this is truly food as medicine in its best form.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 2 hours

Purple Rice Mochi

½ cup soy milk

1 cup purple or white sticky rice flour

Adzuki Bean and Aged Tangerine Peel Sweet Soup

1 piece (10 grams) aged tangerine peel

1 tablespoon cold water

1 tablespoon white sticky rice flour

⅓ cup adzuki beans, rinsed and soaked in water overnight

¼ teaspoon (0.5 gram) ground nutmeg

¼ teaspoon ground amomum fruit

2 tablespoons dark brown sugar, or to taste

1 teaspoon orange zest, for serving

1. Make the purple rice mochi. In a milk pan, bring the soy milk to a boil over medium heat. As soon as it reaches a boil, turn off the heat and let it cool a little.

2. In a medium mixing bowl, place the purple rice flour and slowly pour in the hot milk, mixing well with a spoon. Wearing a pair of food-safe gloves, knead the mixture into a smooth dough. Shape the dough into small bite-size balls (about 1½ inches in diameter) by rolling them between your palms or on a clean, flat surface and set aside.

3. In a medium pot, bring 4 cups of water to a boil over high heat. Drop the mochi balls into the boiling water and cook until they float to the surface, about 5 minutes. Add ½ cup of cold water to the pot and return to a boil. Once the water comes to a boil again, the mochi is done.

4. Take out the mochi and place them in room-temperature water in a small bowl to cool.

5. Make the adzuki bean and aged tangerine peel sweet soup. In a small bowl, soak the aged tangerine peel in warm water until soft. Chop it into smaller pieces.

6. In a separate small bowl, mix the cold water with the white sticky rice flour until there are no lumps. Set aside.

7. In a small pot, combine the soaked adzuki beans, tangerine peel pieces, white sticky rice flour mixture, and 2 cups of water. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to low and simmer, covered, for about 1 hour. Stir occasionally to prevent burning. Add more liquid as needed. When the beans are very soft and mushy, add the nutmeg, amomum fruit, and brown sugar and stir to combine. Taste and adjust the sweetness, adding more brown sugar if necessary. You can also choose to blend the mixture in a blender to achieve a smoother consistency.

8. Divide the purple rice mochi among 4 bowls and top with the sweet soup and the orange zest. Serve warm.

title: Mint and Mung Bean Sweet Soup
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
降暑薄荷绿豆饮

Vegan ◦ Dairy-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Humid, Warm

Energetics: Cold

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Heart, Stomach

Functions: Cooling

Having a sweet bean soup may sound unappetizing, but this recipe will not disappoint. It is a must-have on a hot summer day. It quenches thirst and cools Heat more efficiently than plain water, so much so that schools make this soup especially for their students during summer camps. The addition of mint gives it a refreshing taste and strengthens its Cooling effect. Don’t cook the mint for more than 15 minutes to preserve its maximum efficacy. Although cold beverages are usually not recommended in TCM food therapy, I suggest consuming this one cold.

YIELD: 4 servings

TIME: 13 hours

½ cup (100 grams) mung beans

½ cup (35 grams) dried or fresh lily bulb

2 whole monk fruit or monk fruit extract, to taste

1 bunch (50 grams) fresh mint, both stems and leaves, plus more for garnish

2 quarts water

1. The night before serving this dish, rinse the mung beans, place them in a large bowl with enough water to cover them, and soak them overnight.

2. The next day, drain the mung beans. In a large pot, combine the soaked mung beans, lily bulb, monk fruit (if using whole fruit), and water. Bring to a boil over high heat; reduce the heat to medium-low, and simmer, covered, for 1 hour, until the mung beans are soft and mushy and the liquid turns opaque. Add the mint and monk fruit extract (if using extract). Simmer for another 10 minutes. Taste and adjust the sweetness, adding more monk fruit if necessary.

3. Serve cold as a beverage or a soup and garnish with additional mint.

title: Steamed Ginger and Turmeric Milk Curd
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
双姜撞奶

Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold, Dry

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Spleen, Stomach

Functions: Warming, Tonifies Qi and Blood

Making this classic Cantonese dessert is truly like performing magic. As you pour milk into ginger juice at the right temperature, speed, and ratio, it becomes a solid, smooth, flan-like curd! Originating in Shawan town, in the Guangdong province of China, this dessert was originally called jiang zhuang nai (姜撞奶), which literally means “ginger crushing into milk.” The science behind it is that the protease zingibain in ginger juice denatures the milk protein, transforming it from a water-soluble form to a water-insoluble form, resulting in a beautiful curd. In addition to ginger, I added turmeric to further the Warming, anti-inflammatory, immunity-boosting functions of this classic dish. You can also sprinkle a little ground black peppercorn on top as garnish to strengthen the effect of the turmeric.

Although it sounds like a simple enough idea, this recipe may be one of the most difficult to achieve in this book. Temperature and ratio control needs to be exact. I do not recommend substituting or changing anything in this recipe. Good luck!

YIELD: 1 serving

TIME: 10 minutes

1 cup fresh whole dairy milk

2 teaspoons honey

1 tablespoon ginger juice, at room temperature*

½ teaspoon turmeric powder

1. In a milk pan, heat the milk over medium-low heat. Stir in the honey. Insert an instant-read thermometer to monitor the milk’s temperature. When it reaches 80°C/176°F, remove the pan from the heat.

2. Pour the ginger juice into a small bowl and give it a quick stir. Quickly pour in the warm milk mixture. Do not stir.

3. Leave the ginger milk mixture to set for 5 minutes. Sprinkle with the turmeric powder and serve warm.

title: Sesame Goji Granola
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
枸杞烤麦片

Vegan ◦ Gluten-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Cold

Energetics: Warming

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Liver, Kidney

Functions: Warming, Tonifies Qi and Blood

I had never had granola before I came to the United States, but as soon as I tried it for the first time, I definitely fell in love. It’s crunchy, sweet, nutty, and just perfect with yogurt. The addictive taste does come with the less than ideal fact that store-bought granola is often very high in sugar and fat, which can be easily adjusted if we make our own at home. This is a very simple and quick recipe for granola that has a TCM twist to it to tonify Qi and Blood and warm our body. The aroma of sesame oil pairs well with the gentle sweetness of goji berries and jujube dates. These spiced oats are crunchy, aromatic, and satisfying to have at any time of the day!

YIELD: 2½ cups

TIME: 30 minutes

2 cups rolled oats

2 tablespoons black sesame seeds

½ cup chopped walnuts

2 teaspoons (5 grams) five-spice powder or ground cinnamon

3 tablespoons light brown sugar, or to taste

1 tablespoon finely minced ginger or ginger paste

1 tablespoon sesame oil

½ cup plant-based butter or grass-fed butter, melted

½ cup (25 grams) pitted and chopped jujube dates

¼ cup (25 grams) goji berries

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

2. Place all the dry ingredients, except the jujube dates and goji berries, into a large bowl and mix. Once well combined, incorporate the ginger, sesame oil, and melted butter and toss until the dry ingredients are evenly coated, then spread the mixture in a single layer on a half baking sheet lined with parchment paper.

3. Place the baking sheet in the oven and bake the granola until golden brown, about 20 minutes. Midway through baking, give the mix a stir to ensure even toasting. Three minutes before the end of baking, add the jujube dates and goji berries and continue to bake. Keep a close eye on the granola and berries in the last 3 minutes because they can easily burn at this stage.

4. Remove the sheet from the oven and let the granola cool completely. Enjoy with yogurt, milk, or sweet porridge. Store at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 6 months.

title: Poached Pear with Tofu Cream
author: Zoey Xinyi Gong
body:
润肤药膳炖梨配豆腐奶油

Gluten-free ◦ Nut-free

Five Elements:

Seasonality: Dry

Energetics: Neutral, Cooling

Meridian Affinity: Lung, Heart, Stomach

Functions: Yin Nourishing, Calming, Cooling

A poached pear is one of the best things you can have when you are experiencing Dryness symptoms. In this recipe, rather than using wine as a poaching liquid, I substituted a beautiful blend of Yin-nourishing herbs like glehnia root, coix seeds, lily bulb, and Solomon’s seal to strengthen the hydrating quality of the pear.
