1 large red onion, finely chopped

3 cups (700ml) Vegetable Broth 2.0 (here)

1½ tablespoons white miso paste blended with ¼ cup (60ml) hot water

1 cup (120g) finely chopped red bell pepper

2 cups (320g) fresh or thawed frozen corn kernels

2 teaspoons Savory Spice Blend 2.0 (here)

2 teaspoons fresh lemon juice

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

2 tablespoons pepitas

2 tablespoons chopped cilantro (optional)

4 cups (120g) chopped arugula

Rinse and drain the soaked sorghum, then transfer it to a medium saucepan. Add the red onion and Vegetable Broth 2.0. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat to low, cover, and simmer for 45 to 60 minutes, stirring frequently, or until the sorghum is just tender. Stir in the miso mixture, bell pepper, corn, and Savory Spice Blend 2.0. Cover and cook for about 10 minutes longer, or until the sorghum and vegetables are tender. Transfer to a serving bowl and add the lemon juice, pippali, pepitas, and cilantro (if using). Fluff with a fork, top with the arugula, and serve.

title: SAVORY POLENTA BAKE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: MODERATE

1 cup (155g) medium or coarse cornmeal

5 cups (1.2L) water or Vegetable Broth 2.0 (here)

4 cups (180g) chopped Swiss chard leaves

2 garlic cloves, minced, or 2 teaspoons Roasted Garlic (here)

1 tablespoon white miso paste blended with ¼ cup (60ml) hot water

1 cup (150g) cherry tomatoes, quartered

½ teaspoon dried basil

¼ teaspoon dried oregano

¼ teaspoon ground fennel seeds

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

Drizzle of Balsamic Syrup (here; optional)

Place the cornmeal in a large, deep saucepan. Stir in the water, then cover and set aside at room temperature overnight.

Place the saucepan over medium-high heat. Bring to a boil, stirring frequently, until the polenta begins to thicken. Lower the heat to medium. Stir in the chard leaves, garlic, miso mixture, tomatoes, basil, oregano, fennel seeds, and pippali. Continue to cook, stirring frequently and scraping the bottom of the saucepan to prevent scorching, until the polenta thickens and pulls away from the sides of the saucepan, about 45 minutes. The polenta should be smooth. If there are any lumps, beat them with a whisk until the consistency is smooth. If the polenta becomes too firm or begins to set, stir in a small amount of water.

Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Transfer the polenta mixture to a shallow baking dish. Smooth the top of the polenta until it’s even. Bake, uncovered, until golden brown on top, 15 to 20 minutes. Drizzle each portion with Balsamic Syrup (if using) and serve hot.

Variations: For a Curry Flavor: Add a chopped red bell pepper, a tablespoon of curry powder, and ½ teaspoon of ground fenugreek seeds, and omit the basil and oregano.

For Stuffing: Add minced onions and celery along with ½ teaspoon each of dried sage and thyme.

For a Southwestern Flair: Add a chopped red bell pepper, minced jalapeños, fresh or thawed frozen corn, chopped fresh cilantro, and ½ teaspoon of ground cumin.

title: THREE-GRAIN LOAF
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: MODERATE

1 large red onion, finely chopped

1 large celery rib, minced

4 garlic cloves, minced

1 large carrot, finely grated

⅓ cup (60g) raw barley, rinsed well and drained, or 1 cup (180g) cooked

⅓ cup (60g) raw millet, rinsed well and drained, or 1 cup (180g) cooked

⅓ cup (60g) raw quinoa, rinsed well and drained, or 1 cup (180g) cooked

½ cup (50g) chopped or coarsely crushed walnut or pecan pieces

2 tablespoons ground flaxseeds

2 tablespoons nutritional yeast

1⅓ cup (80g) finely chopped fresh parsley

2 teaspoons Savory Spice Blend 2.0 (here)

½ teaspoon ground thyme

½ teaspoon ground sage

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

¼ teaspoon sodium-free salt substitute (optional)

⅓ cup (40g) whole-grain bread crumbs, or more as needed

2 tablespoons Umami Sauce 2.0 (here)

IF USING RAW GRAINS: In a saucepan, bring 3 cups (700ml) of water to a boil. Add the red onion, celery, garlic, and carrot. Cover and cook until softened, about 5 minutes. Add the barley, cover, and cook for 15 minutes. Stir in the millet and cook for 15 minutes longer. Rinse the quinoa, then stir it into the saucepan and continue to cook for 10 minutes longer or until all the grains are tender. Drain any remaining liquid and set aside to cool.

IF USING COOKED GRAINS: In a small saucepan, combine ¼ cup (60ml) of water with the onion, celery, garlic, and carrot. Cover and cook for 5 minutes, or until tender. Drain any remaining water. Add the cooked grains, then set aside.

Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). In a large bowl, combine the walnuts, flaxseeds, nutritional yeast, parsley, Savory Spice Blend 2.0, thyme, sage, pippali, and sodium-free salt substitute (if using). Add the cooked grain mixture and the cooked vegetables to the bowl. Add the bread crumbs and stir to mix well. If the mixture is too wet to hold together, add additional bread crumbs, a little at a time, until it holds together and you can form a loaf.

Transfer the mixture to a parchment paper–lined 9-inch (23-cm) loaf pan. Press the mixture into the pan and smooth out the top of the loaf. Bake until firm, about 35 minutes. Remove from the oven and let stand at room temperature for 15 minutes, then place a cutting board on top of the loaf pan and flip it over. Remove the pan and parchment paper from the loaf. Rub the top and sides of the loaf with the Umami Sauce 2.0 before slicing and serving.

title: FARRO AND WHITE BEANS WITH RADICCHIO AND BASIL PESTO
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1 cup (165g) raw farro, or 3 cups (600g) cooked

1 medium red onion, chopped

½ cup (120ml) Basil Pesto (recipe below), or more

1½ cups (375g) salt-free cannellini beans, home-cooked or from BPA-free cans or Tetra Paks, drained and rinsed

1 head radicchio, chopped

Ground pippali or black pepper

IF USING RAW FARRO: Add 3 cups (700ml) of water to a saucepan and bring to a boil over high heat. Add the farro and red onion. Lower the heat to medium, cover, and simmer for 40 to 45 minutes, or until the farro is tender. Transfer to a serving bowl and set aside or refrigerate until needed.

IF USING COOKED FARRO: In a small saucepan, add ¼ cup (60ml) of water and the onion, cooking until it is softened, about 5 minutes. In a serving bowl, combine the onion with the cooked farro, and set aside or refrigerate until needed.

Make the Basil Pesto, then add ½ cup (120ml) of it to the cooked farro. Stir in the beans, radicchio, and pippali, to taste. Toss to combine, adding a little more pesto, if needed, and serve.

MAKES: ABOUT 1½ CUPS (350ML) DIFFICULTY: EASY

2 to 3 garlic cloves, crushed

⅓ cup (25g) nutritional yeast

3 tablespoons walnut pieces

2 tablespoons cashews

1 tablespoon white miso paste

3 cups (90g) packed fresh basil leaves

2 teaspoons lemon juice (optional)

In a food processor, combine the garlic, nutritional yeast, walnuts, and cashews, and process to a paste. Add the miso paste, basil leaves, ¼ cup (60ml) of water, and lemon juice (if using), and process until smooth and combined.

title: KASHA WITH PURPLE SWEET POTATOES AND KALE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 TO 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

2 large purple sweet potatoes, peeled and cut into ½-inch (1-cm) dice

1 medium red onion, chopped

1 medium red bell pepper, cored, seeded, and chopped

½ teaspoon onion powder

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

1½ cups (350ml) Vegetable Broth 2.0 (here) or water

1 cup (180g) medium-grain roasted kasha

4 cups (85g) chopped kale, stems removed

1½ cups (370g) salt-free chickpeas, home-cooked or from BPA-free cans or Tetra Paks, drained and rinsed

1 tablespoon white miso paste blended with 2 tablespoons hot water

2 teaspoons Savory Spice Blend 2.0 (here)

Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Spread the sweet potatoes, red onion, and bell pepper on a parchment paper–lined rimmed baking sheet. Season with the onion powder and pippali, and roast until tender, about 25 minutes, stirring once about halfway through.

Meanwhile, in a saucepan, heat the Vegetable Broth 2.0 over medium heat. Stir in the kasha and bring to a boil. Lower the heat to a simmer, then stir in the kale. Cover and simmer until the kasha is cooked, about 10 minutes. (If cooked longer, the grains tend to get mushy). Drain off any remaining liquid. Stir in the chickpeas, miso mixture, and Savory Spice Blend 2.0.

In a serving bowl, combine the cooked kasha and kale with the roasted vegetables. Stir gently to combine. This dish is equally good served hot or at room temperature.

* Be sure to buy toasted (or roasted) kasha, not raw kasha, which takes considerably longer to cook and isn’t as readily available. The one I buy is labeled “Organic Whole Grain Kasha–Roasted Buckwheat Kernels.”

title: BLACK RICE PILAF WITH EDAMAME AND BARBERRIES
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

⅓ cup (40g) dried barberries

1 medium red onion, finely chopped

½ teaspoon ground turmeric

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

1 teaspoon Savory Spice Blend 2.0 (here)

1 cup (120g) cooked shelled edamame

3 cups (525g) cooked black rice

2 scallions (green and white parts), chopped

½ cup (40g) slivered almonds

3 tablespoons minced fresh parsley or cilantro

Place the barberries in a small bowl with enough hot water to cover. Set aside for about 10 minutes to plump up.

In a large skillet or wok, heat ¼ cup (60ml) of water over medium heat. Add the red onion and cook, stirring frequently, until tender, about 5 minutes. Stir in the turmeric, pippali, and Savory Spice Blend 2.0, and cook for about 5 more minutes, stirring often. Add the edamame, rice, and scallions. Cook, stirring, for 5 additional minutes. Drain the barberries, then stir them into the rice mixture along with the almonds. Transfer the pilaf to a serving bowl. Sprinkle with the parsley and serve.

title: PROVENÇAL-STYLE VEGETABLE BAKE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 TO 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1 medium red onion, halved lengthwise and chopped

2 garlic cloves, minced

4 medium red potatoes, scrubbed, unpeeled, and cut into ¼-inch (0.5-cm) slices

1 Japanese eggplant, trimmed, halved lengthwise, and cut into ¼-inch (0.5-cm) slices

3 small zucchini, cut into ¼-inch (0.5-cm) slices

3 plum tomatoes, cut into ¼-inch (0.5-cm) slices

1 teaspoon white miso paste blended with 2 tablespoons hot water

1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves, or 1 teaspoon dried

1 teaspoon dried marjoram

½ teaspoon onion powder

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

¼ teaspoon sodium-free salt substitute (optional)

¼ cup (30g) Nutty Parm 2.0 (here)

¼ cup (30g) wheat germ or whole-grain bread crumbs

Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C). In a medium skillet, heat ¼ cup (60ml) of water over medium heat. Add the red onion and cook, stirring, to soften, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and cook for 1 minute longer. Spread the onion mixture evenly on the bottom of a 9 or 10-inch (23 or 25-cm) baking dish.

Spread the potato slices evenly on top of the onion mixture, followed by the eggplant, zucchini, and tomatoes.

Pour the miso mixture over the vegetables. Sprinkle with the thyme, marjoram, onion powder, and pippali. Cover the dish and bake until the vegetables are tender, about 45 minutes, then uncover and roast for 15 to 20 minutes longer, to cook off any liquid. Remove the dish from the oven, sprinkle the top of the vegetables with the sodium-free salt substitute (if using), Nutty Parm 2.0, and wheat germ. Return the dish to the oven, and bake, uncovered, for about 5 minutes longer. Serve hot.

title: ROASTED ROOT VEGETABLES WITH BALSAMIC SYRUP
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1 small red onion, diced

1 large carrot, diced

1 large parsnip, diced

1 small purple sweet potato, diced

1 small orange sweet potato, diced

1 medium red beet, diced

3 garlic cloves, crushed

1 tablespoon white miso paste blended with ¼ cup (60ml) hot water

1 teaspoon Savory Spice Blend 2.0 (here)

½ teaspoon onion powder

½ teaspoon dried marjoram

½ teaspoon dried thyme

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

¼ cup (60ml) Balsamic Syrup (here)

1 tablespoon minced fresh parsley, thyme, or other fresh herb

Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C). Line one or two large rimmed baking sheets with parchment paper and set aside.

In a large bowl, combine all the vegetables, red onion through garlic. Pour the miso mixture over the veggies, then add the Savory Spice Blend 2.0, onion powder, marjoram, thyme, and pippali. Toss lightly to coat the vegetables with the herbs and spices.

Transfer the seasoned vegetables to the prepared baking sheet(s), spreading them out in a single layer. Roast until tender and beginning to brown, about 45 minutes, turning once about halfway through.

To serve, transfer the vegetables to a large serving bowl, drizzle with the Balsamic Syrup, and sprinkle with the fresh parsley. Serve hot.

title: BRAISED RED CABBAGE WITH APPLES AND WALNUTS
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 TO 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1½ pounds (700g) shredded red cabbage

1 small red onion, minced

2 Granny Smith apples, cored and diced

2 teaspoons grated fresh ginger

¼ cup (60ml) apple cider vinegar

1 tablespoon date sugar

Ground pippali or black pepper

2 teaspoons white miso paste blended with ¼ cup (60ml) hot water

⅓ cup (35g) walnut pieces

In a large saucepan, heat ¼ cup (60ml) of water over medium heat. Add the cabbage and red onion, cover, and cook until slightly softened, about 5 minutes. Add the apples and ginger, then stir in the vinegar, date sugar, and pippali to taste.

Lower the heat to low, cover, and simmer, stirring frequently, until the cabbage and apples are tender, about 20 minutes. Stir in the miso mixture. If the vegetables begin to stick to the pan, add a little more water, 1 tablespoon at a time. When ready to serve, stir in the walnuts and enjoy.

title: GARLICKY MASHED POTATOES WITH CHARD
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

2½ pounds (1kg) Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into chunks

4 cups (180g) finely chopped Swiss chard

⅓ cup (80ml) warm unsweetened soy milk

1 tablespoon white miso paste

1 head Roasted Garlic (here)

1½ teaspoons Savory Spice Blend 2.0 (here)

Ground pippali or black pepper

In a pot of boiling water, cook the potatoes until tender, about 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, steam the chard in a metal steamer basket over an inch (2.5cm) or so of boiling water in a covered saucepan or pot until tender, 3 to 4 minutes. Drain well, press out any remaining water, and set aside.

In a small bowl or cup, combine the warm soy milk with the miso paste and blend well.

When the potatoes are soft, drain them and return them to the pot. Add the miso mixture, Roasted Garlic, Savory Spice Blend 2.0, and pippali to taste, then mash well. Fold in the chard. Serve hot.

title: BROCCOLI WITH SESAME–MISO SAUCE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1 tablespoon Roasted Garlic (here)

¼ cup (60g) tahini

1 tablespoon white miso paste

1 tablespoon rice vinegar

1 teaspoon date sugar

4 to 5 cups (360 to 450g) small broccoli florets

1 tablespoon white or black sesame seeds, for garnish

In a blender, combine the Roasted Garlic, tahini, miso paste, vinegar, date sugar, and 3 tablespoons of water, and blend until smooth. For a thinner sauce, add a little more water, 1 tablespoon at a time, until your desired consistency is reached. Set aside.

Lightly steam the broccoli in a metal steamer basket over an inch (2.5cm) or so of boiling water in a covered saucepan or pot until it’s bright green and just tender, about 5 minutes. Transfer the broccoli to a serving bowl, spoon the sauce over it, sprinkle with the sesame seeds, and serve.

title: GREEN BEANS AND GRAPE TOMATOES WITH GARLIC AND PINE NUTS
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

¼ cup (35g) pine nuts

1 cup (150g) grape tomatoes, halved lengthwise

1 head Roasted Garlic (here)

1 pound (450g) green beans, trimmed

2 tablespoons torn fresh basil leaves

2 tablespoons Balsamic Syrup (here)

Ground pippali or black pepper

In a small skillet, spread out the pine nuts and cook over medium heat, stirring until golden, about 4 minutes. Stir in the tomatoes and Roasted Garlic, then cook until fragrant, about 3 minutes. Remove from the heat and set aside.

Steam the green beans in a metal steamer basket over an inch (2.5cm) or so of boiling water in a covered saucepan or pot until just tender, about 8 minutes. Transfer the cooked green beans to a large serving bowl. Add the pine nut mixture, basil leaves, Balsamic Syrup, and pippali to taste, then toss to combine. Serve warm.

title: ROASTED ASPARAGUS WITH TAHINI LEMON SAUCE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1½ pounds (680g) asparagus

2 garlic cloves, minced

3 tablespoons fresh lemon juice

3 tablespoons tahini

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast

1 tablespoon white miso paste

Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C).

Line a baking sheet with parchment paper and arrange the asparagus in a single layer. Roast the asparagus until tender, 6 to 8 minutes, depending on its thickness.

Meanwhile, in a blender, combine the garlic and lemon juice, and blend until smooth. Then add the tahini, nutritional yeast, and miso paste, and blend again until the sauce is smooth and creamy. Add water, 1 tablespoon at a time until the sauce is as thin or thick as you prefer. Taste to adjust the seasonings, if needed.

Transfer the roasted asparagus to a platter and spoon on as much of the sauce as desired. Serve hot. Transfer any remaining sauce to a small, covered container and refrigerate until needed.

title: INDIAN-INSPIRED SPICED CAULIFLOWER
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 TO 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1 large head cauliflower, cut into small florets

⅓ cup (50g) grated onion

2 teaspoons grated ginger

1 teaspoon minced garlic

¼ cup (60g) tomato puree

1 tablespoon ground coriander

2 teaspoons curry powder

½ teaspoon ground black cumin

½ teaspoon ground turmeric

½ teaspoon ground fenugreek seeds (optional)

⅛ teaspoon ground cayenne, or more to taste

1 tablespoon white miso paste blended with ¼ cup (60ml) hot water

¼ cup (30g) chopped cashews

3 tablespoons chopped fresh cilantro

Steam the cauliflower in a metal steamer basket over an inch (2.5cm) or so of boiling water in a covered saucepan or pot until just tender, about 5 minutes. Set aside.

In a large skillet, heat ¼ cup (60ml) of water over medium heat. Add the onion, ginger, and garlic, then cook, stirring until softened, about 5 minutes. Do not burn. Stir in the tomato puree, coriander, curry powder, black cumin, turmeric, fenugreek seeds (if using), and cayenne.

Add the cauliflower and cook, stirring until the cauliflower is coated with the spice mixture. If the mixture is too dry, add a small amount of water, 1 tablespoon at a time. Lower the heat to low, stir in the miso mixture, cover, and cook until the cauliflower is hot, about 3 minutes. Serve hot, garnished with the cashews and cilantro.

title: ROASTED BRUSSELS SPROUTS WITH PECANS AND SHALLOTS
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

½ cup (50g) pecan halves

1 tablespoon Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

1 pound (450g) Brussels sprouts, trimmed and halved lengthwise

3 or 4 small shallots, quartered lengthwise

1 tablespoon fresh lemon juice

1 teaspoon Savory Spice Blend 2.0 (here)

¼ teaspoon ground pippali or black pepper

Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

In a small bowl, combine the pecans with the Date Syrup 2.0 and stir to coat the nuts. Set aside.

Spread the Brussels sprouts and shallots in a single layer on the prepared baking sheet. Roast in the oven until they are just tender and slightly browned, about 10 minutes (or longer, depending on the size of your Brussels sprouts). About 5 minutes before the end of the cooking time, stir in the pecan mixture.

Transfer the roasted Brussels sprouts, shallots, and pecans to a serving bowl. Add the lemon juice, Savory Spice Blend 2.0, and pippali. Toss gently to combine. Serve hot.

title: SPAGHETTI SQUASH WITH EDAMAME AND BASIL PISTOU
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 TO 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: MODERATE

1 spaghetti squash (about 4 pounds/2kg)

1 head Roasted Garlic (here)

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast

1 tablespoon white miso paste

3 cups (90g) fresh basil leaves

1½ cups (180g) cooked shelled edamame

Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C).

Using a sharp paring knife, pierce the spaghetti squash in about five different places around the vegetable. Place the whole squash on a rimmed baking sheet or in a baking dish.

Roast the squash for 35 to 45 minutes, turning once about halfway through. The squash is done when it is easily pierced with a fork and the skin begins to turn golden brown.

Meanwhile, in a food processor or blender, combine the Roasted Garlic, nutritional yeast, miso paste, and basil leaves, and blend until combined. Add water, 1 tablespoon at a time, pulsing after each addition, until the desired texture is reached for the basil pistou. Set aside.

Remove the roasted squash from the oven, and when cool enough to handle, cut it in half crosswise. Scoop out the seeds and discard, then use a fork to scrape out the flesh into long strands, placing them in a bowl. Discard the skin.

Add the cooked edamame and basil pistou to the squash strands and toss gently to combine. Serve at once.

title: MIXED BERRY CRUMBLE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 TO 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

2¼ cups (400g) fresh or frozen mixed berries

2 teaspoons lemon juice

1 tablespoon date sugar

2 tablespoons chia seeds

1 cup (100g) rolled oats

½ cup (55g) almond flour

¼ cup (75g) almond butter

¼ cup (60ml) Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

¼ cup (25g) walnut pieces (optional)

1 teaspoon vanilla extract

1 teaspoon grated lemon zest, for garnish (optional)

FOR THE FILLING: Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). In a saucepan, combine all the berries and place over medium heat, stirring and crushing the fruit. Cook until the berries are bubbling, 5 minutes. Turn off the heat and stir in the lemon juice, date sugar, and chia seeds. Set aside to let the mixture thicken. Spread the berry filling into the bottom of an 8-inch (20-cm) baking dish. Set aside.

FOR THE CRUMBLE TOPPING: In a food processor, combine all the ingredients except for the lemon zest, from rolled oats to vanilla extract, and pulse until well mixed and crumbly.

Sprinkle the topping over the berry filling. Bake for 20 minutes, or until the topping is golden brown and the filling is bubbling. Remove from the oven and let the crumble cool completely before serving. Garnish with lemon zest (if using).

title: BLUEBERRY CHIA PIE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: MODERATE

¾ cup (190g) pitted dates

1¼ cups (150g) walnut pieces

4 cups fresh (600g) or frozen (620g) blueberries

¼ cup (55g) date sugar

3 tablespoons chia seeds

2 teaspoons fresh lemon juice

FOR THE CRUST: If your dates are not soft, soak them in a bowl for 10 minutes with enough hot water to cover them, then drain well before using. In a food processor, combine the dates and walnuts and process until finely ground. The mixture should be crumbly and beginning to stick together. Press the mixture into the bottom and sides of a 9-inch (23-cm) pie plate. Set aside.

FOR THE FILLING: In a medium saucepan over medium-high heat, combine half the blueberries with ⅓ cup (80ml) of water and the date sugar. Stir to mix well. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered and stirring occasionally, for about 5 minutes, or until the berries begin to break down. Remove the saucepan from the heat. Stir in the chia seeds, lemon juice, and remaining blueberries. Set aside to cool slightly, then evenly spread the berry filling over the prepared crust. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours to allow the filling to set. Cover tightly and store in the refrigerator for up to 4 days, or in the freezer for up to 3 weeks.

title: MOLASSES SPICE COOKIES
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: ABOUT 12 COOKIES DIFFICULTY: MODERATE

⅓ cup (80ml) blackstrap (dark) molasses

⅓ cup (80ml) Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

2 tablespoons almond butter

½ teaspoon pure vanilla extract

1 cup (110g) almond flour

1 cup (120g) oat flour

1 teaspoon aluminum- and sodium-free baking powder

1 teaspoon ground ginger

1 teaspoon ground cinnamon

¼ teaspoon ground allspice

In a large bowl, combine the molasses, Date Syrup 2.0, almond butter, vanilla, and 2 tablespoons of water. Stir until smooth and well blended. Set aside.

In a medium bowl, combine the almond flour, oat flour, baking powder, ginger, cinnamon, and allspice. Mix well. Slowly add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients, stirring to mix well. If the mixture is too dry to form into smooth balls, add more water,* 1 tablespoon at a time. If the dough becomes too wet, add a bit more flour. Chill the dough for 30 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Line one or two baking sheets with parchment paper.

Scoop out 1 tablespoon of the dough and roll it between your hands to shape it into a ball. Place the dough ball on the prepared baking sheet. Repeat until all the cookie dough has been used, making about twelve balls, spaced about 2 inches (5cm) apart on the sheet.

Wet your fingers and gently press each cookie to flatten the dough into a disk about ¼ inch (0.5cm) thick. Bake until the bottom edges are slightly browned, 10 to 12 minutes. Remove from the oven and set aside to cool for about 10 minutes. The cookies will continue to firm up as they cool. When completely cooled, use a metal spatula to transfer the cookies to a plate to serve, or store them in a covered container until ready to enjoy.

VARIATIONS:

* Because the consistencies of molasses, almond butter, and homemade Date Syrup 2.0 can vary, you will need to monitor the amount of additional water, using it only if the dough is too dry.

title: BETTER PECAN SQUARES
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 9 SQUARES DIFFICULTY: EASY

2 very ripe medium bananas, cut into chunks

1 tablespoon almond butter

1½ tablespoons date sugar or Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

2 cups (200g) old-fashioned rolled oats

1 teaspoon aluminum- and sodium-free baking powder

⅓ cup (35g) coarsely chopped pecans

3 tablespoons goji berries

9 pecan halves (optional)

Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Line an 8-inch (20-cm) square baking pan with parchment paper and set aside.

In a food processor, combine the banana chunks, almond butter, date sugar, and 2 tablespoons (30ml) of water, then process until well blended. Add the oats, baking powder, pecans, and goji berries, and pulse to incorporate, adding a little more water if the mixture is too dry. The dough should be fairly stiff.

Transfer the mixture to the prepared baking pan and press it evenly into the pan, smoothing the top. If desired, press the pecan halves into the top of the mixture, in three rows of three. Bake for 15 minutes, then remove from the oven and set aside to cool for at least 15 minutes. When ready to serve, cut into squares and enjoy.

title: BANANA–WALNUT CAKE WITH BLACKBERRY–ALMOND BUTTER SAUCE
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 9 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: MODERATE

1 tablespoon ground flaxseeds

1½ cups (340g) mashed ripe bananas (2 to 3 large bananas)

¼ cup (60ml) unsweetened soy milk

¼ cup (60ml) Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

1 teaspoon fresh lemon juice

1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract

1 cup (110g) almond flour

½ cup (60g) oat flour

1½ teaspoons aluminum- and sodium-free baking powder

½ teaspoon ground cinnamon

½ cup (55g) coarsely crushed walnuts

Blackberry–Almond Butter Sauce (recipe below; optional)

In a small cup or bowl, combine the flaxseeds and 2 tablespoons of warm water. Stir well, then set aside for 10 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Line an 8-inch (20-cm) square baking pan with parchment paper.

In a large bowl, combine the mashed bananas, soy milk, Date Syrup 2.0, lemon juice, vanilla, and flaxseed mixture. Mix well.

Whisk in the almond flour, oat flour, baking powder, and cinnamon until evenly mixed. Fold in the walnuts. If the batter is too thick, stir in a little more soy milk, 1 tablespoon at a time.

Transfer the cake batter into the prepared baking pan and smooth the top. Bake for about 30 minutes, or until lightly browned on top.

Remove the pan from the oven and set aside to cool completely. Once cool, invert the cake onto a plate. Cut the cake into squares and place each serving on a small dessert plate. Spoon some of the Blackberry–Almond Butter Sauce (recipe follows) over each serving (if using).

MAKES: ABOUT 1 CUP (235ML) DIFFICULTY: EASY

¾ cup (110g) fresh or thawed frozen blackberries

¼ cup (60ml) unsweetened soy milk

3 tablespoons almond butter

3 tablespoons Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

1 teaspoon fresh lemon juice

In a blender or food processor, combine all the ingredients and puree until smooth. Use it as is, or cover and refrigerate until needed. The sauce may thicken after sitting awhile, so stir it before using and add up to 1 additional tablespoon of soy milk to thin it, if desired.

title: MOCHA CHIA PUDDING
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

¼ cup (20g) unsweetened cocoa powder

½ cup (120ml) Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

¾ cup (180ml) unsweetened soy milk

¾ cup (180ml) strong brewed coffee

1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract

⅓ cup (80g) chia seeds

In a bowl, combine the cocoa powder with the Date Syrup 2.0, and stir to blend well. Slowly add the soy milk, stirring until smooth. Stir in the coffee and vanilla. Add the chia seeds, then stir to combine well.

Transfer the pudding to individual dessert bowls. Cover and refrigerate for at least 3 hours to thicken. The longer it sits, the firmer it gets. Serve chilled.

title: COCOA–ALMOND BUTTER COOKIES
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 12 TO 16 COOKIES DIFFICULTY: EASY

1 large very ripe banana, mashed well

1 cup (120g) oat flour

¼ cup (30g) almond flour

¼ cup (60ml) Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

¼ cup (75g) almond butter

3 tablespoons unsweetened cocoa powder

1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract

12 walnut halves (optional)

Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Line a rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper and set aside.

In a large bowl, combine the mashed banana, oat flour, almond flour, Date Syrup 2.0, almond butter, cocoa powder, and vanilla. Stir well until thoroughly mixed. Scoop out 1 tablespoon of the dough and roll it between your hands to shape it into a ball. Place the dough ball on the prepared baking sheet. Repeat until all the cookie dough has been used, with the twelve to sixteen balls spaced about 2 inches (5cm) apart on the baking sheet.

Wet your fingers and gently press each ball to flatten the dough into a disk about ¼ inch (0.5cm) thick. Press a walnut half into the center of each disk (if using).

Bake for 12 to 15 minutes, or until lightly browned and set. Remove from the oven. Let the cookies cool completely before carefully removing them from the baking sheet with a metal spatula. If not serving right away, store in an air-tight container at room temperature for up to 3 days, in the refrigerator for up to 1 week, or in the freezer for up to 3 months.

title: COFFEE GRANITA
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 4 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

½ cup (120ml) Date Syrup 2.0 (here)

2 cups (470ml) strong brewed coffee, cooled

In a saucepan, combine the Date Syrup 2.0 and ⅓ cup (80ml) of water, and bring to a boil. Lower the heat to medium and cook, stirring, to blend well. Remove the saucepan from the heat and set it aside to cool. Stir in the coffee, then pour the mixture into a shallow baking dish. Cover and freeze for several hours, or until firm, stirring about once per hour.

When firm, remove the granita from the freezer. Scrape it with the tines of a fork until it is broken up. Spoon the granita into a container, cover, and freeze until serving time. Serve in small bowls. For the best taste and texture, enjoy it within a few hours after it is made.

title: QUINOA PUDDING WITH MANGO
book: The How Not to Age Cookbook
author: Michael Greger
body:
MAKES: 6 SERVINGS DIFFICULTY: EASY

1 cup (180g) quinoa

3 cups (700ml) unsweetened soy milk

½ cup (110g) date sugar

1 teaspoon ground cinnamon

1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract

½ cup (40g) slivered or sliced almonds

1 ripe mango, peeled, pitted, and chopped

6 raspberries, for garnish (optional)

6 fresh mint leaves, for garnish (optional)

Rinse the quinoa in a fine-mesh strainer, then soak in water for about 10 minutes before rinsing again and draining. Transfer the quinoa to a saucepan. Add the soy milk, date sugar, and 1 cup (235ml) of water, then bring to a boil. Lower the heat to low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the quinoa is tender and the liquid is mostly absorbed, 25 to 30 minutes.

Remove the saucepan from the heat, then stir in the cinnamon, vanilla, almonds, and mango. Set aside to cool to room temperature, then spoon the quinoa pudding into shallow dessert bowls and garnish each serving with a raspberry and mint leaf (if using). Serve at room temperature or refrigerate for about 2 hours to serve chilled.

title: Apple Balsamic Vinaigrette
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS

This dressing offers a perfect balance of sweet, sour, and savory. Make extra and keep it in the fridge—you’ll reach for it regularly—to use on salads like the Kale & Fennel Salad With Cherries (see here), crudités, and grain bowls.

½ cup apple cider

½ cup extra-virgin olive oil

¼ cup balsamic vinegar

¼ cup apple cider vinegar

4 teaspoons Dijon mustard

4 garlic cloves, grated or minced

2 teaspoons salt

1 teaspoon thyme

½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Whisk everything together in a medium bowl, or blend in blender, until smooth and emulsified. This will keep in the fridge in an airtight container for up to 2 weeks—just give it a good stir or shake before using.

title: Chamoy Sauce (see image here)
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS

Chamoy, a traditional Mexican condiment, packs a lot of flavor into a very attractive fuchsia-colored sauce. It’s amazing over fruit (try it on fresh mango slices), but the salt and chile make it work on savory dishes, too. You’ll see it called for to dress the Heirloom Tomato & Avocado Salad (see here). Pair it with the Vietnamese Peanut Sauce (see here) to make a pretty fabulous PB&J on sourdough bread.

1½ cups water

½ cup dried hibiscus flowers

½ cup dried apricots, chopped

¼ cup raisins

¼ cup honey

1 tablespoon umeboshi paste or miso paste

2 chiles de arbol, stems and seeds removed

1 teaspoon salt

¼ cup lime juice

Combine all the ingredients except the lime juice in a saucepan and bring to a boil. Lower the heat to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes.

Add the lime juice and use an immersion blender to blend thoroughly until you have a smooth sauce. (You can also use a regular blender for this step.) Store sealed in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.

title: Roasted Tomato Sauce
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 6 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 6 CUPS

This versatile sauce is a wonderful thing to keep on hand in the fridge or freezer. It’s great on pasta, pizza, and more. Roasting tomatoes and caramelizing the garlic concentrates their flavor and adds a nice smoky note to this rich, thick sauce.

½ cup fresh oregano sprigs

4 pounds ripe plum tomatoes, cut in half lengthwise, or whole cherry tomatoes (or a mix of both)

1 head garlic, cloves separated but papery skins left on

1 medium onion, quartered

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

2 teaspoons salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Arrange the oregano sprigs on a sheet pan, then put the tomatoes on top—cut side up for the plum tomatoes. Tuck the garlic cloves and onion chunks between the tomatoes so they’ll be sheltered a little from the heat. Drizzle the oil over the top of the tomatoes, then sprinkle on the salt and pepper.

Bake for 45 minutes, or until the tops or edges of the tomatoes start to blister and get some dark spots. Take the pan out of the oven and let contents cool.

When cool enough to handle, remove the garlic cloves and peel and discard the skins. Discard the oregano stems but keep the leaves. Blend the tomatoes, onion, peeled garlic, and oregano leaves until smooth in a bowl with an immersion blender or in a regular blender.

The sauce will keep in the fridge for a week or in the freezer for months.

If you want an extra-velvety result, strain the finished sauce through a sieve to remove any seeds. You can turn the strained sauce into a wonderful soup by mixing it in a 1:1 ratio with vegetable stock.

title: Slow Cooker Onion Jam
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 16 TO 18 HOURS MAKES 4 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 16 TO 18 HOURS MAKES 4 CUPS

Caramelizing onions unlocks an extraordinary complex sweetness; left alone, they form the base for onion soup. Adding sweet maple syrup and sour vinegar creates a superbly versatile condiment that’s wonderful as a chutney or relish. You can make this on the stove, but it takes two to three hours of attentive work to achieve. A slow cooker makes it very easy.

4 pounds yellow onions, peeled, halved, and cut into thin slivers

1 teaspoon salt

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil

½ cup maple syrup

¼ cup cider vinegar

¼ cup red wine

Set your slow cooker on low.

Put the onions, salt, and oil in the slow cooker, stir well, and let the mixture cook on low for 12 hours.

Stir in the maple syrup, vinegar, and wine and continue cooking for another 4 to 6 hours on low, until there’s just a little bit of liquid left. Let the jam cool, then store in the fridge for up to 2 weeks or in the freezer for months.

Each pound of onions results in about 1 cup of jam. Because the process takes a while, it’s worth making this much. Freeze leftovers in ice cube trays so you can store and defrost just what you need on short notice.

title: Vietnamese Peanut Sauce
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS

This condiment is superbly useful, not to mention very tasty. A match made in heaven for Sesame-Crusted Tofu Summer Rolls (see here), it’s also an excellent dip for vegetables, a sauce for Southern-Style Sheet Pan BBQ Tofu With Sweet Corn & Green Beans (see here), and a great base for an incredible peanut butter sandwich—try it on good whole-grain or sourdough bread with some sliced scallions and cilantro or Quick Pickled Veggies (see here).

½ cup smooth unsalted peanut butter

¼ cup water

Juice of 1 lime

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 tablespoon rice vinegar

2 teaspoons liquid aminos or fish sauce

1 teaspoon ginger, finely grated

1 teaspoon honey or maple syrup

1 teaspoon sriracha

1 garlic clove, finely grated

Put all the ingredients in a small bowl and stir, gently at first, until the mixture begins to emulsify. Then stir more vigorously until everything is thoroughly combined. This sauce is great right away, but it gets better after an hour or so, once the flavors have had time to marry.

Keep tightly covered in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.

Use peanut butter with no additives. The ingredients list on the jar should just say “peanuts.”

title: Red Pesto
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS

This tasty pesto borrows from two traditions: ajvar, a Balkan relish made from roasted red peppers, and muhammara, a Middle Eastern dip that’s thickened with walnuts. Our version is deeply savory and a little sweet and sour. It’s also an excellent way to incorporate more nuts into your diet. Think of it as a versatile alternative to hummus, one you’ll want to have around regularly. You can serve it with warm flatbread or crudités, or use it in wraps or sandwiches.

3 large red bell peppers

1 small Italian eggplant

¼ cup walnuts

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon red wine vinegar

½ teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

½ teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Set your oven to broil on high.

Put the whole peppers and eggplant on a sheet pan and put them under the broiler. Broil for about 20 minutes, turning the vegetables as each side gets black and blistered. Keep an eye on the veggies so they don’t burn. For the last 3 minutes or so, scatter the walnuts around the pan, toasting until fragrant.

Once the vegetables are nice and charred, remove them from the oven. Set the walnuts aside and put the peppers and eggplant in a bowl. Cover and let the veggies steam at least 10 minutes. When cool enough to handle, halve the eggplant lengthwise and scoop the flesh out, discarding the skin. Use a knife to scrape the skin off the peppers and remove the stem and seeds, and discard.

Put the eggplant flesh, peppers, and walnuts, along with all remaining ingredients, in a blender or food processor and blend, scraping sides regularly, until you have a thick, brick-colored puree. If it’s very thick, add a little more oil. Taste for seasoning and serve.

Store in the fridge for up to a week.

You’re looking for about a 2:1 ratio of peppers to eggplant after roasting them, but don’t worry if you don’t have exactly that amount—every vegetable size is different! This is a very flexible recipe; just make sure you taste and adjust the seasonings (particularly salt and vinegar) before serving.

title: Zhug (see image here)
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS

Zhug is a Middle Eastern condiment that beautifully pairs with a wide variety of dishes, including Middle Eastern Roasted Whole Cauliflower (see here). It’s bright, spicy, and delicious. Use it as you would pesto, hot sauce, or relish. Once you’ve tried it, you may find that you can’t live without it.

1 cup parsley leaves

1 cup cilantro leaves

2 garlic cloves, chopped

1 serrano pepper, seeded and chopped

½ teaspoon cumin seeds, toasted

½ teaspoon coriander seeds, toasted

½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Seeds from 1 cardamom pod (about 5 seeds)

½ teaspoon salt

½ cup extra-virgin olive oil

Put everything in a food processor and run it, stopping periodically to scrape down the sides of the bowl with a spatula, until you have a thick, pesto-like green sauce. If you want it slightly thinner, add a bit more oil.

Traditionally, zhug is made using a mortar and pestle; if you have a set, by all means make it that way! You’ll get a more interesting texture, and more important, you’ll experience a physical engagement with your food that promotes mindfulness in what you eat. Start by pounding the garlic and salt together, then pound in the spices, next add the chile and pound some more, and then work through the herbs a bit at a time, adding more as they get incorporated into the paste. Finish by stirring in the oil.

title: Hummus
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS

Hummus is high in fiber and protein thanks to chickpeas and tahini, married with a delicious blend of spices. You can amp up the flavors of your hummus with a variety of garnishes, including fresh herbs, roasted peppers, Garlic Confit (see here), and Zhug (above). Always finish with a drizzle of your best extra-virgin olive oil.

1½ cups cooked chickpeas

¼ cup tahini

3 tablespoons lemon juice

2 tablespoons ice water

2 garlic cloves, grated

½ teaspoon cumin seeds, toasted and ground

½ teaspoon salt

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil

OPTIONAL GARNISH

¼ cup Crispy Roasted Chickpeas (see here)

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

Put all the ingredients except the oil in a food processor and blend until completely smooth, scraping down the sides several times to ensure no lumps remain.

To serve, spread the hummus in a shallow bowl. Use the back of a spoon to make a depression in the center and pour in the oil. If using, sprinkle the roasted chickpeas on top and dust with the paprika.

You can use canned chickpeas for this, but soaking and cooking dried ones will give you a richer flavor. Cook them a day or two ahead for superquick prep when it’s time to eat.

title: Salsa Macha
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 CUP
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 CUP

This popular salsa can be called a Mexican version of chile crisp, and it has just as many uses as its Chinese cousin. You’ll want to have it on hand for the Spicy Creamy Pumpkin Soup (see here), the Yuba Noodle Stir-Fry With Chile Crisp (see here), and anything else that benefits from a sweet-sour-spicy kick—try it on a piece of whole-grain toast!

1½ cups avocado oil

6 ancho chiles, seeded and cut into pieces

4 guajillo chiles, seeded and cut into pieces

4 chiles de arbol, seeded and cut into pieces

6 garlic cloves, sliced

½ cup raw unsalted peanuts

¼ cup sesame seeds

1 bay leaf, crumbled

1 tablespoon apple cider vinegar

1 teaspoon maple syrup

1 teaspoon salt

1 teaspoon Mexican oregano

Heat the oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Add the chiles, garlic, and peanuts and cook until the garlic turns light brown, about 3 minutes. Be careful not to burn the garlic or chiles, as they will turn bitter.

Remove the pot from the heat and add the remaining ingredients, stirring well to combine. Let cool for at least 10 minutes, then blend with an immersion blender until you have a chunky mixture. (If you prefer it smoother, keep blending to your desired texture.)

Store the salsa in an airtight container for up to a month in the fridge.

Most of the heat in this salsa comes from the chiles de arbol. If you want it spicier, add more; if you want it milder, use fewer.

title: Salsa Verde
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 4 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 4 CUPS

This Mexican classic combines mouthwatering tanginess with some heat, a little smokiness, and addictive umami flavor from the tomatillos. If you want a spicier salsa, use serrano peppers instead of jalapeños. This salsa freezes very well, so you can make extra and have it on hand when you need it for making Touchdown Chili (see here).

2 pounds tomatillos

4 jalapeño peppers

1 cup cilantro, loosely packed

6 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped

Juice of 1 lime

1 teaspoon salt

Set your oven to broil on high. Put the whole tomatillos and jalapeños on a sheet pan; broil for about 20 minutes, flipping the vegetables halfway through. You want some nice blackening on the skins, but you don’t want anything to burn.

Remove the pan from the oven and put the jalapeños and tomatillos in a bowl, cover them, and let them steam for at least 10 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, use a knife to scrape the skin off and remove the seeds from both, discarding them.

Return the jalapeños and tomatillos to the bowl and add the remaining ingredients. Use an immersion blender to process everything together, until there are no large pieces of anything left. (You can also use a food processor for this step, using long pulses.) Taste for seasoning and serve, or store in the fridge for up to a week or in the freezer for months.

title: Coconut Raita
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS

Raita, an Indian condiment, is a refreshing yogurt sauce that’s typically used as a cooling counterweight to spicy curries. Coconut yogurt adds a tropical note to this traditional sauce, but don’t just serve this alongside Indian food; it works great with other spicy foods as well, such as Touchdown Chili (see here).

1 cup unsweetened coconut milk yogurt alternative

½ cup cucumber, seeded and diced (leave the peel on for color)

½ cup cilantro leaves, chopped, plus extra leaves for garnish

1 scallion, chopped

½ teaspoon garam masala

½ teaspoon salt

Combine all the ingredients in a small bowl and mix well. Garnish with the extra cilantro leaves and serve.

Raita will keep for about a week in the fridge.

title: Pikliz (see image here)
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 15 MINUTES, WITH 3 TO 48 HOURS MARINATING TIME MAKES ABOUT 4 CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 15 MINUTES, WITH 3 TO 48 HOURS MARINATING TIME MAKES ABOUT 4 CUPS

Pikliz is Haiti’s national condiment—a brightly colored, spicy pickled relish that is truly addictive. Try it with everything from Belizean Rice & Beans (see here) to Easy-Peasy Falafel (see here) to Mushroom & Black Bean Birria (see here). The flavor improves dramatically after a couple of days, so plan ahead!

2 cups green cabbage, finely shredded

1 carrot, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

1 red, orange, or yellow bell pepper, seeded and cut into thin strips

½ yellow or white onion, slivered

3 garlic cloves, sliced

3 scallions, sliced

1½ teaspoons salt

1 habanero pepper, seeded and cut into thin strips

2 whole allspice berries

3 cloves

½ teaspoon peppercorns

Juice of 1 lime

¼ cup apple cider vinegar

Put the cabbage, carrot, bell pepper, onion, garlic, scallions, and salt in a large bowl and toss well, kneading a bit until the vegetables begin to release some liquid.

Pack the vegetable mixture and remaining ingredients into a wide-mouth Mason jar; be sure vegetables are covered by the liquid, adding more vinegar if needed. Seal the jar and set in the fridge. It’s good after a few hours, but for optimal flavor, let the mixture mature in the fridge for 2 days. Pikliz will keep in an airtight container in the fridge for at least 3 weeks.

Habanero peppers are hot, so it’s a good idea to wear gloves when handling them and wash your hands well after preparing them.

title: Pico de Gallo
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 2 CUPS

This classic condiment adds bright flavor and a little heat to everything it touches. Serve it alongside beans, tacos, or roasted squash, or with tortilla chips as an appetizer. For the best flavor, use the freshest, ripest tomatoes you can find. If you want it milder, sub jalapeños for the serrano peppers.

1 pound tomatoes, diced into about ¼-inch pieces

1 small onion (about 4 ounces), diced into about ⅛-inch pieces

3 serrano peppers, seeded and diced into about ⅛-inch pieces (keep the seeds if you like heat!)

½ cup loosely packed cilantro leaves, chopped

Juice of 1 lime

½ teaspoon salt

Combine all the ingredients in a small bowl and mix well. Serve immediately or store in the fridge for about a week. The salt will pull moisture out of the vegetables over time, so always mix leftovers well before serving.

title: Tahini-Miso Sauce (see image here)
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 3 CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 3 CUPS

This simple combination yields serious flavor that works as a spread, a dip, or the base for more elaborate sauces. Plus, it’s packed with protein and probiotics, so it’s supernutritious. Use this condiment in place of mayo as a small step that can produce big results in terms of your health. (If you like heat, stir in a little hot sauce.)

1 cup tahini

1 cup white miso

Juice of 1 lemon

Put the tahini, miso, and lemon juice in a small bowl and gently whisk together. Add ½ cup of water and whisk until everything is fully combined and smooth. For a thinner consistency—say, to use it as a dressing—stir in a bit more water.

Store the sauce, tightly covered, in the fridge for up to a week.

Before you make your sauce, be sure the tahini hasn’t separated, with a layer of oil floating on top. If it has, take a minute or two to stir it until it’s fully combined.

title: Avocado-Herb Sauce
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS

This herbaceous sauce—a cross between green goddess dressing and guacamole—works as a dip, a condiment, or even a salsa. Try it with everything from tacos to salads to Crispy Salt & Pepper Oven Fries (see here).

1 ripe avocado, pitted

½ cup Italian parsley leaves

½ cup cilantro leaves

½ cup raw unsalted pistachios, soaked overnight in 1 cup water and drained, soaking water reserved

¼ cup unsweetened coconut milk yogurt alternative

2 tablespoons lime juice

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 garlic clove, chopped

1 jalapeño pepper, seeded and chopped

½ teaspoon salt

In a blender, blend all the ingredients together until smooth and velvety, adding a little of the pistachio water as needed to get the desired consistency—thicker for a dip, thinner for a dressing. Taste for seasoning, then serve.

This sauce will keep for about a week in an airtight container in the fridge. Give it a stir before using any leftovers.

If you like heat, use a serrano pepper (or two!) instead of the jalapeño.

title: Garlic Confit
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 2 HOURS MAKES ½ CUP CONFIT AND 1 CUP OIL
body:
COOK TIME: 2 HOURS MAKES ½ CUP CONFIT AND 1 CUP OIL

This simple recipe yields two terrific recipe enhancers: more flavorful garlic and garlic-infused oil. They’re wonderful on their own, and even more powerful together. Try spreading the cloves on toasted whole-grain or sourdough bread, or drizzling the oil over almost anything.

1 head garlic, cloves separated and peeled, flat ends trimmed

1 cup (or more) extra-virgin olive oil

Preheat your oven to 275°F.

Put the garlic in a small ovenproof dish, like a ramekin. Pour enough oil to cover the cloves by about ¼ inch. Place the dish in the oven and cook for 2 hours, until the garlic is golden brown and very soft. Let cool, making sure the garlic remains submerged in the oil. Store in the fridge for no more than a week.

Put a roasted clove or two in each compartment of an ice cube tray, fill the compartments with oil, and then put the tray in the freezer. Once solid, pop out the cubes and store them in a zip-top bag in the freezer to use as needed.

title: Garlic Confit Vinaigrette
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 CUP
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 CUP

Nice and creamy, this vinaigrette brightens everything it touches. Use it on salads, in sandwiches, or as a dip for a crudités platter.

¼ cup oil from Garlic Confit (see above)

¼ cup lemon juice

6 cloves garlic from Garlic Confit (see above)

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon red wine vinegar

1 teaspoon Dijon mustard

1 teaspoon honey

½ teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon thyme

½ teaspoon oregano

¼ cup parsley leaves

Using a blender or food processor, blend all the ingredients together until fully emulsified. The vinaigrette can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for about 1 week. Give it a stir or shake before using.

title: Black Tahini Dressing
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS

This dramatic-looking sauce has a creamy texture and wonderfully deep, earthy-nutty flavor. Black sesame seeds are higher in minerals and antioxidants than light ones, which are already powerhouses, so don’t be shy with this sauce. Use it on crudités, on sandwiches, or as a dip or dressing for the Easy-Peasy Falafel (see here) or Roasted Root Vegetable Medley (see here).

½ cup black sesame tahini

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil

¼ cup water

Zest and juice of ½ lemon

1 tablespoon honey

Whisk or blend everything together until you have a smooth, charcoal-gray sauce. This will keep in the fridge for 2 weeks or more in an airtight container.

title: Tex-Mex Breakfast Skillet
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

Our research found that Americans love Mexican and Tex-Mex flavors, even in their breakfasts. This delicious potato, bean, and veggie skillet offers those beloved spices—with loads of nutrition in every bite. It’s great as is in a bowl, and it also works wonderfully as the filling for a burrito.

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1½ pounds Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into roughly 1-inch cubes

1 medium onion, diced

1 red bell pepper, seeded and diced

¾ cup corn kernels (about 1 ear corn)

2 teaspoons Homemade Taco Seasoning (see below, or store-bought)

2 teaspoons salt

2 cups cooked black beans

¼ cup cilantro leaves, chopped, plus more for garnish

1 tablespoon lime juice

1 lime, cut into wedges, for garnish

Heat the oil in a cast-iron skillet or heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat until it starts to shimmer. Add the potatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until they’re nice and brown on all sides and beginning to get tender, about 10 minutes. Add the onion, pepper, and corn, and stir well, then add the taco seasoning and salt, stirring again so everything gets seasoned. Cook for another 10 minutes, stirring occasionally so nothing sticks to the pan or gets too brown.

When the potatoes are fork-tender, add the beans, cilantro, and lime juice; stir again to combine and cook until warmed through, about 5 to 10 minutes. Serve in bowls with lime wedges and cilantro on the side.

HOMEMADE TACO SEASONING

1 tablespoon chipotle powder

1 teaspoon dried Mexican oregano

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

½ teaspoon garlic powder

½ teaspoon onion powder

Combine all the ingredients and mix thoroughly.

You can make the taco seasoning in quantity ahead of time; it’ll keep in your spice cabinet for at least a month.

title: Smoky Southwestern Sweet Potato & Black Bean Hash
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This hearty skillet boasts two Blue Zones all-star ingredients: sweet potatoes and black beans. It’s a great way to start your day—or finish it!

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 white or yellow onion, diced

1 green bell pepper, seeded and diced

2 garlic cloves, sliced

½ teaspoon ground cumin

½ teaspoon ground coriander

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

2 teaspoons apple cider vinegar

1 teaspoon maple syrup

4 cups baked sweet potatoes (about 3 to 4 potatoes), peeled and cut into roughly 1-inch cubes*

2 cups cooked black beans

1½ teaspoons salt

1 scallion, sliced thin

* To quickly bake your sweet potatoes, rinse the potatoes in water and scrub dirt off skin, then pat dry thoroughly with a paper towel. Pierce the skin a few times with a fork, then place on a microwave-safe plate. Microwave for 5 minutes, turning halfway through. Potatoes are done when they are just fork-tender; cook in 30-second increments if they need more time.

Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the onion and pepper and sauté until soft, about 10 minutes. Add the garlic and sauté for 2 more minutes, then add the spices, stir well to combine, and cook for another minute.

Add the vinegar, maple syrup, sweet potatoes, beans, and salt, stirring gently to combine. Cook for 3 minutes, until everything is warmed through, then serve with scallions on top.

Leftovers make great tacos with Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here) and Pico de Gallo (see here).

title: Adventist Coconut Chia Pudding
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES 6 SERVINGS

Chia seeds are a staple of the Adventist diet in the Loma Linda, California, blue zone. These tiny but mighty seeds pack a punch of nutrition in an energy-boosting blend of omega-3 fats, fiber, protein, vitamins, and antioxidants. This smooth, creamy pudding makes for a healthy and bright start to the morning—or a decadent dessert at night.

1 cup coconut cream

1 cup coconut milk

3 tablespoons agave nectar or honey

½ teaspoon finely grated lemon zest

½ cup chia seeds

Whisk the coconut cream, coconut milk, agave nectar or honey, and lemon zest together in a medium bowl. Add the chia seeds and stir well.

Cover with plastic wrap and let the pudding sit in the refrigerator until thickened, at least 40 minutes or overnight.

When ready to eat, stir well and top with fruit, almonds, or other desired toppings.

title: ’Shroom & Bean “Grits”
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

If you like shrimp and grits—a favorite recipe in southern American cuisine—then this savory breakfast is for you. Millet is a tasty grain that’s high in fiber, protein, and good-for-you minerals like calcium and magnesium. Simply said: It’s an easy-to-cook whole grain worth adding to your rotation. Millet originated in China, so to pay homage, this dish features doubanjiang, a fermented spicy Chinese bean paste that gives it a great depth of flavor.

2 tablespoons avocado oil

2 large shallots, diced

2 cups shiitake mushroom caps, sliced

4 garlic cloves, sliced

2 teaspoons fresh ginger, grated

¼ cup doubanjiang (chile bean paste)

¼ cup rice vinegar

2 tablespoons soy sauce

2 tablespoons Chinese rice wine or sherry

2 cups millet

6 cups vegetable stock

2 cups cooked black beans

2 teaspoons sesame oil

2 scallions, sliced, for garnish

1 tablespoon sesame seeds, toasted, for garnish

Heat the oil in a deep pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the shallots and mushrooms and sauté until they begin to color, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute, then add the ginger and cook for 2 more minutes.

Add the doubanjiang and stir well, then add the vinegar, soy sauce, and wine or sherry, stirring to combine. Add the millet, stock, and beans, and stir well. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat to a simmer, cover the pot, and cook for 20 minutes. When the millet is tender, stir in the sesame oil.

Serve garnished with scallions and sesame seeds.

title: Sweet Potato Breakfast Bowls
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 5 TO 10 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS
body:
PREP TIME: 5 TO 10 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

These delicious, satisfying, and beautiful bowls come together very quickly if you bake the sweet potatoes the day before, or use the microwave (see here). You can also prepare the whipped base ahead of time and just heat and garnish it in the morning for a supereasy breakfast.

2 cups sweet potato flesh (from 2 medium potatoes, baked until very soft, then peeled)

¼ cup unsweetened coconut milk yogurt alternative

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon maple syrup

½ teaspoon fresh grated ginger

¼ teaspoon vanilla extract

¼ teaspoon cinnamon

⅛ teaspoon salt

Put all the ingredients in a medium bowl. Use an immersion blender to blend until completely smooth. (You can also use a regular blender for this step.) If not serving right away, warm before serving. Add toppings of your choice or one of the following recommendations.

TOPPING VARIATIONS

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

1 tablespoon unsweetened dried cherries

1 tablespoon slivered almonds, toasted

2 teaspoons cacao nibs

1 teaspoon chia seeds, soaked overnight in water and drained

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

1 tablespoon walnuts, toasted and chopped

1 tablespoon medjool dates, pitted and chopped (about ½ to 1 date)

1 teaspoon orange zest

¼ teaspoon spice blend*

* To make spice blend, combine ¼ teaspoon each of ground cardamom, ground cloves, ground allspice, and ground cinnamon. You can store this mixture in a jar for up to a month.

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

1 tablespoon pecans, toasted and chopped

1 tablespoon medjool dates, pitted and chopped (about ½ to 1 date)

1 teaspoon flax seeds, toasted

1 teaspoon maple syrup

¼ teaspoon pumpkin spice

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

1 tablespoon pomegranate seeds

1 tablespoon macadamia nuts, toasted and chopped

1 tablespoon coconut flakes, toasted

1 teaspoon hemp seeds, toasted

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

2 tablespoons diced tart apple (like Pink Lady)

1 tablespoon Lemon-Ginger Granola (see here)

1 tablespoon walnuts, toasted and chopped

1 teaspoon maple syrup

Orange sweet potatoes are great for this, but purple versions bake to a beautifully cakey consistency that works even better. Purple sweet potatoes get their color from powerful longevity-boosting antioxidants.

title: Okinawan Breakfast Smoothie
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 1 SERVING

Okinawans have used turmeric for hundreds of years in cooking and as a tea. The powerhouse spice is known for its anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and antiaging properties. Scientists are researching its main compound—curcumin—as it may be a factor in slowing the progression of dementia.

Traditionally, Okinawans steep dried turmeric into a tea, but this version uses the spice for a smoothie instead. Sweetened with banana and apple, this provides the perfect zip to start your day, especially if you’re looking for an anti-inflammatory drink.

1 ripe banana, peeled and cut in half

1 apple, cored and cut into a few pieces

1 teaspoon ground turmeric

1 cup vanilla soy milk

5 cups ice

Blend all the ingredients in a blender on high speed until smooth. Drink immediately.

title: Lemon-Ginger Granola
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 3 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 3 CUPS

After researching the recipes Americans love most, one thing was certain: Lemon is one of the most commonly used ingredients. But why save it for your dinner or dessert? In this breakfast bowl, lemon adds a bright flavor to homemade granola (a cost-effective alternative to store-bought breakfast cereals of all kinds). This is a simple recipe to start your day, and it’s easy to double or triple it to make enough for a week or longer.

2 cups rolled oats

¼ cup walnuts, chopped

¼ cup sunflower seeds

¼ cup crystallized ginger, chopped

¼ cup flaked or shredded coconut

3 tablespoons honey

3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

⅛ teaspoon lemon extract

⅛ teaspoon vanilla extract

Zest of 1 lemon

Preheat your oven to 350°F.

Put the oats, walnuts, sunflower seeds, ginger, and coconut in a large bowl and toss with the honey, working the mixture so that it’s as evenly distributed as possible—you do want some clusters to form, though. Add the oil and extracts and toss again to fully combine.

Spread the mixture out on a sheet pan and bake for 20 minutes, stirring once halfway through. You want it to look lightly toasted at the end, but don’t let it get too brown, or it can turn bitter.

Remove the pan from the oven and toss with the lemon zest. Let the granola cool before eating or packing away for later. The granola will keep in an airtight jar in the cupboard for a month or longer.

Feel free to use other nuts, seeds, and dried fruit depending on what you like.

title: Cranberry-Orange Brown Rice Porridge
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Breakfast oats are popular on American tables, but have you ever considered swapping oats for brown rice? It’s a fantastic alternative to the more typical breakfast grain and adds a warm and nutty flavor, along with a great texture, to more traditional bowls.

2 cups short-grain brown rice

2 cups coconut milk

2 cups water

½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries

2 tablespoons maple syrup, plus more for topping

1 teaspoon fresh grated ginger

Zest of 1 orange

¼ teaspoon salt

¼ cup walnuts, toasted and chopped

Put all the ingredients except the walnuts in a pot over medium-high heat. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat to a simmer. Cover the pot and cook for 40 minutes, until the rice is just tender. (If the rice isn’t ready, remove from the heat and let it sit, covered, another 5 minutes.)

Serve with a sprinkle of toasted walnuts and a drizzle of maple syrup on top.

title: Old-Fashioned Oats
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: FIVE-MINUTE OATS COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS
body:
FIVE-MINUTE OATS COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

OVERNIGHT OATS PREP TIME: 24 HOURS MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Oatmeal makes a great breakfast for several reasons: First, it’s incredibly versatile, with myriad flavor combinations, both sweet and savory. Second, it’s satisfying and fiber-rich, which will keep you going through a long day. Finally, it’s a nutritional powerhouse, with tons of protein, vitamins, and minerals.

You can make these oats two ways: an instant five-minute version that you can whip up for a fast breakfast on the go, or an overnight version, for a thicker bowl. For overnight versions of these recipes, add the dried fruit and other ingredients to the jar along with the oats. You can garnish with things that you want to stay crunchy (like chopped nuts) the next day.

2 cups water or plant/nut milk

1 cup rolled oats

Pinch of salt

OPTIONAL FOR OVERNIGHT OATS

Unsweetened coconut milk yogurt alternative (can substitute 1:1 for some of the water or milk)

Chia seeds (1 to 2 tablespoons per cup of oats)

FOR FIVE-MINUTE OATS

Put all the ingredients in a small pot, stir to combine, and bring to a low boil over medium heat. Lower the heat to a high simmer and cook, stirring once or twice, for 5 minutes. Serve with your choice of toppings.

FOR OVERNIGHT OATS

Put the ingredients in a Mason jar or other container, stir well to combine, cover, and put in the fridge for 24 hours.

Use rolled oats, not steel-cut or quick-cooking. Steel-cut oats can take 40-plus minutes to cook (though they’re great if you have the time), and quick-cooking oats turn to mush.

SWEET TOPPING VARIATIONS

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

2 tablespoons fresh blueberries

1 tablespoon almond butter

1 teaspoon chia seeds, soaked overnight in water and drained

1 teaspoon honey

½ teaspoon gingerbread spice

Add all the toppings and serve, stirring well before eating.

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

2 tablespoons walnuts, toasted and chopped

1 tablespoon medjool dates, pitted and chopped (about ½ to 1 date)

1 teaspoon fresh orange zest

1 teaspoon sunflower seeds

1 teaspoon maple syrup

Add all the toppings and serve, stirring well before eating.

SAVORY TOPPING VARIATIONS

For savory oats, omit the salt and sir in a teaspoon of white miso before cooking or soaking overnight. Using a little miso in overnight oats works wonders—enzymes in the miso break down some of the starch into sugar, unlocking a nice sweetness.

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

½ avocado, sliced

4 cherry tomatoes, halved

2 teaspoons pumpkin seeds, toasted

1 teaspoon chives, minced

1 teaspoon everything bagel seasoning

Fan the avocado slices out on the oatmeal, add the tomato halves and pumpkin seeds, then sprinkle the chives and seasoning over the top.

TOP EACH BOWL WITH

¼ cup Garlicky-Good Roasted Mushrooms (see here)

1 tablespoon parsley, chopped

1 teaspoon lemon juice

½ teaspoon sesame oil

Top the oats with the mushrooms, sprinkle on the parsley, then drizzle on the lemon juice and oil.

title: Blue Zones Breakfast Bars
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 35 MINUTES MAKES 12 BARS

Most energy bars are full of additives and refined sugar. These healthy and delicious bars, on the other hand, are made of 100 percent whole ingredients, subbing out sugar for maple syrup and vanilla extract. With chia seeds, soy milk, nuts, and oats, these on-the-go bars are also full of protein, fiber, and healthy fats. They come together easily, and the recipe makes enough to last all week.

FOR THE BASE

3 cups rolled oats

¾ cup soy milk

¼ cup chia seeds, soaked in 1 cup water for at least 10 minutes, then drained

6 tablespoons coconut oil, plus 1 teaspoon for oiling pan

6 tablespoons maple syrup

½ teaspoon vanilla extract

½ teaspoon salt

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Combine all the base ingredients in a large bowl and mix thoroughly.

In a separate bowl, combine your flavor-of-choice ingredients, except chopped or slivered nuts, to make a smooth paste.

Add the flavor paste to your base mix and combine thoroughly.

Oil a 13-x-9-inch sheet pan well with the teaspoon of coconut oil, then spread the mixture out to cover the whole pan evenly. Sprinkle the chopped or slivered nuts (if using) over the top and press them down gently.

Bake for 35 minutes, then let cool. Cut into 12 bars.

Store tightly wrapped in the fridge for up to a week.

FLAVOR VARIATIONS

½ cup pumpkin puree

½ cup almond butter

¼ cup unsweetened dried cranberries

½ teaspoon pumpkin spice

¼ cup pecans, chopped (optional)

½ cup medjool dates, pitted and chopped (about 4 to 5 dates)

½ cup tahini

¼ cup raisins

½ teaspoon fresh ginger, grated

¼ cup cashews, chopped (optional)

½ cup unsweetened applesauce

½ cup walnut butter

¼ cup unsweetened dried apples, chopped

½ teaspoon cinnamon

¼ cup walnuts, chopped (optional)

½ cup very ripe banana, mashed

½ cup almond butter

¼ cup unsweetened dark chocolate chips

½ teaspoon cardamom

¼ cup almonds, slivered (optional)

title: Tofu Shakshuka
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 25 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Shakshuka originated in North Africa, then spread throughout the Middle East. It’s commonly eaten for breakfast, but works just as well for lunch or dinner. Silken tofu makes an excellent substitute for the traditional eggs, and scooping the tofu into ovals adds to the effect. If you want it spicier, add more harissa or some cayenne.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 red bell pepper, seeded and cut into thin strips

1 medium onion, halved and thinly sliced

3 garlic cloves, minced

1 teaspoon ground cumin

1 teaspoon ground coriander

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

Pinch of saffron threads (about ¼ teaspoon)

1 teaspoon harissa

1 teaspoon salt

1 tablespoon tomato paste

1 (28-ounce) can crushed or diced tomatoes

1 (16-ounce) container silken tofu

Freshly ground black pepper

½ cup cilantro leaves, chopped

Put the oil in a large skillet or deep pan (one you can bring directly to the table) and set it over medium heat until shimmering. Add the bell pepper and onion and sauté until soft and translucent, about 10 minutes. You don’t want them to brown, just get nice and tender.

Add the garlic, spices, harissa, salt, and tomato paste. Stir well and cook for another 5 minutes or so, then add the tomatoes and their liquid. Stir well.

Use a soup spoon to scoop roughly egg-size balls of tofu into the pan. Push down gently on all the tofu to submerge it in the sauce.

Reduce the heat to low and simmer for about 10 minutes, until the liquid thickens a bit.

Taste for seasoning, twist a few turns of black pepper over the top, sprinkle on the cilantro, and bring the bubbling pan right to the table. Serve it with extra harissa on the side and some crusty whole-grain or sourdough bread to mop up the sauce.

title: Sunrise Banana Bread Smoothie
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 3 (1-CUP) SERVINGS
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 3 (1-CUP) SERVINGS

Banana bread is one of the most sought-after recipes, but a loaf often includes bad-for-you sugars and unhealthy white flour. This equally decadent breakfast uses no added sugar, just the natural sweetness of bananas and dates. It’s nutritious, satisfying—the cashews add plenty of protein—and supersimple. Just remember to soak the cashews the night before! If you want a real morning pick-me-up, add a shot of espresso or cold brew coffee per serving before blending.

1 cup raw unsalted cashews, soaked overnight in 2 cups water

6 medjool dates, pitted

2 cups soy or oat milk

1 banana

¼ teaspoon vanilla

¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon

⅛ teaspoon ground cardamom

⅛ teaspoon ground star anise

Grated whole nutmeg, for garnish

Drain the cashews and discard their soaking water. They will have absorbed water during soaking, so you’ll have more than a cup. Use all of them. Put all the ingredients except the nutmeg into a blender and run it until you have a completely smooth, creamy texture.

Pour into glasses, grate a little nutmeg on top of each one, and serve.

If you have a professional-quality blender, this can be made without presoaking the cashews. Just add an extra ½ cup or so of whatever milk you’re using along with the raw nuts and slowly bring the blender up to high speed over the course of about 30 seconds. Let it run until everything is nice and smooth.

If this becomes a regular breakfast, mix a week’s worth of the spices for convenience by combining 2 teaspoons of cinnamon with 1 teaspoon each of cardamom and star anise and store your prepared mix in an airtight container. But grate the nutmeg each time—it’s so much more aromatic when fresh.

title: Quick Pickled Veggies
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 PINT
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 PINT

These easy pickles are based on Vietnamese do chua, which is a popular topping on banh mi. Use them to brighten up everything from salads to sandwiches with a nice sour crunch. You’ll also want to have these on hand for Sesame-Crusted Tofu Summer Rolls (see here).

FOR THE BRINE

½ cup apple cider vinegar

½ cup water

2 teaspoons salt

1 bay leaf

1 clove

6 black peppercorns

½ teaspoon coriander seeds

½ teaspoon mustard seeds

FOR THE PICKLES

2 medium carrots, peeled and cut into 3-by-⅛-inch matchsticks

1 large daikon, peeled and cut into 3-by-⅛-inch matchsticks

1 fresh or dried hot pepper (optional)

In a small pot, bring all the brine ingredients to a boil, then reduce to a simmer for 5 minutes. Meanwhile, pack the vegetables into a heatproof container, like a canning jar, so that they’re all parallel; it’s easier to do this with the jar on its side.
