Turn the jar upright and add hot brine until the vegetables are completely covered.

If you want a spicy kick, tuck a hot pepper into the jar before you close it. Let the jar stand on the counter until cool, then cover it with a lid and move it to the fridge. These can be served as soon as they’re cool, but they are even tastier the next day.

The pickles will keep in the fridge for at least 2 weeks.

You can strain the spices out of the brine as you pour it in the jar, or leave them in for more flavor over time.

title: Homemade Corn Tortillas
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES 8 (4-INCH) TORTILLAS

Making corn tortillas at home might seem daunting, but they’re pretty easy—and the health benefits and flavor are incomparable, a world away from store-bought. Be patient; after a few tries you’ll get the hang of it. And once you do, you’ll never go back.

1 cup masa harina

¼ teaspoon salt

¾ cup hot water

Combine the masa harina and salt in a medium bowl. Add the water and mix well so there’s no dry masa harina in the bowl. Gently work the dough with your hands for a minute until it’s no longer sticky, then form it into a ball. Cover with a damp tea towel and let it rest for 5 to 10 minutes.

Preheat a cast-iron skillet, griddle, or comal over medium heat.

Pinch off a walnut-size piece of dough, roll it into a ball, and press it into a tortilla shape. Cook the tortilla for about a minute, until brown spots begin to appear, then flip it over for another minute. Repeat and stack the cooked tortillas on a plate next to the stove so they keep each other warm; the steam helps them stay pliable.

Serve right away, or freeze tightly wrapped in plastic once they cool down.

Masa harina is a flour made from corn that’s been nixtamalized (soaked in an alkaline solution), which improves its nutritional content, gives the tortillas the characteristic flavor you’ll recognize, and makes them hold together properly. Regular cornmeal won’t work!

Don’t throw away stale tortillas—they can be used in tortilla soup or baked or fried to make chips.

title: Crispy Salt & Pepper Oven Fries
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Among beloved recipes, crispy fries and potatoes reign supreme for Americans. These better-for-you oven fries deliver with a crisp outside and fluffy inside. Tossing them in seasoning before and after cooking really boosts the flavor. Have some fun trying other herbs and spices, too.

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided

2 pounds russet potatoes, peeled and cut into roughly ¼-inch sticks

Hot water

1 teaspoon salt, divided

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

¼ cup chives, minced (optional)

Nutritional yeast or freshly grated pecorino (optional)

Preheat your oven to 400°F.

Use half the oil to coat the surface of a sheet pan.

Put the potatoes in a bowl and cover them with hot water. Let soak for 10 minutes, then drain the potatoes and dry thoroughly on kitchen towels.

Toss the potatoes in the remaining oil, then add half the salt and the pepper, tossing again to coat evenly. Spread the potatoes in a single layer on the sheet pan, taking care that they don’t touch.

Bake for 20 minutes, then use a thin spatula to flip the potatoes over—the sides touching the pan will brown first. After another 10 minutes, use the spatula to roll the potatoes over onto a third side for 10 more minutes. This turning will help them get brown and crispy all the way around.

At this point, they should be nice and brown, but you can turn them one more time if you think they need it. Remove them from the oven and toss with the remaining salt and, if using, the chives and nutritional yeast or pecorino. Serve immediately.

title: Roasted Broccoli Rabe
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Broccoli rabe has a slight bitterness that roasting transforms into an addictive sweetness. The many members of the Brassica genus, such as broccoli, cabbages, turnips, and mustard greens, are renowned for their health benefits—including cancer-fighting properties.

1 teaspoon sesame seeds, plus 1 teaspoon for garnish

½ teaspoon mustard seeds

½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

12 ounces broccoli rabe (about 3 small bunches)

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, plus another tablespoon to finish

½ teaspoon salt

1 tablespoon lemon juice

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Mix the seeds and pepper in a ramekin or small bowl and set aside.

Put the broccoli rabe on a sheet pan and drizzle with the oil, tossing to coat the stalks and florets evenly. You want a nice shine all over. Sprinkle the salt on top and toss again. Then arrange the stalks in one layer and pop the pan into the oven for 15 minutes.

Pull the pan out, sprinkle the spices onto the broccoli rabe, and use tongs to give a gentle shake to the greens to let the spices settle in. Put the pan back in the oven for 5 more minutes, then remove.

Serve with a sprinkle of lemon juice, plus the remaining oil and sesame seeds over the top to finish.

You can substitute broccolini or Chinese broccoli, or even regular broccoli—but you’ll need to cut the heads into quarters lengthwise before roasting.

title: Crispy Roasted Chickpeas
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS

Chickpeas are a superfood commonly found across all the blue zones, especially Ikaria and Sardinia. This crispy version makes for a delicious snack on its own, or it can be used as a longevity-boosting add-on to soups, salads, and more.

2 cups cooked chickpeas, drained and dried on a tea towel

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

½ teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon ground coriander

½ teaspoon herbes de Provence

¼ teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

¼ teaspoon garlic powder

¼ teaspoon onion powder

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Put the chickpeas in a medium bowl and toss with the remaining ingredients until evenly coated, then arrange them in a single layer on a sheet pan. Bake for 40 minutes, until they have shrunk, darkened a bit, and become crisp on the outside. Serve immediately, or cool and then store in a jar in the fridge.

This is a great recipe to double or triple so you can always have a jar on hand. They’ll keep in the fridge for at least a week and will crisp back up after a couple of minutes on the stove or in a hot oven.

title: Roasted Root Vegetable Medley
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

Root vegetables are full of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. Choosing a variety of colors means you’re also getting lots of different antioxidants and nutrients, since the orange and purple colors, for example, indicate the presence of longevity-promoting compounds like beta carotene and anthocyanins, respectively.

FOR THE MARINADE

3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

2 tablespoons red wine vinegar

2 teaspoons liquid aminos

1 tablespoon Dijon mustard

1 teaspoon herbes de Provence

1 garlic clove, grated

½ teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

FOR THE VEGETABLES

4 carrots, peeled and cut into ¼-inch-thick sticks about 3 inches long

2 yellow beets, peeled and cut lengthwise into thin wedges

1 to 2 parsnips (about 12 ounces), peeled and cut into ¼-inch-thick sticks about 3 inches long

1 bunch red radishes (about 6 radishes), greens removed and bulbs quartered lengthwise

½ red onion, slivered

TO FINISH

Black Tahini Dressing (see here), or store-bought tahini dressing

1 tablespoon chives or other fresh herbs, finely minced

Preheat your oven to 425°F.

In a large bowl, whisk all the marinade ingredients together until everything is thoroughly combined and emulsified. Add the vegetables to the bowl and toss until they are thoroughly coated.

Spread the mixture out on a sheet pan and roast until everything is tender and beginning to brown nicely in places, about 30 minutes. If you give the pan a little shake and stir at around the 20-minute mark, that will help things cook more evenly.

Put the vegetables on a warmed serving dish, drizzle the tahini sauce on top, and sprinkle with the chives.

This combination of vegetables works especially well, but don’t feel limited to this exact mixture. This recipe will work with whatever root veggies are available or in season.

title: Honey Roasted Carrots
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 35 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

You don’t have to wait for Thanksgiving to enjoy good roasted carrots. These healthy veggies marry well with warm spices, and this dish features four of them: cumin, caraway, coriander, and fennel. A little smoked paprika warms things up even more, and the caramelized honey glaze takes it over the top. This is a wonderful side dish and is easy to make ahead.

FOR THE GLAZE

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon lemon juice

1 tablespoon honey

FOR THE CARROTS

12 ounces carrots, peeled (about 5 medium carrots)

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

½ teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon cumin seeds

¼ teaspoon caraway seeds

¼ teaspoon coriander seeds

¼ teaspoon fennel seeds

¼ teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

¼ cup chopped carrot greens or parsley, for garnish

Preheat your oven to 350°F.

In a ramekin or small bowl, whisk together the glaze ingredients until the honey is dissolved, then set aside.

Cut the carrots lengthwise in half or quarters so that the widest ends are about ¼ inch thick. Toss the carrots in the oil to coat evenly, then add the salt and spices and toss again. Spread the carrots in a single layer on a 13-x-9-inch sheet pan, with curved sides facing up.

Roast the carrots for 30 minutes, then remove the pan from the oven, drizzle the glaze over the carrots, and return to the oven for 5 more minutes.

Garnish with the chopped greens before serving.

If your carrots come with the greens attached, chop some of those leaves for a garnish. Or use parsley instead.

title: Muesli
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 5 CUPS
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 5 CUPS

Muesli was invented around the turn of the 20th century by Swiss doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner, who developed it for his recuperating patients. His recipe called for soaking oats overnight; our version can be eaten right away, but soaking overnight adds to the flavor. And it’s not just for breakfast. Try it as a tasty lunch or midday snack, or any time of day. Make sure to use rolled oats; instant oats will turn to mush, and steel-cut oats won’t get soft enough.

FOR THE MUESLI

3 cups rolled oats

¼ teaspoon cinnamon

½ cup pecans, chopped

¼ cup flaked or grated coconut

¼ cup pumpkin seeds

¼ cup sunflower seeds

½ cup dried apricots, chopped

½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries

TO SERVE

¾ cup plant/nut milk

Fresh fruit, for garnish

To make the muesli, put the oats and cinnamon in a medium bowl and mix well. Toast the pecans, coconut, and seeds in a dry pan over medium-high heat until aromatic and beginning to color, 3 to 5 minutes. Add the toasted mixture to the oats and stir to combine, then add the dried fruit and stir again. Store the muesli in a lidded jar in a cupboard for up to a month.

To serve, pour milk of your choice over 1 cup muesli and garnish with some seasonal fresh fruit.

For overnight oats, prepare the muesli and pour into a jar with a pinch of salt and ¾ cup milk per cup of muesli. Seal and refrigerate for at least 12 hours.

This recipe is very flexible. You can use any combination of nuts, seeds, and dried fruit depending on what you have on hand. Wheat germ is a great addition, as are chia seeds if you’re going to be soaking the muesli overnight.

title: Garlicky-Good Roasted Mushrooms
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Mushrooms aren’t always a go-to for American diners, but you should consider giving them a try. They’re not only delicious but also beneficial for gut health, immunity, and preventing certain cancers. They also provide umami, the savory fifth taste, making them an excellent way to add deep flavor—what you might be used to getting from meat—to a meal.

FOR THE MUSHROOMS

1 pound cremini or button mushrooms

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

½ teaspoon salt

Freshly ground black pepper

½ teaspoon herbes de Provence

1 sprig rosemary

5 to 6 garlic cloves, separated from the head but with papery skin still on

FOR THE DRESSING

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon red wine vinegar

1 teaspoon liquid aminos

¼ cup flat-leaf parsley, chopped

Preheat your oven to 350°F.

Wipe the mushrooms with a damp cloth to remove any dirt, and trim any discolored stem ends. Quarter the large mushrooms and halve the smaller ones so the pieces are all roughly the same size. In a medium bowl, toss the mushrooms with the oil, then toss again with the salt, pepper, and herbes de Provence.

Put the rosemary on a 13-x-9-inch sheet pan and arrange the mushrooms and garlic cloves in a single layer on top. Bake for 30 minutes, until the mushrooms are brown and tender, giving the pan a gentle shake and stirring at about halfway through.

While the mushrooms are cooking, make the dressing by whisking the ingredients together in a small bowl.

When the mushrooms are done and the garlic is soft, remove the pan from the oven. Using tongs, grab the rosemary spring and the garlic cloves and set them aside to cool for a few minutes. Strip the leaves off the rosemary and peel the skins off the garlic (they should come off easily) and coarsely chop them both. Toss the mushrooms, rosemary, and garlic together with the dressing in a bowl, top with parsley, and serve.

If you have access to a grill, the oiled and seasoned mushrooms are wonderful threaded onto skewers and grilled. Instead of roasting the garlic cloves, you can just toss the grilled mushrooms with a little Garlic Confit (see here).

These are great served warm, but they’re even better the next day after they’ve had a chance to marinate in the dressing.

title: Refried Beans
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

A protein-packed powerhouse, this is an excellent way to use up leftover cooked beans. Plus, you can serve these refried beans on the side of myriad dishes to up their nutritional value, including Jollof Rice (see here), Butternut Squash & Pineapple al Pastor (see here), and Guacamole & Bean Tacos (see here). Pinto and black beans are most commonly used, but any bean or legume—even lentils or chickpeas—will work. If the beans were cooked with seasoning, adjust the salt accordingly.

2 tablespoons avocado oil

½ onion, diced

2 garlic cloves, sliced

1 teaspoon Mexican oregano

2 cups cooked pinto or black beans

½ teaspoon salt

½ cup vegetable stock

In a skillet, heat the oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and sauté until it begins to brown, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and oregano and cook for another 2 minutes, then add the beans and salt, stirring well.

Use a potato masher to break the beans up, mixing them with the onion and garlic, until you have a chunky paste. Lower the heat to medium and add the stock, stirring well to combine. Cook, stirring regularly, for another 5 minutes.

Taste for seasoning and serve.

title: Not-Your-Mom’s Whipped Potatoes
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

These aren’t Mom’s mashed potatoes. Instead, this version of creamy mash is a take on a French dish called pommes écrasées (crushed potatoes). Traditionally, they are mashed by hand for a chunky, rustic texture, but this version uses an immersion blender to whip the potatoes into a smooth puree.

Yukon Gold potatoes are best for this dish for two reasons: First, their skins are superthin, so you don’t need to bother peeling them. Second, their waxiness makes for a gorgeously rich and creamy texture that’s perfect on the side of almost any meal.

1 pound Yukon Gold potatoes

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil

1 teaspoon salt

2 tablespoons chives, minced

Trim any dark spots off the potatoes, then halve or quarter the potatoes so all the pieces are roughly the same size, about 2 inches across. Put the potatoes in a deep pot that’s large enough to hold them with plenty of room to spare. Cover the potatoes with water by about 2 inches. Bring the water to a boil and cook until a knife can pierce the potatoes with minimal resistance, about 20 minutes.

Use a colander to drain the water, then return the potatoes to the pot. Add the oil, salt, and chives and use an immersion blender to whip it all into a smooth, velvety puree. Taste for seasoning and serve.

title: Creamy White Bean & Tomato Soup
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

I was pleasantly surprised when our research revealed white bean soup is a favorite recipe among Americans. Folks adding longevity-powerhouse beans to a meal always makes me happy. We also found that American cooks love creamy soups. So we made this hearty, velvety version, packed with flavor and a nutritional upside.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish

½ onion, chopped

3 garlic cloves, sliced

2 teaspoons herbes de Provence

3½ cups Roasted Tomato Sauce (see here) or 1 (28-ounce) can crushed or diced tomatoes

½ pound silken tofu, cubed

2 cups cooked white beans, divided

¾ teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Fresh chives, parsley, or basil, for garnish (optional)

Put the oil in a large soup pot over medium-high heat until it starts to shimmer. Add the onion and sauté until it begins to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and herbes de Provence, stir well, and sauté for another 2 minutes.

Add the tomato sauce, tofu, half the beans, and the salt and pepper; stir to combine. Take the pot off the heat and use an immersion blender to puree everything until smooth, then return to the heat and add the rest of the beans; stir to combine.

Once the soup begins to bubble, lower the heat and simmer for 5 more minutes. Ladle the soup into bowls and garnish with the fresh herbs and a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.

Pairing suggestion: Consider serving with Easy Spelt Flatbreads (see here) for dunking.

title: Kickin’ Potato & Corn Chowder
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This southwestern riff on corn chowder (an American favorite) is creamy, complex, and darn tasty. It doesn’t really need anything paired with it, but a stack of fresh Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here) for dipping is never a bad idea.

2 cups vegetable broth

2 cups unsweetened soy milk

1 teaspoon cornstarch

2 whole poblano peppers

1½ cups corn kernels (about 2 ears corn)

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 medium onion, chopped

1 jalapeño, seeded and chopped

3 garlic cloves, chopped

½ teaspoon ground cumin

½ teaspoon ground coriander

½ teaspoon Mexican oregano

1 teaspoon salt

1 pound Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into ¾-inch cubes

Juice of 1 lime

¼ cup cilantro leaves, chopped, plus more for garnish

Combine the vegetable broth and soy milk in a medium bowl, then whisk in the cornstarch until it’s fully incorporated with no lumps.

Heat a large heavy-bottomed soup pot over medium-high heat. Put the poblanos in the dry pot and char their skin, turning every 5 minutes or so, until they blacken and blister all the way around. Place the poblanos in a bowl and cover them to steam for 20 minutes.

Add the corn kernels to the dry pot over medium-high heat and blister them, stirring regularly, for about 2 minutes. Remove from the pot and set aside. When cool enough to handle, stem and seed the poblanos with a knife, then remove the skin and dice the peppers.

Pour the oil into the pot, then add the onion, jalapeño, and garlic; sauté for 2 minutes or until they begin to soften. Add the cumin, coriander, oregano, and salt, stir to combine, and let it cook for one more minute.

Add the broth–soy milk mixture to the pot, stirring well. Let everything come to a boil before adding the potatoes. Stir and bring to a boil again. Lower the heat to a simmer. Add the lime juice and cilantro, stir again, and let simmer until the potatoes are fork-tender, about 20 minutes.

Garnish each bowl with fresh cilantro and serve.

title: Grilled Veggie Kebabs
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

This is a vibrant summer side dish you can whip up easily on the grill—a favorite pastime for Americans. The best part: It features a rainbow assortment of fresh produce (use what you have!) and a bright, tangy protein- and probiotic-rich ginger-miso dressing.

FOR THE MARINADE

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 tablespoon rice vinegar

1 tablespoon soy sauce

FOR THE GINGER-MISO DRESSING

1 tablespoon white miso or soy sauce

1 tablespoon lime or yuzu juice

1 teaspoon fresh ginger, grated

1 garlic clove, grated

FOR THE KEBABS

12 ounces button mushrooms, wiped and trimmed, large ones halved

1 zucchini, sliced into half circles about ¾ inch thick

1 yellow summer squash, sliced into half circles about ¾ inch thick

1 small eggplant, quartered lengthwise and cut into ¾-inch slices

1 red bell pepper, seeded and cut into 1½-inch pieces

½ red onion, cut into 1½-inch pieces

FOR GARNISH

1 tablespoon toasted sesame seeds

1 scallion, thinly sliced

Light your grill and set to high heat.

Whisk the marinade ingredients together in a small bowl until combined. In another bowl, do the same with the dressing ingredients.

Thread the various vegetables onto grill-safe skewers, pushing them together to fit as many as possible without crowding too tightly. Brush each skewer with the marinade, taking care to coat all sides evenly.

Grill the kebabs, rotating them every few minutes, until they’re nicely browned and a little charred in places, about 10 to 15 minutes.

When they’re done, serve the skewers topped with the dressing, sesame seeds, and scallions. Or use tongs to pull all the vegetables off the skewers into a serving bowl and toss everything with the dressing until thoroughly coated. Garnish with the sesame seeds and scallions.

If you don’t have a grill, just toss all the vegetables in the marinade in a baking pan and roast them in the oven at 400°F for 20 to 25 minutes until they’re nicely browned. Then toss them in the dressing and serve.

title: West African Peanut Stew
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 35 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Peanuts aren’t just one of America’s most sought-after ingredients; they’re also an easy and delicious way to boost your longevity. This hearty stew is inspired by maafe, a Senegalese spicy peanut stew typically made with beef, sweet potatoes, and carrots. We’ve left out the beef but kept the good-for-you peanuts and sweet potatoes in the mix. Plus, we give an extra dose of fiber with heart-healthy kale.

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 yellow or white onion, diced

1 red bell pepper, seeded and diced

1 teaspoon ginger, grated

3 garlic cloves, grated or finely minced

½ teaspoon ground cumin

¼ teaspoon chipotle powder, plus more to taste

1 (14-ounce) can whole or crushed tomatoes

4 cups vegetable stock

1 teaspoon salt

½ cup smooth unsalted peanut butter

2 sweet potatoes, peeled and cut into roughly 1-inch cubes

2 cups kale, hard stems removed and leaves finely chopped

¼ cup raw, unsalted peanuts, chopped

Cilantro, for garnish

Heat the oil in a large soup pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and pepper and sauté until they soften and just begin to brown, about 10 minutes. Add the ginger, garlic, cumin, and chipotle powder, stir well, and cook for another 2 minutes.

Add the tomatoes, stock, and salt, and stir well. Remove the pot from the heat and use an immersion blender to make a smooth puree. Return the pot to medium-high heat and whisk in the peanut butter until fully combined.

Add the sweet potatoes and kale, stirring to combine. As soon as the stew begins to bubble, lower the heat to a simmer and cover the pot. Cook until the sweet potatoes and kale are tender, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, about 20 minutes.

Garnish each bowl with chopped peanuts and cilantro and serve.

Use peanut butter with no additives. The ingredients list on the jar should just say “peanuts.”

title: Spinach & Roasted Radicchio Salad With Chile-Maple Vinaigrette
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 2 TO 4 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 2 TO 4 SERVINGS

This salad is full of superfoods, starting with immune-boosting spinach, which is also great for bone and eye health. The pecans bring the protein, while roasted radicchio, known for being heart-healthy, brings a wonderful sweetness, especially when paired with the bright, chile-infused maple vinaigrette. This is a satisfying side salad for four or a wonderful lunch for two.

FOR THE SALAD

1 head radicchio, cut into 8 wedges (include a bit of core in each slice so they hold together)

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

¼ teaspoon salt

½ cup pecan halves

¼ cup Slow Cooker Onion Jam (see here, or store-bought)

8 ounces baby spinach

¼ cup flat-leaf parsley, chopped, to finish

FOR THE VINAIGRETTE

½ cup extra-virgin olive oil

¼ cup red wine vinegar

1 Fresno chile, seeded and finely minced

1 teaspoon thyme

1 teaspoon Dijon mustard

1 teaspoon maple syrup

1 garlic clove, grated or finely minced

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

To make the salad, arrange the radicchio wedges in a shallow baking dish, drizzle with the oil, and sprinkle on the salt. Put the dish in the oven for 45 minutes, adding the pecans for the last 5 minutes so they toast.

While the radicchio cooks, make the vinaigrette, whisking all the ingredients together until glossy and emulsified. Set aside. (This makes about 1 cup of dressing, more than you’ll need for this recipe. Keep leftovers covered in the fridge for up to a week.)

When the radicchio is ready, take it out of the oven and let cool for a couple of minutes. Mix the onion jam into ¼ cup of the vinaigrette and toss with the spinach, then spread the mixture out on a serving dish. Arrange the radicchio wedges on top of the spinach, scatter the pecans on top, and finish with the parsley. Drizzle a little more vinaigrette over the radicchio wedges before serving.

title: Creamy Carrot & Tahini Soup
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This cheerful soup is loaded with fiber, protein, and flavor. And you can have it two ways: served warm for a tasty fall comfort dish or served cold as a refresher on a hot day.

½ cup pine nuts

1 teaspoon harissa

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

1½ pounds carrots, peeled and cut into ¼-inch rounds

4 cups vegetable stock

½ cup tahini

½ cup orange juice

Juice of 1 large lemon

2 tablespoons miso

In a large soup pot, toast the pine nuts over medium-high heat until they begin to brown, 3 to 5 minutes. Remove the nuts to a small bowl and toss them with the harissa and oil until they’re nicely coated. Set aside to use as a garnish later.

Put the carrots and vegetable stock in the pot over medium-high heat and bring to a boil, then lower to a simmer. Cook until the carrots are tender, about 20 minutes. Remove the pot from the heat and add the remaining ingredients. Use an immersion blender to blend everything until you have a smooth puree. (You can also do this in a regular blender.)

If serving warm, bring the soup back to a simmer over medium heat to warm everything through. Serve, garnishing each bowl with a spoonful or two of the pine nuts.

If you have leftovers, this soup is easily transformed into a Japanese-style salad dressing, similar to what you’d get on salad at many sushi restaurants in the United States. For each ½ cup of soup, add 2 teaspoons of rice vinegar, 1 teaspoon of freshly grated ginger, and ½ teaspoon of liquid aminos or fish sauce. Mix well and enjoy over your favorite greens!

title: Easy Fennel Salad
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Fennel is a staple ingredient in two blue zones: Sardinia and Ikaria. It’s likely helped centenarians reach a healthy old age because it’s high in antioxidants and may reduce the risk of chronic diseases like cancer and heart disease.

This salad also borrows from Japanese culture, using the technique of kneading thinly sliced vegetables with salt to tenderize them and concentrate their flavor. If you have a mandoline or food processor with a slicing blade, those will get you the thinnest slices. If not, just use a good sharp knife and get the veggies as thin as you can.

FOR THE SALAD

2 medium fennel heads, halved, cored, and sliced as thinly as possible

½ medium onion, sliced as thinly as possible

½ teaspoon salt

Peel from one mandarin orange or clementine, finely chopped, or the zest from one orange

½ cup fennel fronds, chopped

1 teaspoon toasted sesame seeds, to finish

FOR THE DRESSING

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

2 tablespoons red wine vinegar

1 teaspoon liquid aminos

1 teaspoon ground fennel

½ teaspoon dry ground mustard

½ teaspoon maple syrup or honey

Put the fennel and onion slices in a large bowl and add the salt. Mix well to combine, then begin kneading the mixture. You’ll notice the texture changing, and within a minute or so, a handful will drip liquid when squeezed.

Keep kneading until there’s a small pool of liquid at the bottom of the bowl, then put the fennel mixture into a sieve and rinse under cold water, giving it a few more squeezes to rinse away the salt. Turn off the water and squeeze the mixture thoroughly to drain away the excess liquid; you want it damp but not wet. You can also use a salad spinner or wrap the mixture in a dish towel and wring it out.

Rinse the bowl, then add the dressing ingredients and whisk to combine. Return the fennel mixture to the bowl, along with the citrus peel and fennel fronds. Toss, combining everything thoroughly. Top with sesame seeds and serve.

Most fennel is sold with the stalks and fronds intact. If yours isn’t, then just omit the fronds.

title: Spicy Creamy Pumpkin Soup
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 25 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This simple soup marries two American favorites: pumpkin and Mexican flavors. With its beautiful color, velvety texture, and rich flavor of warmth and sweetness, this crowd-pleaser is as good for you as it is delicious. Squash and pumpkin are rich in calcium as well as vitamins A and C, which are all great for bone health; they’re also high in cancer-fighting beta carotene and gut-healthy fiber.

4 guajillo or ancho chiles, seeded and torn into pieces

2 tablespoons avocado oil

¼ cup pumpkin seeds

1 tablespoon chile powder

1 onion, diced

2 garlic cloves, sliced

1 teaspoon ground cumin

1 teaspoon ground coriander

1 small pumpkin (or kabocha squash), peeled, seeded, and cut into roughly 1½-inch cubes

4 cups vegetable stock

1 cup silken tofu, cubed

2 teaspoons salt

1 tablespoon Salsa Macha (see here, or store-bought)

Heat a large soup pot over medium-high heat and toast the chiles until they soften and become aromatic, about 30 seconds per side. Remove and set aside.

Put the oil in the pot, then add the pumpkin seeds, stirring well to coat the seeds. Fry the seeds until they begin to brown, about 1 minute. Remove the seeds with a slotted spoon and put them in a bowl with the chile powder, tossing well to coat. Set aside.

Add the onion to the pot and sauté until it begins to turn translucent, about 3 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 more minute, then add the cumin and coriander, stirring well, and cook for another minute.

Add the chiles back to the pot, along with the pumpkin, stock, tofu, and salt, and stir. Bring the soup to a boil, then turn the heat to low and cover the pot. Simmer until the pumpkin is fork-tender, about 20 minutes.

Take the pot off the heat and use an immersion blender to make a smooth puree. Taste for seasoning, then serve with a tablespoon of pumpkin seeds and a drizzle of salsa macha in each bowl.

title: Three Bean Chili Sin Carne
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

A flavorful chili in less than 30 minutes. Yes, it’s true! This beloved classic combines three different beans (the number one longevity ingredient in the blue zones), as well as heart-healthy walnuts. Be sure to make enough for leftovers: It’s even better after a day or two in the fridge—make it ahead of time if you can.

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 onion, diced

4 garlic cloves, sliced

1 teaspoon ground cumin

1 teaspoon ground coriander

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

1 teaspoon chipotle powder

1 teaspoon Mexican oregano

1 teaspoon unsweetened cocoa powder

2 bay leaves

½ cup walnuts, finely chopped

2 teaspoons salt

1 (28-ounce) can crushed tomatoes

1½ cups cooked kidney beans

1½ cups cooked pinto beans

1½ cups cooked black beans

Juice of 1 lime

1 avocado, halved and sliced, for garnish

Cilantro sprigs, for garnish

Chile powder or Homemade Taco Seasoning (see here, or store-bought)

Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers, then add the onion and sauté for 3 minutes, until translucent. Add the garlic and cook for 1 more minute, then add the spices, cocoa powder, bay leaves, and walnuts, stirring well; cook for 1 minute more.

Add the salt, tomatoes, beans, and lime juice, stir to combine, and bring to a low boil. Turn the heat to medium-low and cover the pot. Simmer for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until the walnuts begin to soften.

Serve with avocado slices fanned out on top of each bowl, sprinkled with chile powder or taco seasoning. You can also offer fresh Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here) and lime wedges on the side.

You want the walnuts to be finely chopped, the size of large breadcrumbs. They will soften as they absorb liquid and, along with the starch from the beans, help thicken this chili to a rich consistency that’s great for scooping up with Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here).

title: Melis Family Minestrone
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 2 HOURS, PLUS SOAKING BEANS OVERNIGHT MAKES 8 TO 10 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 2 HOURS, PLUS SOAKING BEANS OVERNIGHT MAKES 8 TO 10 SERVINGS

This veggie-packed, big-batch soup is eaten every day for lunch by the Melis family of Sardinia, the world’s longest-lived family, with nine siblings totaling more than 850 years in age. It can be made with seasonal vegetables from the garden but always includes beans.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 medium onion, chopped

5 stalks celery, chopped

5 carrots, peeled and chopped

8 garlic cloves, chopped

⅓ pound dried chickpeas, soaked overnight and drained

⅓ pound dried white beans, soaked overnight and drained

⅓ pound dried pinto or red beans, soaked overnight and drained

6 to 8 cups vegetable stock

1 (14-ounce) can diced tomatoes

1½ cups potatoes, cut into 1- to 2-inch cubes (about 1 large potato)

1 bay leaf

1 teaspoon dried oregano

Salt, to taste

1 teaspoon freshly ground red or black pepper

¼ cup finely grated pecorino (optional)

Heat a heavy-bottomed soup pot over low heat and add the oil. Once it’s shimmering, add the onion, celery, carrots, and garlic. Cook until the onions are translucent.

Add the beans, stock, tomatoes, potatoes, bay leaf, oregano, salt, and pepper to the pot, stir to combine, and bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat to low and simmer, uncovered, until the beans are tender, about 1½ hours.

Divide the soup into bowls, and serve with grated pecorino (if using).

If you forgot to soak the beans overnight, you can quickly microwave dried beans in a bowl of water for 15 minutes on high, stirring halfway through. Double the amount of water to the beans; for example, 1 cup beans should have 2 cups water. Or just use canned versions, drained of their liquid.

For a faster version of the soup, use a pressure cooker. Set to cook for 10 to 15 minutes and use the natural release.

title: Deluxe Blue Zones Minestrone
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 25 TO 30 MINUTES MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 25 TO 30 MINUTES MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS

This version of minestrone uses all the classic ingredients but adds more herbs, leafy greens, and some pasta to make a satisfying and complete meal in a bowl. An optional rind of pecorino adds a great savory note if you eat dairy.

Don’t feel that you have to follow this recipe to the letter—soups like this are a great way to use up all sorts of things in the fridge. Half a zucchini? Add it! Some leftover farro? Perfect! Just remember that grains (including pasta) are thirsty and you may want to add a bit more liquid to keep the soupy consistency.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 onion, diced

2 carrots, peeled and diced

3 celery ribs, diced

½ red bell pepper, seeded and diced

½ fennel bulb, diced

5 garlic cloves, chopped

½ cup parsley, chopped

4 sprigs thyme, leaves stripped and chopped

2 sprigs oregano, leaves stripped and chopped

1 sprig rosemary, leaves stripped and chopped

1 bay leaf

½ teaspoon red pepper flakes

¼ head green cabbage, cored and shredded

1 bunch kale, thick stalks removed and leaves chopped

2 red or yellow potatoes, diced

1 (14-ounce) can crushed or whole peeled tomatoes

1½ cups cooked chickpeas

1½ cups cooked white beans

1½ cups cooked red or kidney beans

6 cups vegetable stock (or water)

1 cup small durum wheat pasta (like ditalini or macaroni)

2 teaspoons salt

1 rind pecorino, about 2 inches square (optional)

Red Pesto (see here, or store-bought)

Heat the oil in a large soup pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion, carrots, celery, bell pepper, fennel, and garlic; cook until the onion turns translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the herbs, pepper flakes, cabbage, and kale; stir well and cook until the greens wilt, about 2 more minutes.

Add the potatoes, tomatoes, beans, stock, pasta, salt, and pecorino rind (if using), and stir gently to combine. When the liquid begins to boil, lower the heat to medium-low and simmer until the carrots and potatoes are fork-tender, 15 to 20 minutes. Remove the bay leaf and pecorino rind.

Ladle soup into bowls. If you want to take it over the top, serve each with a dollop of pesto.

title: Heirloom Tomato & Avocado Salad
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

When it comes to ingredients, Americans crave tomatoes, avocados, and corn. So we put them together in this garden-fresh salad. This summery combo makes a wonderful meal on its own, or you can pair it with everything from Mushroom & Black Bean Birria (see here) to Butternut Squash & Pineapple al Pastor (see here).

1½ cups sweet corn kernels (about 2 ears sweet corn)

½ cup pumpkin seeds

1 teaspoon, plus 1 tablespoon avocado oil, divided

1 teaspoon Homemade Taco Seasoning (see here, or store-bought)

1 pound heirloom tomatoes, cut into roughly 1-inch cubes

2 avocados, pitted and cut into roughly 1-inch cubes

½ red onion, slivered

½ teaspoon salt

¼ cup Chamoy Sauce (see here, or store-bought), plus more for topping

Add the corn to a dry skillet over medium-high heat, stirring as the kernels begin to char and pop a bit. Let them color for a couple of minutes, then put them in a large bowl.

While the pan is still hot, add the pumpkin seeds and let them toast, stirring occasionally, about 2 minutes. Put the pumpkin seeds in a small bowl with 1 teaspoon of the oil and the taco seasoning and stir well to combine. Set aside.

Add the tomatoes, avocados, onion, salt, and the remaining tablespoon of oil to the bowl with the corn, then toss gently to combine. Add the chamoy sauce and toss again.

Serve, topping each portion with an extra drizzle of chamoy and some of the pumpkin seeds.

Heirloom tomatoes are readily available at farmer’s markets and most grocery stores, but if you can’t find any, vine-ripe tomatoes will work just fine for this recipe.

title: Kale & Fennel Salad With Cherries
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

This easy salad makes for a great lunch by itself or a wonderful first course or side for a larger meal. The Apple Balsamic Vinaigrette (see here) adds subtle sweetness that plays beautifully with the cherries.

1 bunch kale (about 6 ounces), stems removed and leaves finely shredded

1 bulb fennel, cored and halved lengthwise, sliced very thinly

¼ cup Apple Balsamic Vinaigrette (see here), plus more to finish

½ cup cherries, pitted and halved

¼ cup pine nuts, toasted

Fennel fronds or other fresh herbs like parsley or chives, for garnish

Put the kale and fennel in a large bowl and toss with 2 tablespoons of vinaigrette. Knead the mixture vigorously for 1 to 2 minutes, squeezing hard to coat everything with the dressing and wilt the vegetables a bit, making them silky. Add the rest of the vinaigrette and toss well to combine.

Serve the salad with the cherries and pine nuts sprinkled on top, and garnish with a few fennel fronds or other herbs.

title: Tofu Dumpling Miso Soup
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 10 MINUTES, PLUS 1 HOUR PREP MAKES 4 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 10 MINUTES, PLUS 1 HOUR PREP MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Our research showed that Americans love Asian flavor profiles, which is wonderful given the number of longevity ingredients found in Okinawa, Singapore, and other blue zones–adjacent regions across the continent. Most Americans are likely familiar with miso soup—one of the world’s most nourishing comfort foods—and wonton soup, typically found on American Chinese restaurant menus. This recipe combines those familiar flavors and textures with plump dumplings loaded with healthy mushrooms and tofu.

This is a delicious meal, but it takes some time to assemble the dumplings. So consider this a recipe for a celebratory feast or a dinner party. The effort will be well worth it—and you can even turn making dumplings into a fun activity for your family, friends, or personal moai (the Okinawan word for a dedicated group of lifelong friends).

FOR THE DUMPLINGS

½ pound fresh shiitake mushrooms, finely chopped

½ teaspoon salt

½ pound firm tofu, pressed, drained, and finely chopped

2 scallions

1 garlic clove, minced or grated

1 teaspoon liquid aminos or fish sauce

¼ cup cilantro leaves, chopped

1 teaspoon sesame oil

1 package 3-inch square wonton wrappers

FOR THE SOUP

8 tablespoons white miso paste

2 teaspoons lemon juice

8 cups Dashi (see here, or store-bought instant dashi)

4 shiitake mushroom caps, sliced into thin strips

2 heads baby bok choy, bases cut off, separated into individual leaves

1 teaspoon sesame oil

1 teaspoon soy sauce

1 scallion, sliced

To make the dumplings, heat a dry heavy-bottomed soup pot over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and salt and stir, letting the mushroom pieces give up their liquid and shrink, browning a little, about 10 minutes. When they’re dry, remove the mushrooms from the pot and add them to a bowl with the rest of the dumpling ingredients except the wonton wrappers; mix well to combine.

Set a small bowl of water in easy reach. Lay a wonton wrapper flat in front of you and dip a finger in the water; lightly wet the edge of the square so it will stick to itself when you form the dumpling.

Put a heaping teaspoon of filling in the center of the wrapper, then fold one corner over so it touches the opposite corner, making a triangle shape. Pinch the edges together, gently pressing air out of the filling. You can leave the dumpling like this, or you can pinch the two opposite corners together to make a little packet. Put the finished dumpling on a sheet pan lined with parchment. Repeat until you have 24 dumplings or have used up all your filling.

To make the soup, wipe the soup pot clean, then add the miso, lemon juice, and dashi, whisking until the miso is dissolved. Bring the soup to a gentle boil. Add the shiitake caps and bok choy to the boiling soup, stirring to submerge the vegetables; blanch the greens for about 30 seconds until they’re a vivid green.

Use a slotted spoon to remove the vegetables and place them in a small bowl. Gently toss the vegetables with the sesame oil and soy sauce and set aside. Bring the soup back to a gentle boil and add the dumplings, stirring well so they don’t stick together. Let them cook for 5 minutes.

Use a slotted spoon to put six dumplings in each soup bowl. Ladle the soup over the dumplings, then add the bok choy and sliced mushrooms to each bowl. Garnish with the scallion and serve.

You can double or triple the dumpling recipe to freeze some for later. Just put the dumplings on parchment-lined sheet trays (making sure the dumplings don’t touch and stick together) directly in the freezer. Once they’re frozen solid, place the dumplings in zip-top freezer bags.

title: Touchdown Chili
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

Our research proved something we probably already knew: Americans love their chili. Especially come fall and football season. This hearty version is a blue zones touchdown, made with longevity-boosting legumes, whole grains, and lots of vegetables. Charring the peppers and other vegetables beforehand takes a bit of time (you can skip this step if you just don’t have the spare minutes), but the smoky notes and silky texture are well worth the effort.

This chili freezes particularly well, so it’s an excellent dish to make ahead for easy weeknight dinners served with a pile of fresh Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here). If you want it spicier, use serranos in place of the jalapeños, or keep the jalapeño seeds and membranes—that’s where most of a pepper’s heat lives!

1 cup water or vegetable stock

1 tablespoon white or yellow miso

2 poblano peppers

2 yellow bell peppers

1 cup tomatillos (about 3 to 4)

2 small zucchini

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 medium onion, diced

4 garlic cloves, chopped

2 jalapeños, seeded and diced

½ teaspoon ground coriander

½ teaspoon ground cumin

1 bay leaf

1 teaspoon salt

4 cups cooked white beans

¼ cup quinoa, rinsed for a couple of minutes and drained

2 cups Salsa Verde (see here, or store-bought)

½ cup cilantro leaves, chopped, plus more for garnish

1 ripe avocado, diced

1 to 2 limes, cut into wedges

Pour the water or stock into a bowl, add the miso, and stir until the miso dissolves. Set aside.

Heat a heavy-bottomed large soup pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Put the poblanos and bell peppers in the dry pan and char them thoroughly on all sides (do them in batches if they don’t all fit at once). You want the skin to be black in many places, and wrinkling in the rest. Use your vent fan—this can get a bit smoky.

Remove the peppers and place them in a bowl, cover it, and set the peppers aside to steam for at least 10 minutes. Add the tomatillos and zucchini to the pot, charring them on several sides, then remove them and place on a cutting board. Once cool enough to handle, chop the tomatillos and zucchini into small chunks about ½ inch across.

Use a knife to scrape the skin off the peppers and remove the seeds, discarding both, and dice the peppers.

Put the oil in the pan, heat it on medium until it shimmers, then add the onion and garlic. Sweat them, stirring regularly, until they’re translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the charred vegetables and the jalapeños and stir. Once everything is sizzling, add the coriander, cumin, and bay leaf, stir well, and let the mixture cook for another couple of minutes.

Add the salt, beans, quinoa, miso broth, and salsa verde to the pot, and stir to combine. Once the mixture begins to bubble, reduce the heat to low and let it simmer for about 15 minutes until the quinoa is cooked.

Remove the bay leaf and stir in the chopped cilantro. Taste for seasoning.

Garnish each bowl with the diced avocado and some cilantro, and bring them to the table with lime wedges.

This recipe calls for a pint of Salsa Verde (see here). You can buy some at the store if you don’t have time to make your own—or if you plan ahead, keep a container of fresh-made Salsa Verde in the freezer so you can defrost it for this tasty dish.

title: Japanese Curried Sweet Potato Stew
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Purple sweet potatoes, known as beni imo, are the cornerstone of the Okinawan diet. They’re packed with fiber and nutrients. Their purple color comes from anthocyanins, which are powerful antioxidants that make this type of sweet potato even healthier than the orange varieties.

This rich, nourishing stew uses curry powder, an Indian blend that’s also popular in Japan. Dashi, miso, and the garnishes bring the flavor firmly back to Japan.

3 cups Dashi (see here, or store-bought instant dashi)

2 tablespoons white miso

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 medium onion, diced

3 garlic cloves, minced

1 tablespoon ginger, grated

1 tablespoon curry powder

2 tablespoons yuzu juice (or lemon juice)

1 teaspoon salt

4 cups purple sweet potato, peeled and cut into ½-inch cubes (about 2 large potatoes)

1 cup cooked short-grain brown rice

1 teaspoon sesame oil, to finish

1 scallion, sliced into thin rounds, for garnish

Furikake seasoning, for garnish

Put 3 cups of the dashi in a medium bowl and gently whisk in the miso until it dissolves.

In a heavy-bottomed soup pot, heat the avocado oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and stir; let it sweat until it starts to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger, and curry powder, stir again, and let the mixture cook for another minute or so.

Add the miso broth mixture, the yuzu juice, and the salt, then add the sweet potato and stir to combine. Bring everything to a boil, then lower the heat to medium-low so it simmers gently.

Cook until the sweet potato pieces are just tender, about 15 minutes, then add the rice, stir gently, and let the stew simmer for another 5 minutes or so.

Taste for seasoning and serve with a dribble of sesame oil and some scallion and furikake on top.

The starches from the sweet potatoes and rice make this quite thick, suitable for eating with chopsticks or a spoon. If you want more of a soup, add another cup of dashi. Just remember to taste and adjust the seasoning if needed before serving.

title: Mediterranean White Bean Soup
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This hearty soup evokes the flavors of the landscape in two of the blue zones—Ikaria and Sardinia—where the hillsides are often covered in wild fennel and other aromatic herbs. It’s also packed with beans, the king of longevity foods. A long, slow simmer marries the flavors and lets the starch from the rice and beans thicken this into almost a stew. It’s even better the next day—though you may want to add a little water to thin it when reheating since the rice will soak up liquid overnight. This soup is an excellent opportunity to use some top-quality extra-virgin olive oil as a finishing touch.

1 tablespoon white miso

2 cups vegetable broth

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil (preferably oil from Garlic Confit, see here), plus 2 tablespoons to finish

4 cloves Garlic Confit (see here)

1 head fennel, tops and cores removed, sliced crosswise as thinly as you can (about 1/16 inch), fronds reserved

1 medium onion, diced

2 carrots, diced

1 rib celery, diced

1 teaspoon herbes de Provence

1 bay leaf

Juice of ½ lemon, plus zest reserved for garnish

1 teaspoon salt

2 cups cooked white beans

½ cup cooked long-grain brown rice

2 tablespoons fennel fronds, finely minced, for garnish

2 tablespoons fresh dill, finely chopped, for garnish

Whisk the miso into the broth until the miso dissolves.

In a heavy-bottomed soup pot, add 2 tablespoons of the oil and the garlic confit cloves. Use a spoon to smash the garlic into a paste and mix it into the oil.

Heat the garlic oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the fennel slices, onion, carrots, and celery, and stir well. Sweat the vegetables until they soften but do not brown, about 10 minutes.

Add the herbes de Provence and bay leaf and stir. Stir in the miso broth, lemon juice, and salt. Add the beans and rice and reduce the heat to medium-low, so it’s just bubbling; cook gently for another 10 minutes, stirring periodically to make sure nothing sticks to the pot.

Remove the bay leaf before serving. Serve topped with the lemon zest, fennel fronds, and dill, and add a drizzle of oil around the outside of each bowl.

If you have some whole-grain or sourdough bread handy, that would be a wonderful way to scoop up every drop.

title: Dashi
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 12+ HOURS (SEE SIDEBAR FOR FASTER TIME) MAKES 4 CUPS
body:
PREP TIME: 12+ HOURS (SEE SIDEBAR FOR FASTER TIME) MAKES 4 CUPS

Dashi is the mother stock of Japanese cuisine, and we use it quite a bit in some of the soups in this book. Most versions use cured, smoked bonito, but vegetarian versions—like this one—are also popular. This overnight technique makes it a no-cook breeze. Plan ahead and you can basically ignore it until it’s time to make dinner—then it takes just minutes to assemble.

4 cups water

4 dried shiitake mushrooms

1 piece kombu (dried kelp), about 4 x 4 inches

Combine all the ingredients in a large bowl, cover, and put it in the fridge overnight. When you’re ready to use the dashi, strain out the mushrooms and kelp. They can be chopped and used in other soups or stews.

If you don’t have time to let this sit overnight, combine all the ingredients in a pot and bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then lower to a bare simmer, cover the pot, and let the ingredients infuse for 20 minutes. It won’t be as nuanced as the overnight version, but it will work perfectly.

title: Easy-Peasy Falafel
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAKING IF USING DRIED BEANS MAKES 4 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAKING IF USING DRIED BEANS MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Falafel is a Blue Zones superhero that benefits from the longevity power of the mighty chickpea—a common ingredient in both Ikaria and Sardinia. Also known as garbanzo beans, chickpeas are good for digestive, bone, and cardiovascular health. Baking falafel is much easier (and healthier) than deep-frying it.

If you use dried chickpeas, you’ll have to soak them overnight. Canned chickpeas make the recipe speedier, but you’ll need to incorporate a filler, like whole wheat flour, to absorb some of the extra liquid (see sidebar).

1½ cups dried chickpeas, soaked overnight in 6 cups water and drained thoroughly (about 4 cups); or 2 (15-ounce) cans, drained and dried thoroughly on a kitchen towel

2 garlic cloves, chopped

½ medium onion, chopped

¾ cup parsley leaves, chopped

½ cup cilantro leaves and stems, chopped

¼ cup fresh dill, chopped

1 tablespoon ground cumin

1 tablespoon lemon juice

1 tablespoon plus ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided

2 teaspoons ground coriander

1 teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon baking soda

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Preheat your oven to 400°F.

Put all the ingredients except the ¼ cup of oil in your food processor and pulse repeatedly, using a spatula to scrape down the sides several times. You want the mixture to have the texture of wet sand. Put the mixture in the refrigerator for at least 10 minutes or up to an hour. This rest helps your falafel stick together, so don’t skip it.

Pour 2 tablespoons of the remaining oil onto a sheet pan and spread it around to evenly coat the surface.

Wet your hands and grab ¼-cup-size handfuls of the falafel mixture and form them into small patties about 2 inches across and ½ inch thick. Place the patties on the pan, taking care not to crowd them. You should end up with at least 12 patties. (If you want to serve these like burgers, make the patties larger, about 4 inches across.)

Brush the remaining 2 tablespoons of oil over the tops of the patties and put the tray in the oven. Bake for 30 minutes, flipping the patties halfway through. You want crispy brown outsides and fluffy, tender insides.

Serve on a salad of arugula, cherry tomato, cucumber, and slivered red onion with Black Tahini Dressing (see here) or Tahini-Miso Sauce (see here), as burgers on whole-grain buns, or as part of a Mediterranean platter with Hummus (see here) and veggies.

If you use canned chickpeas, your patties won’t hold together without a filler because they’ll be too wet. Add 4 to 6 teaspoons whole wheat flour to your mixture to help canned beans hold together better.

title: Pesto Polenta
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Italian flavor profiles are superpopular with America’s home cooks—and in the blue zones—and this recipe delivers those in spades. Whisking pesto into polenta results in a creamy and intensely flavorful base for just about any sauce. Try it with our Roasted Tomato Sauce (see here) or Roasted Root Vegetable Medley (see here).

1 cup polenta

¼ cup Red Pesto (see here, or store-bought)

In a saucepan, bring 3 cups of water to a boil over high heat. Whisk in the polenta, mixing until there are no lumps, and return the pot to a boil. Lower the heat to a simmer; use the whisk to stir the polenta regularly so it doesn’t stick to the bottom.

The polenta will begin to thicken and bubble; adjust the heat if it’s spattering too much. Keep whisking well every couple of minutes until the polenta is tender, about 20 minutes. Then add the pesto and whisk vigorously to combine thoroughly, digging down into the corners of the saucepan with the whisk to get it all.

Pairing suggestion: Spoon some polenta onto each plate and top with a generous dollop of Roasted Tomato Sauce (see here) and some fresh basil.

Leftover polenta solidifies into a pretty firm texture. Take advantage of this by storing it in a lightly oiled rectangular container. The next day, you can easily remove the block of polenta and slice it. It’s wonderful sautéed or grilled.

title: Yuba Noodle Stir-Fry With Chile Crisp
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Yuba is a great high-protein, legume-rich alternative to pasta. It’s a product of tofu making, but it’s formed into dry sheets that work beautifully as wide noodles—almost like pappardelle or sen yai (like you’d find in pad see ew). They just need to be soaked in hot water for 10 minutes to soften. Most brands of chile crisp are quite spicy; if you want a milder dish, cut the amount in half and add an extra teaspoon of sesame oil.

FOR THE SAUCE

¼ cup soy sauce

3 tablespoons rice vinegar

2 tablespoons chile crisp

2 teaspoons fresh ginger, grated

2 garlic cloves, grated

1 teaspoon sesame oil

¼ teaspoon cornstarch

FOR THE STIR-FRY

2 tablespoons avocado oil

½ pound yuba sheets, soaked in hot tap water for at least 10 minutes, drained, then sliced into noodle-size strips

1 cup edamame

1 cucumber, halved lengthwise and sliced about ⅛ inch thick

1 tablespoon toasted black and white sesame seeds, for garnish

2 scallions, thinly sliced, for garnish

More chile crisp, for garnish (optional)

Whisk together all the sauce ingredients in a small bowl until thoroughly combined. Set aside.

Heat the avocado oil in a wok or large sauté pan over high heat until it shimmers, then add the yuba and toss well to coat, about 30 seconds. Add the edamame and the cucumber and stir well, then add the sauce and toss well to combine. Cook until the sauce begins to thicken a bit, another 3 minutes or so.

Put the stir-fry in a serving bowl, top with sesame seeds and scallions, and serve with more chile crisp on the side (if desired).

Be sure to buy yuba sheets, not sticks. The sticks are thicker and generally require cooking or a much longer soak to hydrate.

title: Southern-Style Sheet Pan BBQ Tofu With Sweet Corn & Green Beans
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Research showed us that Americans enjoy southern flavors, and in particular they love a good barbecue. You can skip the burgers and dogs and sub in this crowd-pleasing sheet pan dinner, which packs all the smoky, spicy barbecue flavors you crave into a longevity-friendly assortment of vegetables.

FOR THE MARINADE

3 tablespoons avocado oil

1 tablespoon red wine vinegar

1 tablespoon honey

FOR THE BBQ SPICE RUB

1 teaspoon onion powder

1 teaspoon garlic powder

1 teaspoon ground cumin

1 teaspoon chipotle powder

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (sweet or hot, according to taste)

1 teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

FOR THE TOFU AND VEGETABLES

1 block firm tofu, pressed and drained, halved lengthwise and then cut into ½-inch slices

6 ounces green beans, trimmed

2 ears sweet corn, cut into ribs (see sidebar)

1 cup sweet potatoes, peeled and cut into roughly ¾-inch slices (about 1 large potato)

1 medium onion, quartered lengthwise, quarters halved crosswise

Preheat your oven to 400°F.

In a small bowl, whisk the marinade ingredients together until combined. In another small bowl, mix the spice rub ingredients together until combined.

Put the tofu and vegetables on a large sheet pan and toss them in the marinade until evenly coated. Then toss again in the spice mixture, making sure everything gets a nice coating. Spread everything into a single layer and bake for 30 minutes, using a spatula to flip the tofu and vegetables over after about 20 minutes so they can brown on both sides.

Transfer to a serving dish and bring to the table family style.

Pairing suggestion: This is wonderful with the rich, cooling Avocado-Herb Sauce (see here).

To cut corn into ribs safely, trim the ends off each ear so they have a flat top and bottom. Stand each ear on its thicker end and place the blade of your knife right in the middle of the central cob. Rock the knife back and forth to work the blade down while holding the corn from the top with your other hand, taking care to keep that hand above the knife blade at all times. Keep rocking the blade and pushing down until you reach the bottom. Do the same thing with each half ear so you end up with long rib-shaped quarters.

title: Tropical Poke Bowls
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

We’ve founded Blue Zones Project Cities in a number of Hawaiian communities across the islands. While the community-led initiative aims to improve well-being by making healthy choices easier, there’s an existing rich food culture in Hawaii with plenty of its own longevity benefits. We skipped the fish for our version, replacing it with Blue Zones all-stars—legumes, purple sweet potatoes, leafy greens, whole grains, sea vegetables, and fresh fruit.

FOR THE DRESSING

1 cup coconut milk

¼ cup cilantro leaves

Juice of 1 lime

1 tablespoon white miso

1 teaspoon fresh galangal or ginger, grated

1 green Thai chile, chopped

FOR THE BOWLS

1 cup cabbage, finely shredded

1 scallion, sliced

Salt

4 cups cooked short-grain brown rice

1 cup edamame

1 cup ripe pineapple, diced

1 cup cooked black beans

1 cup purple sweet potato, mashed*

¼ cup dried ogo or hijiki seaweed, soaked in water for at least 10 minutes

* See instructions for baking potatoes in the microwave on see here.

Put all the dressing ingredients in a blender and blend until smooth and creamy. Set aside.

Put the cabbage and scallion in a bowl with a pinch of salt and knead for 1 minute until the cabbage begins to wilt.

To assemble the bowls, put a cup of rice in each bowl, then top with ¼ cup each of edamame, pineapple, black beans, sweet potato, and the cabbage mixture. Garnish each bowl with seaweed and drizzle dressing on top before serving.

Thai chiles are hot! If you want a milder dressing, substitute a jalapeño.

title: Misir Wot
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Misir Wot is a traditional recipe from Ethiopia, a country that knows a thing or two about cooking flavorful, veggie- and fiber-rich dishes, as I explored in The Blue Zones American Kitchen. These spicy lentils are creamy and easy to make because dried lentils don’t require presoaking or cooking ahead of time. This makes a fantastic side or a standalone meal paired with some Easy Spelt Flatbreads (see here) and a salad.

2 tablespoons coconut oil

1 red onion, diced

4 garlic cloves, grated

1 teaspoon fresh ginger, grated

2 tablespoons berbere

2 plum tomatoes, diced

1 cup dried red lentils

1 to 1½ teaspoons salt (see sidebar)

2½ cups water or vegetable stock

Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed soup pot over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the onion and sauté until it softens, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, stir, and cook for 2 more minutes.

Add the berbere, stir, and cook for 1 more minute before adding the tomatoes and stirring again. Cook until the tomatoes soften, about 2 more minutes.

Add the lentils, salt, and water or stock, and stir well. As soon as the liquid begins to boil, lower the heat to medium-low. Cover the pot and cook until the lentils are soft, about 20 minutes.

Berbere is a spice blend used in many Ethiopian dishes. Some versions contain salt, which will determine how much additional salt you add to this recipe. If the berbere you buy contains salt, add only 1 additional teaspoon to the recipe. As always, let your taste buds be your guide.

title: Sunday Supper Lasagna
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 1 HOUR MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Lasagna is always a crowd-pleaser—and it’s one of the most sought-after recipes, according to our research. This version skips most of the dairy ingredients in traditional lasagna in favor of longevity-friendly ingredients, so it’s packed with tons of nutrition and great flavor. Yes, it takes some time to make, but if your family has a Sunday supper tradition, this will be a great addition to your recipe rotation.

FOR THE WHITE BEAN–PINE NUT CREAM

1 cup cooked white beans

1 cup pine nuts, soaked overnight in 2 cups water and drained, a bit of the soaking water reserved

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil

2 tablespoons nutritional yeast

2 teaspoons liquid aminos

2 teaspoons red wine vinegar

1 teaspoon honey

½ teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon smoked paprika

⅛ teaspoon freshly grated nutmeg

FOR THE TOMATO SAUCE

1 (28-ounce) can crushed tomatoes or tomato puree

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 garlic clove, grated

½ teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon dried oregano

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

FOR THE LASAGNA

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

1 package durum wheat lasagna noodles, boiled in salted water until just al dente

1 butternut squash, peeled and sliced into thin (⅛ inch or thinner) sheets using a mandoline

8 ounces spinach

½ cup nutritional yeast or grated pecorino

Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

To make the cream, put all the ingredients in a large bowl. Use an immersion blender to blend until smooth, adding a bit of the reserved pine nut soaking water to thin out if needed. (You can also use a regular blender for this step.) Taste for seasoning and set aside.

To make the tomato sauce, blend all the sauce ingredients together in a large bowl using an immersion blender until smooth. (You can also do this in a regular blender.) Set aside.

To make the lasagna, pour the oil into a 9-x-9-inch baking dish and spread to coat evenly. Add a layer of noodles, then a scant ¼ cup of the white bean–pine nut cream, smoothing it out into an even layer. Add a layer of squash, then a scant ¼ cup of tomato sauce, spreading evenly. Top that with a layer of spinach. Repeat the layers in order, ending with a final layer of noodles at the top of the dish. Spread a layer of white bean–pine nut cream on top. Sprinkle the nutritional yeast or pecorino on top, then add a few twists of pepper. Bake for 1 hour; let rest for 5 to 10 minutes before serving.

If you don’t have a mandoline, you can slice the squash as thinly as possible using a knife, or use a vegetable peeler to shave the squash into thin sheets. Thinner slices cook faster, yielding a more tender result.

If you’re short on time, you can use store-bought tomato sauce instead of making your own. Or if you’ve made and frozen our Roasted Tomato Sauce (see here), you can defrost it and use that.

title: Chile Tofu With Charred Snow Peas
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Our research showed a lot of things Americans look for in a recipe. At the top of that list: a quick and easy meal that’s cooked in 30 minutes or less. This stir-fry delivers on that with a ton of flavor from spicy gochujang sauce, which you can find at most grocery stores.

FOR THE SAUCE

2 tablespoons gochujang

2 tablespoons water

2 tablespoons soy sauce

1 tablespoon honey

1 tablespoon lemon or lime juice

2 teaspoons sesame oil

1 teaspoon ginger, freshly grated

1 garlic clove, grated

FOR THE STIR-FRY

2 tablespoons avocado oil

6 ounces snow peas

1 carrot, peeled and thinly sliced on the bias

6 ounces Chinese broccoli, chopped

1 block firm tofu, pressed and drained, cut into 1- to 1½-inch cubes

1 tablespoon toasted sesame seeds, for garnish

1 scallion, thinly sliced, for garnish

In a small bowl, whisk the sauce ingredients until fully combined. Set aside.

Heat a wok or large sauté pan over high heat and add the oil, turning the pan to coat evenly. Add the snow peas and cook, stirring occasionally, letting the pea pods blacken in a few spots, about 3 minutes. Add the carrot and cook for another 2 minutes, then add the broccoli, tossing well to combine. Cook for 3 more minutes, then add the tofu and stir well. Add the sauce, tossing to thoroughly combine.

Lower the heat to medium and let everything cook for another 2 minutes, then put the mixture in a serving bowl. Top with sesame seeds and scallions.

Pairing suggestion: Serve over steamed short-grain brown rice with some kimchi on the side.

title: Easy Spelt Flatbreads
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 15 TO 20 MINUTES, PLUS 40 MINUTES PREP MAKES 6 (8-INCH) OR 8 (6-INCH) FLATBREADS
body:
COOK TIME: 15 TO 20 MINUTES, PLUS 40 MINUTES PREP MAKES 6 (8-INCH) OR 8 (6-INCH) FLATBREADS

This five-ingredient recipe makes quick, easy, and nutritious flatbreads that are perfect as a base for open-faced sandwiches and personal-size pizzas or for mopping up soups and stews.

2 cups spelt flour, plus more for dusting

1 teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon baking soda

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil

Put the flour, salt, and baking soda in a large bowl and mix well to combine. Add the oil and mix again, then stir in ¼ cup of water until you have a shaggy dough with no dry flour remaining in the bowl. Let the dough rest, covered, for 5 minutes, then use your hands to knead the dough gently in the bowl. After a couple of minutes you’ll see it come together, sticking to itself rather than to the bowl or your hands.

Lightly dust a work surface with a little flour, move the dough to the surface, and gently knead it for about 5 minutes, pulling it toward you and folding it over on itself, then pushing it away from you before rotating the dough a quarter turn and repeating the fold-and-push motion. Once it’s glossy and the surface is a little bouncy, form the dough into a ball, wrap it in plastic, and let it rest for 20 minutes.

To make the flatbreads, heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over medium heat. Unwrap the dough and flatten the ball a bit; cut it like a pizza into 6 or 8 wedge-shaped slices. Roll each wedge into a ball with your hands, then use a rolling pin to flatten each ball into a circle about 1/16 inch thick. Don’t worry if they’re not perfectly round—they’ll still work and taste great.

Cook each flatbread in the skillet for 1 to 2 minutes per side—you’ll want to see nice dark brown spots but no blackening. Stack the cooked breads on a plate as you go; they’ll keep each other warm and the steam will help them stay flexible.

Don’t throw your flatbreads away if they get stale! Just break or cut them into pieces and toast them in a pan with a little extra-virgin olive oil, salt, and garlic powder to make wonderful croutons that add a tasty crunch to soups and salads.

FLATBREAD TOPPING IDEAS

PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES

FOR THE SEASONED SALT

1 teaspoon coarse salt

1 teaspoon nutritional yeast

1 teaspoon herbes de Provence

½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

FOR EACH FLATBREAD

1 clove garlic, chopped, and 1 tablespoon oil from Garlic Confit (see here)

½ teaspoon seasoned salt

1 fresh ripe heirloom tomato or vine-ripe tomato, sliced

5 to 6 basil leaves

Extra-virgin olive oil, to finish

To make the seasoned salt, put everything in a mortar or spice grinder and pound or grind until you have a powder. Store leftovers in an airtight container in the pantry for up to a month.

Spoon some garlic confit and its oil onto each flatbread and spread evenly. Sprinkle on about ¼ teaspoon of the seasoned salt, then add a layer of tomato. Tuck a basil leaf under each tomato slice to create a pinwheel effect, then sprinkle another ¼ teaspoon of seasoned salt over the top. Finish with a drizzle of your best extra-virgin olive oil.

PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES

FOR EACH FLATBREAD

2 tablespoons Red Pesto (see here)

2 oil-cured Calabrian chiles, sliced

4 artichoke hearts, halved (or quartered if large)

Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

1 tablespoon Italian parsley leaves, chopped

Extra-virgin olive oil, to finish

Spread the pesto on each flatbread, then add the chiles and artichokes, distributing them evenly over the pesto. Add a few twists of pepper, scatter the parsley around, and finish with a drizzle of your best extra-virgin olive oil.

COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES

FOR EACH FLATBREAD

3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, divided

1 garlic clove, grated

½ teaspoon salt, divided

¼ teaspoon herbes de Provence

Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

1 king trumpet mushroom, sliced about ⅛ inch thick

1 tablespoon lemon juice

2 teaspoons white miso

1 cup baby arugula

Set your oven to broil on high.

Brush each flatbread using 1 tablespoon of the oil, then sprinkle with the garlic, ¼ teaspoon of the salt, the herbes de Provence, and the pepper. Arrange the mushroom slices in an even layer, extending to the edges of the flatbread, then brush with another tablespoon of the oil and sprinkle with the remaining salt.

Broil for 5 minutes, until the mushrooms are beginning to brown. Be careful that the edges of the flatbreads don’t start to burn.

While the flatbreads bake, whisk the remaining oil and the miso in a medium bowl until smooth. Toss the arugula in the miso dressing until evenly coated.

Arrange the salad on top of each flatbread and serve.

PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES

FOR EACH FLATBREAD

2 tablespoons Hummus (see here, or store-bought)

½ roasted red pepper in oil, drained and sliced

¼ cup Crispy Roasted Chickpeas (see here)

1 tablespoon Italian parsley, finely chopped

Extra-virgin olive oil, to finish

Spread the hummus on the flatbread in an even layer. Arrange the pepper slices on top, then fill in the open areas with chickpeas. Finish with parsley and a drizzle of your best extra-virgin olive oil and serve.

title: Spanakopita Pasta
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This recipe is a two-for-one: Spanakopita is a popular dish in Greece (we featured a version in the Ikaria chapter of The Blue Zones Kitchen), and pasta recipes are among the most favored in American kitchens. In this recipe, we infuse a tasty pasta dish with the flavor profiles of Greece’s spinach-and-herb pie. The result is tangy, creamy, and satisfying—and the sauce comes together in the time it takes to boil the pasta.

1 box durum wheat spaghetti

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 medium onion, diced

3 garlic cloves, chopped

12 ounces spinach, washed and dried

½ cup marinated artichoke hearts

1 teaspoon herbes de Provence

¼ cup fresh dill, coarsely chopped, plus extra for garnish

¼ cup Italian parsley, coarsely chopped, plus extra for garnish

½ cup silken tofu, cubed

1 tablespoon lemon juice

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast

1 teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

1 tablespoon white or yellow miso

½ cup crumbled feta or vegan substitute, for garnish (optional)

Cook the spaghetti until al dente according to the package instructions, reserving ½ cup of the cooking water.

While pasta is cooking, put the oil in a pot over medium-high heat. When it starts to shimmer, add the onion and garlic; let them sweat, stirring, for a couple of minutes. Add the spinach and stir, mixing to help it wilt. Once the spinach is evenly wilted and dark green, about 5 minutes, add the artichoke hearts and herbs, stirring to combine, and cook until fragrant, another 3 minutes. Add the tofu, lemon juice, nutritional yeast, salt, pepper, and miso, and stir again until combined.

Remove the pot from the heat and use an immersion blender to puree everything until you have a smooth green sauce. If it’s very thick, add a little pasta water 1 tablespoon at a time to thin it.

Put the cooked spaghetti in a serving bowl, add ¾ of the sauce, and toss thoroughly to combine. Taste for seasoning.

To serve, spoon the remaining sauce over the top of the pasta and garnish with the herbs and feta (if using).

title: Cauliflower Steaks With Tomatoes & Grapes
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Roasting cauliflower in thick, steaklike slices makes it tender but substantial and serves as a good alternative to a slab of meat. Liven the flavors of the earthy cauliflower with warm spices and sweetness from grapes and tomatoes.

1 cauliflower

1 teaspoon ground coriander

½ teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

½ teaspoon turmeric

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

½ teaspoon salt

8 ounces cherry tomatoes
