8 ounces seedless grapes

3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

¼ cup hazelnuts, chopped

¼ cup Garlic Confit Vinaigrette (see here)

Fresh cilantro sprigs, for garnish

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Trim the leaves off the cauliflower and cut the stalk so it’s flush with the bottom of the head. Turn the head on its side and cut roughly 1-inch-thick round slices so that the core holds them together. Some florets and bits will inevitably fall off, but don’t worry—use them, too.

Combine all the spices and the salt in a small bowl. Arrange the cauliflower slices on a sheet pan, and sprinkle the spice mixture evenly over them. Add the tomatoes and grapes to the pan so that they fill in the gaps between the cauliflower pieces. Drizzle the oil over everything, using a brush or your hand to spread it around so all the food is coated.

Roast in the oven until the cauliflower stalks are fork-tender and the tomatoes and grapes start to get nice and brown on top and split open, about 40 minutes. Scatter the hazelnuts around the pan and roast for another 5 minutes to toast them.

To serve, plate each cauliflower steak with nuts and a few grapes and tomatoes, pushing down on them a bit so they pop and release their juices. Spoon a tablespoon of the vinaigrette over each cauliflower steak, add a few cilantro sprigs, and enjoy.

Leftovers make a wonderful (and very packable) lunch the next day. Just cut the steaks into individual florets and toss everything well with vinaigrette before putting your leftovers in the fridge to marinate overnight.

title: Mushroom & Black Bean Birria
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Birria is a slow-cooked Mexican stew that’s often strained and served alongside tacos as a dipping sauce. And it’s becoming more popular in recipe trends in America, too—no surprise, since our research found U.S. diners love Mexican flavor profiles. You can choose to serve this dish strained as a taco filling or as is as a stew. Traditionally, birria is made with meat, but this Blue Zones version delivers great flavor and tons of fiber along with the magical health benefits of black beans.

FOR THE CHILE PASTE

4 ancho chiles

4 pasilla chiles

2 chiles de arbol

8 peppercorns

2 whole cloves

1 teaspoon ground cumin

1 teaspoon ground coriander

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

½ cinnamon stick

1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves, chopped

1 teaspoon Mexican oregano

8 garlic cloves

2 bay leaves

½ white or yellow onion

1 (14-ounce) can crushed tomatoes

¼ cup apple cider vinegar

½ teaspoon salt

FOR THE BIRRIA

2 tablespoons avocado oil

½ white or yellow onion, diced

1 pound button mushrooms, halved or quartered into bite-size pieces

1 pound cremini mushrooms, halved or quartered into bite-size pieces

½ teaspoon salt

2 cups cooked black beans

6 cups vegetable stock or Dashi (see here)

TO SERVE (OPTIONAL)

Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here)

1 cup cilantro sprigs, chopped

½ cup onion, diced

1 to 2 jalapeños, sliced

2 limes, quartered

To make the chile paste, in a large dry pot, toast the chiles over medium-high heat until soft and fragrant, about 2 minutes per side. Remove the chiles and use a knife to remove their stems and seeds, discarding both. Set the chiles aside in a bowl.

In the same pot, toast the peppercorns, cloves, cumin, coriander, paprika, and cinnamon until fragrant and just beginning to smoke, 1 to 2 minutes. Put the toasted spices and remaining chile paste ingredients in a high-power blender with the peppers and puree until you have a smooth paste. Set aside.

To make the birria, wipe the pot clean, then add the oil and heat over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and sauté until it begins to turn translucent, about 3 minutes. Add the mushrooms and stir well, then add the salt and stir again. Sauté the mushrooms until they give up their liquid and begin to brown, about 5 minutes.

Add the beans, stock, and chile paste mixture to the pot and stir well to combine. Bring everything to a boil, then lower the heat to medium-low and let simmer to meld the flavors, about 15 minutes.

Taste for seasoning and serve as a stew. If you want to make tacos, strain the birria and put the mushroom-bean mixture in one serving bowl and the liquid in another. Either way, serve with the tortillas and garnishes, taco bar style.

title: Cozy Roasted Vegetables With Cider-Horseradish Glaze
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS AS A MAIN; 8 SERVINGS AS A SIDE
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS AS A MAIN; 8 SERVINGS AS A SIDE

Cozy season brings cooks back into the kitchen, and this combination of squash, brussels sprouts, sage, and apple cider practically screams autumn. It’s a great one-pan dinner, or the perfect side dish for a holiday gathering.

FOR THE GLAZE

2 tablespoons apple cider

1 tablespoon prepared horseradish

1 tablespoon maple syrup

FOR THE VEGETABLES

1 pound butternut squash, peeled, seeded, and cut into 1-inch cubes

1 pound brussels sprouts, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise

½ red onion, chopped

½ cup walnuts, chopped

¼ cup dried currants or raisins

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

2 teaspoons balsamic vinegar

½ teaspoon salt

1 teaspoon sage leaves, chopped

¼ teaspoon ground allspice

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

2 tablespoons chives, minced, for garnish

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

In a small bowl, whisk the glaze ingredients together and set aside.

Toss the remaining ingredients except the chives together on a sheet pan and spread evenly onto the pan. Roast for 30 minutes, then drizzle the glaze over the vegetables, stir gently, and return to the oven for another 15 minutes.

Sprinkle chives over the top before serving.

title: Beans & Greens “Risotto”
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAKING FOR FARRO MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAKING FOR FARRO MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

The Italian word farro covers three kinds of ancient wheat: spelt, emmer, and einkorn. Whole farro grains have a nutty flavor and are great cooked al dente like risotto. Soaking the grain overnight requires advance planning, but it makes night-of cooking quick and easy. This version of risotto uses dandelion greens, which are closely related to some of the wild greens that centenarians in Sardinia and Ikaria regularly enjoy in meals and as teas.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

½ yellow or white onion, finely diced

2 garlic cloves, minced

3 sprigs oregano, leaves stripped and chopped

3 sprigs rosemary, leaves stripped and chopped

3 sprigs thyme, leaves stripped and chopped

1 bay leaf

8 ounces dandelion greens, chopped

1 cup farro, rinsed and soaked overnight in 4 cups water and drained

2 cups cooked cannellini beans

2 cups vegetable stock

Juice of ½ lemon

1 teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

½ cup Italian parsley, chopped, for garnish

In a heavy-bottomed skillet, heat the oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and sauté until it begins to turn translucent, about 3 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 2 more minutes, then add the oregano, rosemary, thyme, and bay leaf, stirring well.

Add the greens, stirring to combine, and cook until they’re completely wilted and dark green, about 5 minutes. Add the farro, beans, stock, lemon juice, salt, and pepper, and stir gently to combine.

Bring everything to a boil, then lower to a simmer and cover the pot. Cook until the farro is tender, about 20 minutes. Taste for seasoning, remove the bay leaf, and serve with parsley sprinkled on top.

If you can’t find dandelion greens, you can substitute escarole, frisée, or another type of endive.

title: Spiced Chickpeas & Spinach
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 2 HOURS, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAKING FOR BEANS MAKES 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 2 HOURS, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAKING FOR BEANS MAKES 6 SERVINGS

Infused with harissa for warmth, this versatile dish serves as a great vegetarian main, offering protein, greens, and plenty of spice. Easy to make and rich in flavor, it’s perfect for a comfort meal on a chilly evening, or you can make a big batch to reheat for lunch throughout the week.

½ cup dried chickpeas, soaked overnight, rinsed, and drained

8 to 10 curry leaf sprigs, or more to taste if you like spicier

2 tablespoons harissa

1 tablespoon avocado oil

2 shallots, thinly sliced

4 garlic cloves, crushed

4 cups fresh spinach (about 32 ounces)

Fresh mint or cilantro, chopped, for garnish

Chile flakes (optional)

Put the chickpeas in a large, ovenproof sauté pan and cover with fresh water. Add the curry leaves, then bring the mixture to a simmer over medium heat. Once simmering, lower the temperature to low or simmer; cover the pan and cook until the chickpeas are tender, about 1 hour.

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Strain the chickpeas, reserving 1 cup of the cooking liquid. Mix the reserved liquid with the harissa in a small bowl. Set aside.

In the same sauté pan, heat the oil over medium heat. Once it begins to shimmer, add the shallots and garlic; cook until translucent, about 2 minutes. Add the spinach, cooking until wilted, about 3 to 5 minutes.

Add the chickpeas and remaining cooking liquid back to the pan; stir to combine. Cover and put in the oven to roast for 90 minutes.

Serve garnished with fresh mint or cilantro and a sprinkle of red chile flakes for an optional extra kick.

title: Portobello Fajitas
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

These incredibly delicious fajitas get loads of flavor from simple ingredients like mushrooms, onions, peppers, and household spices. Our version calls for portobellos, but other types of mushrooms would also work well, depending on what you have handy.

6 tablespoons avocado oil

4 tablespoons lime juice

4 teaspoons liquid aminos or fish sauce

2 garlic cloves, finely grated

2 teaspoons chipotle powder

2 teaspoons ground cumin

1 teaspoon salt

6 portobello mushroom caps, cleaned and cut into ¼-inch strips

2 medium white or yellow onions, slivered

2 red, yellow, or orange bell peppers, seeded and cut into ¼-inch strips

Fresh cilantro sprigs, for garnish

1 lime, quartered, for garnish

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

In a large bowl, whisk the oil, lime juice, liquid aminos or fish sauce, garlic, chipotle powder, cumin, and salt together until fully combined.

Add the mushrooms, onions, and bell peppers to the bowl and toss in the marinade until everything is fully coated.

Spread the mixture in a single layer on a sheet pan and bake for 45 minutes, until everything is tender and starting to brown nicely in places. Give the pan a little shake and stir at around the 30-minute mark to help things brown a bit more. Garnish with cilantro and lime wedges before serving.

Pairing suggestion: Serve with Refried Beans (see here), Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here), and the salsa of your choice, such as Salsa Verde (see here), Pico de Gallo (see here), or Avocado-Herb Sauce (see here).

title: Butternut Squash & Pineapple al Pastor
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS

This showstopper dish brings the deep, spicy flavors of a Mexican al pastor marinade to alternating layers of butternut squash and pineapple. The result is wonderfully complex and satisfying—perfect on its own or folded inside corn tortillas.

FOR THE MARINADE

4 dried guajillo chiles

2 dried ancho chiles

Boiling water

3 garlic cloves

1 chipotle in adobo sauce (optional; use more if you want extra spice)

¼ cup apple cider vinegar

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 teaspoon Mexican oregano

1 teaspoon ground cumin

1 teaspoon achiote or annatto powder (or hot paprika)

1 tablespoon honey

1 teaspoon salt

FOR THE SQUASH AND PINEAPPLE

1 large butternut squash neck, cut right where the bulbous part begins, peeled and halved lengthwise, then sliced into ¼-inch-thick half circles

1 pineapple, peeled, cored, and sliced in half lengthwise, then sliced into ¼-inch-thick half circles

1 cup cilantro leaves, chopped, for garnish

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

To make the marinade, put the dried guajillo and ancho chiles in a small bowl and pour just enough boiling water over them to cover. Let them soften in the water for 10 minutes, or more if needed (they should be pliable and plump), then remove from the bowl, reserving the soaking water. Remove and discard the seeds and stems.

In a medium bowl, combine the softened chiles, garlic, chipotle (if using), vinegar, oil, oregano, cumin, achiote or annatto powder, honey, and salt, and use an immersion blender to blend into a paste. Use a little of the chile soaking water if needed to loosen the paste, making sure to scrape down the sides of the bowl so that everything gets pureed. (You can also use a regular blender for this step.) You want a smooth, spreadable paste.

In a 13-x-9-inch baking dish, arrange the squash and pineapple in alternating rows, cut sides down, making two columns that look like half-cylinder loaves. Rub the pineapple and squash all over with the marinade, using a spatula or your hands (wear gloves if using your hands). Make sure everything is evenly coated.

Bake for 40 minutes, or until the squash is completely fork-tender. Remove from the oven and sprinkle with cilantro.

Pairing suggestion: Serve with a big stack of Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here); a plate of fresh cilantro sprigs, sliced jalapeños, and lime wedges; and the salsa of your choice, such as Pico de Gallo (see here) or Avocado-Herb Sauce (see here).

When peeling the squash, be sure to get all the way down to the orange flesh since the inner skin will remain tough even after cooking.

title: Mushroom & Walnut Bolognese
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 1 TO 4 HOURS MAKES 4 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 1 TO 4 HOURS MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Spaghetti and meatballs or meat sauce tops the recipe charts in the United States, so we decided to make a Blue Zones version of a classic Sunday sauce that’s well worth the time and effort to impress family and friends at dinnertime. But we’ve reinvented the classic with longevity ingredients: mushrooms, walnuts, red wine, and a variety of fiber-rich vegetables. You can also make this in the slow cooker (see sidebar) and set it and forget it.

2 tablespoons plus ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided

1 pound button or cremini mushrooms, trimmed and wiped with a damp towel, shredded with a food processor or large holes of a box grater

1 medium onion, diced

1 carrot, peeled and diced

1 celery rib, diced

4 garlic cloves, chopped

½ teaspoon red pepper flakes

1 teaspoon dried oregano

½ teaspoon dried thyme

2 bay leaves

½ cup walnuts, finely chopped

1 teaspoon salt

½ cup red wine

1 (14-ounce) can crushed or pureed tomatoes

1 teaspoon liquid aminos or fish sauce

½ cup unsweetened soy milk

1 box durum wheat spaghetti, cooked according to package instructions, cooking water reserved

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast or ¼ cup pecorino, plus more for garnish (optional)

½ cup basil leaves, torn, for garnish

In a heavy-bottomed soup pot, heat 2 tablespoons of the olive oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the mushrooms and stir well; sauté until they give up their liquid and begin to brown a bit, about 10 minutes. Add the onion, carrot, celery, garlic, red pepper flakes, oregano, thyme, bay leaves, walnuts, and salt, and stir well to combine. Continue sautéing until the vegetables soften and begin to color, another 10 minutes or so.

Add the red wine and stir, scraping up any brown bits off the bottom of the pot. Then add the tomatoes, liquid aminos or fish sauce, and soy milk, and stir well. Lower the heat to a bare simmer and let the sauce cook, stirring occasionally to be sure it isn’t sticking, for an hour. If the sauce starts to stick, add ¼ cup of water and stir well. Let it continue simmering for at least another 40 minutes or up to 4 hours for deeper flavors. Remove the bay leaves.

Add the pasta to the pot and stir well. Add the remaining ¼ cup of oil and the nutritional yeast or pecorino, stir again, and add a ladle of pasta water if the sauce needs to be thinned out.

Serve immediately, topping each mound of pasta with a little extra sauce from the pot, the basil leaves, and a sprinkling of nutritional yeast or pecorino if desired.

For a slow cooker version, put all the ingredients except the spaghetti and garnishes in a slow cooker, mix well, and set to low heat. Let it cook, covered, for 12 hours. Keep it warm until you’re ready to serve with freshly made spaghetti.

title: Roasted Cabbage Steaks With Apples
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS AS A MAIN; 8 SERVINGS AS A SIDE
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS AS A MAIN; 8 SERVINGS AS A SIDE

This is one steak the Blue Zones can get behind. Cabbage and apple are a classic fall pairing. Roasted together, they offer a sweet and savory dish that’s as flavorful as it is filling. The Apple Balsamic Vinaigrette (see here) makes this completely irresistible.

1 red cabbage, leaves and stalk trimmed

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, divided

2 tart baking apples, halved and cored

½ teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon ground caraway seeds

¼ teaspoon ground juniper berries

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

½ cup walnuts, chopped

3 tablespoons Apple Balsamic Vinaigrette (see here), plus more to taste

¼ cup Italian parsley, chopped

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Turn the cabbage on its side and slice it into roughly 1-inch-thick rounds with the core at the center to hold each slice together. Drizzle 1 tablespoon of the oil onto a sheet pan and spread it around evenly. Place the cabbage rounds on the pan and drizzle the remaining oil on top. Arrange the apple halves cut side down in between the cabbage.

In a small bowl, mix the salt and spices together; sprinkle the mixture over the cabbage slices, rubbing gently to spread evenly. Bake for 40 minutes, then scatter the walnuts on top of the cabbage and apples and bake for another 5 minutes.

Serve each cabbage steak with an apple half on top, some walnuts, and a generous drizzle of vinaigrette. Top with some parsley.

title: Middle Eastern Roasted Whole Cauliflower
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 1 HOUR MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Cauliflower is a versatile member of the superhealthy cruciferous vegetable family, which is known for its heart-healthy, anti-inflammatory, and immune-boosting properties, among other benefits. This recipe is a showpiece of a side dish, bursting with flavor from its Middle Eastern spice blend—a growing popular flavor trend in U.S. homes.

The key to a perfectly roasted cauliflower is to steam it first, getting it nice and tender before removing the lid to let the water evaporate, giving it a beautiful roasted exterior.

FOR THE SPICE RUB

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

1 teaspoon harissa

½ teaspoon ground cinnamon

½ teaspoon ground allspice

¾ teaspoon ground cloves

½ teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

½ teaspoon turmeric

½ teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

FOR THE CAULIFLOWER

1 whole cauliflower, leaves trimmed and stalk cut flush to the base of the head

½ cup boiling water

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Combine the spice rub ingredients in a small bowl, then spread the rub all over the outside of the cauliflower—don’t put any on the bottom—working it into the crevices between the florets as best you can. Put the cauliflower in a deep, ovenproof pot with a lid, then carefully pour the boiling water into the pot, but not directly over the cauliflower (to avoid washing off any of the spice rub). Put the lid on the pot and put it in the oven for 30 minutes.

Remove the lid and return the pot to the oven. Let the cauliflower roast for another 30 minutes. You should be able to push a metal skewer or knife easily straight down through the head without meeting much resistance. If it’s not as tender as you’d like, give it another 5 minutes or so.

Remove the pot from the oven and carefully put the cauliflower on a serving plate or cutting board. Cut it into slices, like a cake.

Pairing suggestion: Serve each piece with a generous dollop of Zhug (see here) or other dipping sauce.

title: Sheet Pan Potatoes With Mushrooms, Kale & Beans
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This easy sheet pan dinner has it all: protein, fiber, carbs, leafy greens, and tons of flavor. It’s even great for lunch the next day as a fresh take on potato salad.

FOR THE DRESSING

1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil

1 teaspoon liquid aminos or fish sauce

1 teaspoon balsamic vinegar

½ cup parsley, chopped

¼ cup dill, chopped

FOR THE VEGETABLES

1 pound lacinato kale (also known as Tuscan or black kale), thick stems removed, chopped

¼ teaspoon salt

1 head garlic, separated into cloves but papery skins left intact

1 medium onion, slivered

1 pound cremini mushrooms, cleaned and halved or quartered depending on size

1 pound new potatoes

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

2 teaspoons liquid aminos or fish sauce

1 tablespoon herbes de Provence

2 teaspoons balsamic vinegar

1 teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

2 cups cooked white beans

¼ cup Italian parsley, chopped, for garnish

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

To make the dressing, whisk together all the ingredients in a small bowl until combined. Set aside.

Put the kale in a bowl with the salt and knead it for a couple of minutes until it wilts and darkens. Spread the kale out on a sheet pan and tuck the garlic cloves underneath so that they’ll be sheltered from the heat.

Put the onion, mushrooms and potatoes in a bowl and toss them with the oil, liquid aminos or fish sauce, herbes de Provence, vinegar, salt, and paprika, then spread the mixture out over the kale. Roast for 40 minutes, then scatter the beans over the top of everything and roast for another 5 minutes.

Remove the pan from the oven and peel the garlic, discarding the skins. Put everything in a serving bowl, toss with the dressing, and serve garnished with parsley.

title: Broccoli & Lemon Risotto
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 25 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Risotto is a wonderfully versatile dish, but home cooks are often scared to make it on their own. Skip dining out in favor of this 25-minute version that’s perfectly creamy and chewy, as risotto should be. This Blue Zones take uses broccoli and lemon for flavors that are cheerful and comforting in equal measure. It’s also highly nutritious, providing the health benefits of cruciferous broccoli, protein from the miso, and tons of fiber from the rice and veggies. This dish is even better with some Roasted Broccoli Rabe (see here) on top.

½ pound broccoli florets

3 tablespoons white miso

Juice and zest of 1 lemon

6 cups Dashi (see here) or vegetable stock

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided

1 medium onion, finely diced

1½ cups arborio or carnaroli rice

3 garlic cloves, chopped

1 teaspoon salt

1 teaspoon thyme

1 tablespoon nutritional yeast or ¼ cup freshly grated pecorino

1 tablespoon chives, minced

1 tablespoon fennel fronds, minced

Freshly ground black pepper

Cut the stems off each broccoli floret and cut them crosswise into thin slices; set aside. Pull or cut the florets apart into mini-florets about one inch across; set aside.

In a large bowl, whisk the miso and lemon juice into the dashi or vegetable stock until the miso is dissolved.

Put 2 tablespoons of the oil in a heavy-bottomed skillet or sauté pan over medium-high heat. When the oil starts to shimmer, add the onion and stir well, cooking it until it becomes translucent, 3 to 5 minutes. Add the rice, stirring well to coat each grain with a little oil, and let it toast for another minute or so, stirring several times.

Add the broccoli stem slices, garlic, salt, and thyme, and stir again; cook for a minute or so, until the garlic becomes aromatic. Add a ladleful of the miso-lemon broth, stirring well to incorporate it; continue adding broth one ladleful at a time as the rice absorbs it. After 10 minutes, add the broccoli florets and stir well to combine.

Continue adding broth one ladleful at a time until the rice is just shy of al dente, about another 10 minutes. Add the remaining 2 tablespoons of oil, the nutritional yeast or pecorino, and the rest of the broth, and stir vigorously, shaking the pan back and forth and really working the rice to create a creamy emulsion, for about a minute. Then stir in the herbs and a couple generous twists of pepper, taste for seasoning, and serve immediately. Garnish each bowl with some lemon zest.

The secret to perfect risotto is the mantecatura. There’s no exact translation, but it roughly means “creaming” in Italian. This is the vigorous mixing in the final minutes of cooking that creates an emulsion between fat (extra-virgin olive oil) and water (vegetable stock), using the starch from the rice or pasta as a binder. The result is wonderfully creamy and rich, so make sure to use some elbow grease! Be sure to use arborio or carnaroli rice; other types will not yield the al dente texture you want from a risotto.

title: Bibimbap
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 15 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This classic Korean bowl is equally delicious served hot or cold, and it comes together very fast if you have the rice and beans made ahead of time. (A little Sunday night prep goes a long way in having meals at the ready in 30 minutes or less.) Speed things up even more with store-bought gochujang sauce, available at most grocery stores.

FOR THE GOCHUJANG SAUCE

4 tablespoons gochujang

2 tablespoons orange juice

2 teaspoons rice vinegar

2 teaspoons sesame oil

2 teaspoons honey

2 teaspoons freshly grated ginger

2 garlic cloves, grated

FOR THE BOWL

1 cup shredded kale

1 teaspoon soy sauce

1 teaspoon rice vinegar

½ teaspoon sesame oil

4 cups cooked brown jasmine rice

1 cup cooked adzuki beans

1 red bell pepper, seeded and sliced thin

1 carrot, peeled and cut into ¼-inch matchsticks

1 tablespoon toasted sesame seeds, for garnish

To make the gochujang sauce, whisk together all the ingredients in a small bowl until fully combined. Set aside.

Put the kale in a separate bowl, add the soy sauce, vinegar, and sesame oil, and knead it well for a minute or so until the kale wilts and darkens, turning shiny. Set aside.

To assemble your bowls, put 1 cup of rice in each bowl and top it with ¼ cup beans, ¼ of the pepper slices, ¼ of the carrot, and ¼ of the dressed kale. Spoon a tablespoon of gochujang sauce onto the middle of each bowl and sprinkle sesame seeds on top. Serve with extra sauce on the side.

In Korean, bibim means “mixing” and bap is cooked rice. So be sure to mix this thoroughly, getting the sauce all over everything, before eating.

title: Guacamole & Bean Tacos
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Creamy and crunchy, these tacos seem simple, but the flavors and textures show off in a complex combination. The addition of spicy, crunchy Salsa Macha and fresh Homemade Corn Tortillas makes for one of the best tacos you’ll ever eat. Plus, these are Blue Zones supertacos, with healthy veggies, protein-packed beans, and nuts and seeds from the salsa. And they only take 20 minutes to make!

FOR THE GUACAMOLE

4 ripe avocados, halved and pitted

2 jalapeños, seeded and minced

4 garlic cloves, grated or finely minced

½ teaspoon salt

½ cup cilantro leaves, chopped

Juice of 1 lime

FOR THE SLAW

1 red cabbage, quartered, cored, and finely shredded

1 medium onion, halved and sliced thin

½ teaspoon salt

½ teaspoon ground cumin

½ teaspoon ground coriander

1 teaspoon fresh Mexican oregano, minced (or scant ½ teaspoon dried)

Juice of 1 lime

FOR THE BEANS

1 teaspoon avocado oil

1 garlic clove, chopped

½ teaspoon ground cumin

½ teaspoon ground coriander

1½ cups cooked black beans

1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar

¼ teaspoon salt

To make the guacamole, put the avocados in a bowl and mash gently with a fork until you have a mixture that’s part smooth, part chunky. Add the jalapeños, garlic, salt, cilantro, and lime juice, and stir gently until thoroughly combined.

To make the slaw, put the cabbage and onion in a large bowl along with the salt, cumin, coriander, and oregano. Knead everything gently but firmly, grabbing, squeezing, and mixing a handful and then repeating, making sure to work your way through all of it. You’ll notice that the cabbage quickly starts to get a bit shiny as the salt pulls water out of the vegetables. It will also start to smell really good as the flavors combine. Once the cabbage’s texture has changed, becoming limp and looking somewhere between raw and cooked, add the lime juice and mix well.

To make the beans, heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute, then add the cumin and coriander, stir, and cook for 1 more minute. Add the beans, vinegar, and salt, stir well, and cook until the beans are hot, about 3 minutes.

Pairing suggestion: Serve everything family style along with a pile of Homemade Corn Tortillas (see here) and a bowl of Salsa Macha (see here, or store-bought) so diners can build their own tacos.

title: Belizean Rice & Beans
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 50 MINUTES MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 50 MINUTES MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS

One of the key pillars of a Blue Zones lifestyle is community: Loma Linda centenarians gather on the Sabbath to share a potluck meal; Nicoyans celebrate often with family and friends; Okinawans have moai, groups of friends connected for life; Ikarians and Sardinians gather with friends and family regularly and on Sundays following church services. In Belize, there’s a similar culture of community with regular Sunday gatherings, and none of these occasions is complete without a big pot of rice and beans cooked in coconut milk. This Blue Zones version uses aromatic brown basmati rice for a lower glycemic index number and more fiber. The traditional accompaniment for this heart-healthy, protein-packed meal is a spicy habanero-onion salsa, but our Pikliz (see here) works just as nicely.

2 tablespoons avocado oil

½ yellow or white onion, diced

1 green bell pepper, seeded and diced

3 garlic cloves, chopped

1½ cups cooked kidney beans

2 cups brown basmati rice

2 cups coconut milk

2 cups water or vegetable stock

½ teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

1 tablespoon lime juice

3 sprigs fresh thyme, leaves stripped and chopped

¼ cup cilantro leaves, chopped, plus more for garnish

Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and bell pepper and sauté until they soften and just begin to color, about 10 minutes. Add the garlic and sauté for 1 minute, then add the remaining ingredients except the cilantro; stir well to combine.

Bring everything to a boil, then lower the heat to a simmer, cover the pot, and let it cook for 40 minutes. Fluff the rice, taste for seasoning, and serve garnished with cilantro.

Leftovers make a wonderful base for other recipes, including Bibimbap (see here), Tropical Poke Bowls (see here), and ’Shroom Bowls With Creamy Dressing (see here).

title: Slow Cooker Bourguignon
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 8 HOURS MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 8 HOURS MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS

Four kinds of mushrooms give this rich stew its flavor and texture. What’s nice about this easy dinner is you can set it and forget it—the slow cooker does all the work for you. You don’t need to use fancy, expensive wine for this, but remember that the wine is a significant part of the dish, so use something you’d enjoy drinking. If you have trouble finding oyster or maitake mushrooms, just substitute more cremini or button, or use portobello or shiitake.

½ cup extra-virgin olive oil

8 ounces cremini mushrooms, cleaned, trimmed, and quartered

8 ounces button mushrooms, cleaned, trimmed, and quartered

8 ounces oyster or king trumpet mushrooms, cleaned and sliced about ¼ inch thick

8 ounces maitake mushrooms, cleaned and cut into bite-size pieces

1 medium onion, diced

5 carrots, peeled and diced

2 celery ribs, diced

6 garlic cloves, chopped

2 tablespoons herbes de Provence

2 bay leaves

4 cups red wine

4 tablespoons miso

2 tablespoons liquid aminos

2 teaspoons cornstarch

2 teaspoons balsamic vinegar

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

¼ cup Italian parsley, chopped, for garnish

Set your slow cooker on high. Add the oil and let it heat up.

Add the mushrooms, vegetables, and herbs to the slow cooker and stir well to combine. Cover and let the mixture cook for 2 hours.

While the mushroom mixture cooks, put the red wine and remaining ingredients except the parsley in a medium bowl. Whisk until the miso is dissolved.

After 2 hours, pour the wine mixture into the slow cooker, stir well, and cover again. Let it cook for 6 more hours.

Keep warm until ready to eat. Serve garnished with parsley.

Pairing suggestion: This is wonderful served on top of Not-Your-Mom’s Whipped Potatoes (see here) with some Honey Roasted Carrots (see here) on the side.

If you can’t add the liquid two hours after adding the mushroom mixture, just put everything in at once and let it cook. It’ll still be great!

title: Rice & Lentil Pilaf
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This Middle Eastern–inspired dish combines hearty and protein-rich rice and lentils with the bright flavors of lemon and fresh herbs, similar to a rice pilaf. The lentils don’t need to be soaked, and they cook at the same time as the brown rice, so this comes together easily.

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided

1 yellow or white onion, diced

4 garlic cloves, chopped

2 teaspoons baharat spice blend

4 sprigs thyme, leaves stripped

Juice of 1 lemon, divided

1 cup brown basmati rice

1 cup green lentils

4 cups vegetable stock

1 teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

½ cup dill, chopped

½ cup cilantro, chopped

½ cup parsley, chopped

½ cup mint, chopped

2 scallions, chopped

1 tablespoon Aleppo pepper, for garnish

1 tablespoon sumac powder, for garnish

Heat half the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat until it starts to shimmer. Add the onion and sauté until it begins to turn translucent, about 3 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute, then add the baharat and thyme, stirring well, and cook for another 2 minutes.

Add half the lemon juice and scrape up any brown bits from the bottom of the pot, then add the rice, lentils, stock, salt, and black pepper, and stir well to combine. Bring to a boil, then lower to a simmer. Cover the pot and cook for 40 minutes.

Check that the rice and lentils are both tender, then stir in the remaining 2 tablespoons of oil, the remaining lemon juice, and all the fresh herbs. Taste for seasoning and serve with a sprinkle of Aleppo pepper and sumac powder on top of each dish.

title: Blue Zones Burgers
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES, PLUS 1 HOUR SET TIME MAKES 4 PATTIES
body:
COOK TIME: 20 MINUTES, PLUS 1 HOUR SET TIME MAKES 4 PATTIES

There’s no question that Americans love their burgers. In fact, some studies suggest the average American eats about 60 burgers per year. That’s a lot of not-so-good-for-you red meat. These burgers, on the other hand, combine two quintessential good-for-you Blue Zones ingredients—legumes and purple sweet potatoes—into tasty patties that work just as well on a salad as they do on a bun. The mushroom coating gives them extra flavor and a nice crust.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, divided

1 cup cooked black lentils

½ cup purple sweet potato flesh (from 1 medium potato), baked until very soft and peeled*

1 teaspoon liquid aminos or fish sauce

1 teaspoon salt

1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar

1 teaspoon smoked paprika (hot or sweet, according to taste)

1 garlic clove, grated

1 cup shiitake mushroom caps, grated or very finely chopped

4 whole wheat burger buns (optional)

* For quick baked potatoes, follow the microwave instructions on see here.

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Oil a 13-x-9-inch sheet pan with 1 tablespoon of the oil.

Put the remaining tablespoon of oil and the rest of the ingredients except the mushrooms in a large bowl, and use a potato masher to thoroughly combine everything. You want most of the lentils to be broken and mixed with the sweet potato, and all the seasoning should be evenly distributed. Chill the mixture for at least 1 hour.

Put a 4-inch ring mold on the oiled sheet pan and add 2 tablespoons of the mushrooms in an even layer inside the ring. Take ¼ of the burger mixture and use a rubber spatula to spread it evenly on top of the mushrooms, forming a patty about ⅓ inch thick.

Sprinkle another 2 tablespoons of mushrooms over the top and gently press down so the mushrooms stick to the burger mixture. Repeat 3 more times to make 4 patties.

Brush the remaining oil over the tops of the 4 patties, then bake for 20 minutes, flipping halfway through, until a nice brown crust forms on both top and bottom.

Use a metal spatula to place the patties on buns (if using) or plates and serve with the condiments and toppings of your choice.

Pairing suggestion: These are great with Crispy Salt & Pepper Oven Fries (see here), Pikliz (see here), and Tahini-Miso Sauce (see here).

The patty mixture can be made ahead of time and kept in the fridge, tightly covered, for a day or two, or frozen for up to a month. To freeze, place the patties on parchment paper directly in the freezer, then once they’re frozen solid, store in a tightly closed freezer bag.

title: Three Sisters Pot Pie
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 1 HOUR, PLUS AT LEAST 1 HOUR REFRIGERATION MAKES 4 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 1 HOUR, PLUS AT LEAST 1 HOUR REFRIGERATION MAKES 4 SERVINGS

The “three sisters” are the foundational ingredients of Indigenous American agriculture: corn, beans, and squash. And they make for a powerfully healthy and delicious combination. So we combined their flavors and nutritional benefits in a classic American dish: pot pie.

FOR THE CRUST

4 ounces coconut oil, frozen and cut into cubes

1 cup whole wheat pastry flour

½ cup fine semolina flour

Pinch of salt

¼ cup ice water

FOR THE FILLING

2 tablespoons avocado oil

½ onion, diced

1 red bell pepper, seeded and diced

1 ancho chile, seeded and chopped

2 guajillo chiles, seeded and chopped

2 garlic cloves, chopped

1 tablespoon Mexican oregano

½ teaspoon ground cumin

½ teaspoon ground coriander

½ teaspoon chipotle powder

1½ cups corn kernels (about 2 ears)

1½ cups cooked pinto beans

½ winter squash like kabocha or acorn, peeled, seeded, and cut into roughly 1-inch cubes

4 ounces spinach

1½ teaspoons salt

2 cups vegetable stock

Juice of 1 lime

To make the crust, put the coconut oil chunks, all the flour, and the salt in a food processor and pulse until the oil is broken up, with the largest pieces no bigger than a pea.

Add the water and pulse again until the dough starts to come together. Don’t overwork it or it will get tough. Turn the dough out onto your work surface, gather into a ball, and wrap tightly. Rest in the fridge for at least an hour or up to overnight.

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

To make the filling, in a cast-iron pan or shallow heatproof casserole, heat the oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and bell pepper and sauté until they begin to soften, about 5 minutes. Add the chiles, garlic, oregano, and spices, stir well, and cook for 2 more minutes.

Add the corn, beans, squash, and spinach. Stir well, then add the salt, stock, and lime juice. Stir to combine, bring to a simmer, and then turn off the heat.

To assemble the pot pie, roll the crust out into a sheet large enough to cover the pan. Drape the crust over the pan, trimming the edges, and use a fork to poke holes in the top so steam can escape.

Bake for 45 minutes, then rest for 5 to 10 minutes before serving.

The crust can be made ahead of time and kept tightly wrapped in the fridge overnight or stored in the freezer for up to a month.

title: ’Shroom Bowls With Creamy Dressing
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 20 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

In just one bowl, you can pack fiber-rich grains, gut-healthy veggies, and plenty of flavor to satisfy all taste buds. Make this ahead of time (keep the dressing on the side) for a great lunch during the workweek. If you have precooked rice on hand, all of this comes together in 20 minutes or less!

FOR THE MARINATED MUSHROOMS

4 large shiitake mushrooms (fresh not dried), stems removed

1 tablespoon soy sauce

1 tablespoon rice vinegar

1 teaspoon fresh ginger, thinly sliced

1 garlic clove, sliced

¼ cup boiling water

FOR THE DRESSING

½ cup kimchi

½ cup Kewpie mayo

FOR THE BOWLS

4 cups cooked brown jasmine rice

1 tablespoon sesame oil

2 tablespoons furikake seasoning

1 cup cooked edamame

1 carrot, peeled and grated

1 avocado, sliced

1 scallion, thinly sliced, for garnish

Put the mushrooms in a medium bowl with the soy sauce, vinegar, ginger, and garlic, and toss well to combine. Pour the boiling water over the mushrooms; cover the bowl and let the mixture sit for 10 minutes. Remove the mushrooms and slice thinly when cool enough to handle.

Using an immersion blender or regular blender, blend the kimchi and Kewpie mayo together until smooth, scraping down the sides of the container a couple of times. Set aside.

Put the rice in a medium bowl with the sesame oil and furikake and toss well until thoroughly combined.

To assemble your bowls, put 1 cup of the rice mixture in each serving bowl, spreading it out to make a flat surface. Arrange ¼ cup edamame, ¼ of the carrot, ¼ of the avocado, and ¼ of the sliced mushrooms on top of the rice, then drizzle some dressing over the top. Garnish with scallions.

title: Creamy Mac & “Cheese”
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 25 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

The sauce in this recipe is rich and decadent—so much so that you wouldn’t believe it’s fully Blue Zones–approved. But it’s true! This dish is full of fiber and soy protein. Try it as a healthy (and delicious) alternative to mac and cheese—a beloved American classic that came up time and time again in our research.

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish

¼ cup fresh sage leaves (about 3 leaves per person)

½ white or yellow onion, diced

½ acorn squash, peeled and cut into roughly 1-inch cubes

2 garlic cloves

½ pound silken tofu, cubed

2 tablespoons white wine vinegar

2 tablespoons nutritional yeast

2 tablespoons Dashi (see here, or use vegetable stock or water)

1 teaspoon salt

1 pound durum wheat pasta, cooked according to package instructions, cooking water reserved

Freshly ground black pepper, for garnish

Put the oil in a deep saucepan over medium-high heat. When it begins to shimmer, add the sage leaves, taking care to keep them separate, and let them fry for about a minute on each side. Remove the leaves and place them on a paper towel–lined plate to drain.

Add the onion, squash, and garlic to the saucepan and stir well to coat everything with oil. Sauté until the onion begins to soften, about 5 minutes, then add the tofu, vinegar, nutritional yeast, dashi, and salt, stirring to combine. Lower the heat to medium, cover the saucepan, and let the mixture simmer until the squash is tender, about 15 minutes.

Remove the saucepan from the heat and use a blender to puree the mixture until it’s silky smooth with no lumps. Taste for seasoning and keep warm.

Add the cooked pasta to the saucepan, tossing well to coat. Add a ladleful of reserved pasta water, if needed, stirring to fully combine.

Serve immediately, finishing each bowl with a drizzle of oil, a couple twists of pepper, and a few fried sage leaves.

title: Blue Zones Biryani
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 50 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Biryani likely originated in Iran, but today it is most associated with North India—though variations appear across South Asia. This version includes longevity-powered red lentils in addition to the traditional green peas.

4 tablespoons coconut oil, divided

1 onion, halved; one half slivered, one half diced

¼ cup cashews

2 tablespoons raisins

Pinch of saffron threads (optional)

½ cinnamon stick

1 star anise

5 cloves

10 cardamom seeds (or two pods)

1 teaspoon cumin seeds

1 teaspoon coriander seeds

1 teaspoon mustard seeds

1 teaspoon fennel seeds

1 teaspoon Kashmiri chile powder or other chile powder (optional; add more for extra heat)

½ teaspoon powdered turmeric

1 teaspoon garam masala

1 teaspoon fresh ginger, grated

1 teaspoon garlic, grated

1 plum tomato, diced

½ head cauliflower, cut into florets, large ones halved or quartered

½ cup fresh or frozen green peas

½ cup fresh or frozen green beans, cut into ½-inch pieces

2 carrots, peeled and sliced into thin rounds

½ cup unsweetened coconut milk yogurt alternative

2 teaspoons salt

½ cup red lentils, rinsed and drained

2 cups brown basmati rice, rinsed and drained

4 cups water or vegetable stock

In a deep pot or casserole, heat 2 tablespoons of the oil over medium-high heat. When it begins to shimmer, add the slivered onion, stir, and cook until the thin parts begin to brown, about 5 minutes. Add the cashews, raisins, and saffron (if using), and cook for another 5 minutes or so to brown the onion and nuts. Remove the mixture from the pan, along with some of the oil, and set aside.

Add the remaining 2 tablespoons of oil to the pan and let it melt. Add the diced onion and all the ingredients through the garam masala and stir. When the mustard seeds begin to pop, about 1 minute, add the ginger and garlic and stir again. Cook for 1 more minute, then add the tomato and stir, using the liquid to scrape up any brown bits from the pan.

Add the cauliflower, peas, beans, and carrots, and stir again. Add the yogurt, salt, and lentils, stir, and cook for 3 minutes. Spread the rice out in an even layer on top of the vegetable mixture, pushing down gently to create a smooth surface. Pour the water or vegetable stock slowly over the rice.

As soon as the mixture begins to simmer, lower the heat to medium-low and cover the pot. Cook for 40 minutes, until the rice is just tender and most of the liquid has been absorbed.

Garnish the biryani with the cashew-onion mixture and its oil, and bring it to the table, family style.

Pairing suggestion: Serve with Coconut Raita (see here).

title: Jollof Rice
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAK FOR RICE MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 30 MINUTES, PLUS OVERNIGHT SOAK FOR RICE MAKES 6 TO 8 SERVINGS

West Africa has many recipes for jollof rice. We won’t claim one is better than another, but this version is based on a Nigerian version of the beloved dish. Traditionally, jollof is cooked in large pans over an open fire for parties, so a little smoked paprika helps give a bit of that flavor to our version. This recipe also adds beans—not typically part of jollof—to make it more Blue Zones appropriate.

1 red bell pepper, seeded and roughly chopped

1 onion, halved; one half roughly chopped, one half slivered

3 plum tomatoes, roughly chopped

3 garlic cloves, chopped

1 habanero or Scotch bonnet pepper, stem and seeds removed, chopped

1 tablespoon tomato paste

1 teaspoon fresh ginger, grated

2 tablespoons avocado oil

1 bay leaf

2 sprigs thyme, leaves stripped

1 teaspoon curry powder

1 teaspoon sweet smoked paprika

2 cups brown basmati rice, soaked overnight in 6 cups water with a pinch of salt and drained

1½ teaspoons salt

1 cup vegetable stock, plus more as needed

1½ cups cooked pinto beans

1 scallion, sliced thin

Put the bell pepper, chopped onion, tomatoes, garlic, habanero or Scotch bonnet, tomato paste, and ginger in a blender, and blend into a smooth puree. Set aside.

In a heavy-bottomed skillet, heat the oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the slivered onion and sauté until it begins to turn translucent, about 3 minutes. Add the bay leaf, thyme, curry powder, and paprika, and stir well, cooking for another 2 minutes.

Add the rice, salt, stock, and beans to the skillet and stir well to combine. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat to medium-low and cover the skillet. Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring gently at about the 10-minute mark, until the rice is just tender. If it’s still quite wet, take the lid off and let it cook for another 5 minutes or so to evaporate some liquid. If it’s very dry, add ½ cup more stock.

Taste for seasoning and remove the bay leaf. Use a fork to fluff up the rice; sprinkle the scallion over the top and serve, giving everyone some of the browned rice from the bottom.

Pairing suggestion: Serve this with West African Peanut Stew (see here) or sprinkle some Crispy Roasted Chickpeas (see here) on top.

One of the keys to good jollof rice is letting the rice at the bottom brown so that it’s just shy of burning. This crispy, extra-flavorful rice is widely prized as the best part.

title: Balsamic Mushroom & Lentil Wild Rice
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 45 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

Wild rice has about twice the protein and fiber of brown rice, making it a superbly Blue Zones–friendly ingredient. And its nutty flavor and texture pair beautifully with mushrooms and black lentils.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

2 cups shiitake mushroom caps, cleaned and sliced

1 large shallot, chopped

2 garlic cloves, chopped

4 large fresh sage leaves, chopped

2 sprigs oregano, leaves stripped and chopped

2 sprigs rosemary, leaves stripped and chopped

2 sprigs thyme, leaves stripped and chopped

1¼ cups (6 ounces) wild rice, rinsed and drained

½ cup black lentils

1 teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

6 cups vegetable stock or water

2 tablespoons balsamic vinegar

¼ cup chives, minced

White truffle oil (optional), for garnish

Heat the olive oil in a large soup pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the mushrooms, stir, and sauté until they give up their liquid and begin to brown, about 5 minutes. Add the shallot and garlic, stir, and cook for another 3 minutes.

Add the herbs, stir, and cook for 2 more minutes, then add the rice, lentils, salt, pepper, and stock or water. As soon as the mixture begins to boil, lower the heat to medium-low and cook uncovered at a moderate simmer for 40 minutes, until the rice is tender and the grains are beginning to split lengthwise.

Taste for seasoning and stir in the vinegar and most of the chives. Serve with more chives sprinkled on top and a drizzle of truffle oil (if using).

Pairing suggestion: Serve topped with Garlicky-Good Roasted Mushrooms (see here) and a salad on the side.

title: Veggie-Forward Shepherd’s Pie
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 55 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
COOK TIME: 55 MINUTES MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

Americans love comfort foods, and is anything more comforting than a shepherd’s pie? This version combines three kinds of mushrooms with lentils for loads of flavor and fiber. The aromatic broth includes red wine vinegar and miso, and it’s all topped with Not-Your-Mom’s Whipped Potatoes (see here), then baked until it’s browned and bubbling.

2 cups water or vegetable stock

1 tablespoon miso

1 teaspoon liquid aminos or fish sauce

1 tablespoon cornstarch

¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil

8 ounces shiitake mushrooms, cleaned, stems removed, and sliced

8 ounces cremini mushrooms, cleaned and chopped

8 ounces button mushrooms, cleaned and chopped

1 cup cooked green or brown lentils

1 medium onion, diced

3 carrots, peeled and diced

3 celery ribs, diced

1 teaspoon herbes de Provence

1 bay leaf

2 garlic cloves, chopped

¼ cup red wine vinegar

1 teaspoon salt

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

3 cups Not-Your-Mom’s Whipped Potatoes (see here)

¼ cup flat-leaf parsley, chopped, for garnish

¼ cup chives, chopped, for garnish

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

In a medium bowl, combine the water or stock, miso, liquid aminos or fish sauce, and cornstarch; whisk together until the miso and cornstarch are fully incorporated, with no lumps remaining. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a large cast-iron skillet or heat-safe 12-inch casserole over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the mushrooms, stir well, and sauté until they release all their liquid and begin to sizzle again, about 10 minutes. Add the lentils, onion, carrots, and celery, and sauté, stirring regularly, until they have begun to soften, another 5 minutes or so. Add the herbs and garlic and cook, stirring every minute or so, for 5 minutes.

Deglaze the pan with the vinegar, stirring to scrape up any bits stuck to the pan, and then pour in the stock mixture. Stir well to combine everything, add the salt and pepper, then let the mixture bubble and thicken for a couple of minutes.

Take the pan off the heat and remove the bay leaf. Carefully spread the potatoes over the top using a spatula or wooden spoon. This is easiest if the potatoes are freshly made and still warm. If they’re cold and stiff, the best way to cover the stew is by using a pastry bag to pipe the potato mixture evenly over the top.

Put the pan in the oven and bake for 30 minutes. If you want the top to be more browned, switch the oven to broil for the final few minutes (but keep an eye on it). Remove the pan from the oven, garnish with parsley and chives, and serve.

title: Sesame-Crusted Tofu Summer Rolls
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 25 MINUTES MAKES 8 ROLLS

These Vietnamese-style rolls are a perennial favorite, and they meet a lot of the flavor profiles Americans are looking for in their recipes. They’re light and fresh but satisfying—and between the tofu and noodles, they’ve got legumes in two forms (three if you add the peanut sauce). Plus, you can make them in under 30 minutes!

5 ounces bean thread noodles

Very hot tap water

½ cup black and white sesame seeds

1 pound firm tofu, pressed and drained, cut crosswise into ¼-inch slices

1 tablespoon avocado oil

8 Vietnamese rice wrappers

1 cup Quick Pickled Veggies (see here), drained, or ½ cup each carrot (about 1 medium carrot) and daikon (about 1 medium daikon), cut into thin matchsticks

1 cup mint leaves

1 cup cilantro leaves

1 cup Vietnamese Peanut Sauce (see here, or store-bought), for serving

Put the noodles in a large bowl and cover them with very hot tap water. Let them soak until they’re soft, at least 10 minutes. Drain and set aside.

Put the sesame seeds on a shallow plate. Dredge the tofu slices in the seeds so both sides are coated. Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat and fry the tofu until lightly browned on both sides, about 5 minutes per side.

Pour about 2 inches of hot water into a wide container (like a cake pan) that’s large enough to hold the rice wrappers. Add a wrapper to the bowl, pushing it down until fully submerged, then let it soak until just soft, about 1 minute.

Remove the wrapper from the water, letting it drip for a few seconds, then lay it out flat on your work surface. Place two pieces of tofu in a horizontal line about ½ inch from the wrapper’s edge that’s closest to you and ½ inch from either side, then spread about ¼ cup of noodles on top of the tofu, followed by a layer of veggies and then one of mint and cilantro. Roll the wrapper away from you, pulling gently on the roll as you go—you want to make it as tight as possible. Repeat with the remaining wrappers.

Serve the rolls with the peanut sauce. They’re also great with Tahini-Miso Sauce (see here) or Avocado-Herb Sauce (see here).

title: Roasted Ratatouille
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

This Provençal dish combines the best of summer’s bountiful nightshades—tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, and zucchini—in a savory stew. This version simplifies the process without sacrificing any flavor and borrows a little of the presentation from a certain movie with the same name.

2 zucchini, cut into ⅛-inch rounds

1 eggplant (or 2 to 3 thin Japanese eggplants), cut into ⅛-inch rounds

1 teaspoon salt, divided

¼ cup, plus 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, divided

1 red bell pepper, seeded and roughly chopped

½ onion, roughly chopped

2 plum tomatoes, roughly chopped

2 garlic cloves, chopped

4 sprigs thyme, leaves stripped, divided

4 sprigs oregano, leaves stripped and chopped, divided

1 sprig rosemary, leaves stripped and chopped, divided

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Put the zucchini and eggplant slices in a large bowl, sprinkle with half the salt, and toss well. Add ¼ cup of the oil and toss again to coat each slice evenly. Set aside.

Put the bell pepper, onion, tomatoes, garlic, half the herbs, the remaining salt, and the black pepper in a blender and run it until you have a smooth puree. Pour half the puree into a wide, round casserole, spreading into an even layer.

Arrange the zucchini and eggplant slices on top of the puree, alternating slices to make a scalloped pattern, continuing until the whole dish is covered. Pour the other half of the sauce over the top and spread it evenly, then sprinkle on the rest of the herbs.

Bake for 40 minutes, remove from the oven, and drizzle on the rest of the oil. Let it rest for 5 more minutes before serving.

Pairing suggestion: This is great with Not-Your-Mom’s Whipped Potatoes (see here), Beans & Greens “Risotto” (see here), or Spinach & Roasted Radicchio Salad With Chile-Maple Vinaigrette (see here).

Ratatouille is even better the next day; make this ahead of time and reheat it before serving.

title: Moroccan Tagine
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 40 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

In Morocco, “tagine” is the name of both a shallow ceramic vessel with a tall conical lid and the savory stews cooked in it. But you don’t need a tagine to cook this delicious dish, loaded with veggies, chickpeas, and spices—any deep skillet or casserole with a lid will work fine.

2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 onion, diced

3 garlic cloves, chopped

2 teaspoons ras el hanout (Moroccan spice blend)

2 teaspoons ground cumin

1 teaspoon ground coriander

½ teaspoon turmeric powder

¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

¼ teaspoon cayenne

Pinch of saffron threads (optional)

1 bay leaf

¼ preserved lemon, finely chopped (or juice and zest of one lemon)

1 carrot, peeled and cut into 1-inch rounds

1 zucchini, halved lengthwise and cut into half moons

1 cauliflower, cut into bite-size florets

2 cups chickpeas, cooked

¼ cup Niçoise or kalamata olives

2 cups vegetable stock

½ cup tomato puree

2 teaspoons salt

Cilantro, for garnish (optional)

Heat the oil in a large skillet or casserole over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and sauté until it softens, about 3 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 2 more minutes.

Add the spices and the bay leaf, stir, and cook for 3 minutes, then add the preserved lemon and cook for 2 more minutes. Add the vegetables, chickpeas, and olives, and stir gently to coat with the onion mixture in the pan.

Add the stock, tomato puree, and salt, and stir gently; as soon as the liquid begins to boil, lower the heat to medium-low and cover the pot. Simmer until the vegetables are very tender, about 30 minutes. Remove the bay leaf. Taste for seasoning and serve.

Garnish with sprigs of cilantro (if using). This is great with harissa and couscous—which is made from semolina (durum wheat) and thus Blue Zones–approved.

Preserved lemons can be found online or at specialty shops, or you can substitute the juice and zest of one lemon. Ras el hanout is easy to find online.

title: Hibiscus-Mint Tea
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES 4 (1-CUP) SERVINGS

Tea is a key beverage for centenarians in Okinawa, Sardinia, and Ikaria. Typically made with a variety of herbs, the flavor combinations are endless. This version uses wonderfully tart and fruity hibiscus flowers, which also give it a vivid purple color. Mint, lime, and honey take things to another level. Drink this hot or iced (and with a splash of seltzer).

½ cup fresh mint leaves, plus sprigs for garnish

¼ cup wildflower honey

½ cup dried hibiscus flowers

Peel from ¼ lime, sliced

4 cups boiling water

Put the mint leaves in a heatproof container (like a wide-mouth 1-quart canning jar) along with the honey. Muddle the honey and mint with a wooden spoon to crush the leaves a bit, then add the hibiscus and lime peel. Pour the boiling water into the jar, cover it, and let steep for 5 minutes. Strain and serve garnished with a sprig of fresh mint.

title: No-Bake Pecan Bars
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 9 BARS

Pecans are one of the most favored dessert ingredients for Americans—from pecan pie to pecan bars, there’s something about this actually-good-for-you nut that brings out everyone’s sweet tooth. But rather than being coated in sugar, these easy dessert bars get their sweetness from longevity-boosting purple sweet potatoes, as well as dates and a hint of maple syrup. Make sure to bake the sweet potatoes rather than steam them—you want them as dry as possible. (See our microwave trick on see here.)

FOR THE CRUST

2 cups pecans

8 medjool dates, pitted

¼ teaspoon cinnamon

FOR THE FILLING

2 cups purple sweet potato flesh (from about 2 large potatoes, baked until very soft, then peeled)

1 teaspoon cardamom

1 teaspoon fresh ginger, grated

4 teaspoons maple syrup

¼ teaspoon vanilla extract

FOR THE CARAMEL

½ cup coconut milk

2 tablespoons maple syrup

To make the crust, blend the ingredients in a food processor until you have a homogeneous mixture that looks like wet sand. Transfer to a bowl and set aside.

To make the filling, wipe the food processor clean and puree the ingredients until smooth. Set aside in a bowl.

To make the caramel, boil the ingredients together in a small saucepan until the mixture reduces and thickens. When the caramel has thickened, a spatula dragged across the bottom will leave a trail of bare pan for a few seconds before the liquid flows back.

To assemble the bars, trim a sheet of parchment paper to fit the bottom of a 9-x-9-inch square cake pan so that it hangs over two of the sides. You’ll use these overhangs as handles to remove the bars at the end.

Spread half the crust mixture around the bottom of the pan in an even layer, pressing down firmly to compact it. Spread the sweet potato mixture on top in an even layer, then top that with the rest of the crust mixture, making it as even as possible.

Spread another sheet of parchment out over the top of the bars, then use a second cake pan to press down gently but firmly on the bars to compact them. Remove the top pan and use the parchment to carefully lift the bars out of the bottom pan. Set them on a cutting board and drizzle the caramel evenly over the top. Cut into 9 equal squares and serve.

This recipe calls for two 9-x-9-inch cake pans—the second one is used to press down on the bars to compact them.

title: Fall Fantasy Dark Chocolate Truffles
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES, PLUS 1 HOUR CHILL TIME MAKES ABOUT 8 TRUFFLES
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES, PLUS 1 HOUR CHILL TIME MAKES ABOUT 8 TRUFFLES

Pumpkin and cranberry evoke the festive flavors of fall and winter. We combined them with chocolate in these bite-size treats that make for a celebratory end to a meal.

½ cup unsweetened dark chocolate chips

¼ cup pumpkin puree

1 tablespoon maple syrup

¼ teaspoon pumpkin spice

¼ teaspoon vanilla extract

¼ cup freeze-dried cranberry powder

Melt the chocolate chips in a double boiler or microwave. Stir in the pumpkin puree, maple syrup, pumpkin spice, and vanilla extract; mix well to combine. Put the ganache in the fridge, covered, until completely cold, about 1 hour.

Once it’s chilled, spread the cranberry powder in an even layer onto a small plate. Use a dessert spoon to scoop out some ganache. Use a second spoon to scoop the ganache from the first, passing the ganache back and forth a couple of times to make a roughly round ball about the size of a quarter in diameter.

Roll each truffle in the cranberry powder until coated on all sides, then place the truffle on a plate or small sheet tray lined with parchment. Keep the truffles refrigerated until you’re ready to serve.

The ganache can be made ahead of time and kept in the fridge for a day or two. This recipe scales up well, so you can make a big batch of truffles and then freeze them for future use.

title: Lemon Longevity Bars
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: BAKE TIME: 45 MINUTES, PLUS SEVERAL HOURS CHILL TIME MAKES 9 BARS
body:
BAKE TIME: 45 MINUTES, PLUS SEVERAL HOURS CHILL TIME MAKES 9 BARS

Lemon squares are a perennial favorite dessert, but this version skips the added sugar, eggs, and butter while still delivering on all the tangy, sweet-tart flavor you desire.

FOR THE CRUST

1½ cups almond flour

6 medjool dates, pitted

3 tablespoons coconut oil

¼ teaspoon salt

FOR THE LEMON CURD

2 cups coconut milk

¾ cup lemon juice

¼ cup maple syrup

1 heaping tablespoon lemon zest

Pinch of salt

¼ cup arrowroot starch or cornstarch

Preheat your oven to 375°F.

Line a 9-x-9-inch cake pan with parchment paper.

Put the crust ingredients in a food processor and run it until you have an even mixture that looks like wet sand. Spread the crust mixture evenly around the bottom of the cake pan. Use your hands to press down on the mixture to make it compact.

Bake the crust for 20 minutes, until the edges begin to brown.

While the crust bakes, make the curd: Whisk all the ingredients except the starch in a bowl until fully combined. Add the starch a little at a time as you whisk to be sure there are no lumps.

When the crust is ready, pour the curd mixture into the pan; return to the oven and bake for 22 to 25 minutes, until the edges are set and the center is still a little loose and wiggly. Remove the pan from the oven and let cool, then put it in the fridge until it’s completely chilled, at least 2 to 3 hours. Cut into 9 squares and serve.

title: No-Bake Peanut Butter & Honey Cookie Bites
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 12 BALLS
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 12 BALLS

These bite-size sweet treats have the texture of cookie dough and the longevity-boosting properties of peanuts and chickpeas. It’s much easier to shape these with wet hands.

½ cup cooked chickpeas

¼ cup smooth unsalted peanut butter

6 medjool dates, pitted

2 teaspoons honey

Pinch of salt

½ cup pistachios, finely chopped

Put all the ingredients except the pistachios in a food processor and blend until smooth.

Use your hands to form balls about 1¼ inches in diameter. Roll each ball in the pistachios to coat, then roll again between your hands briefly to push the nuts into the dough.

Serve immediately, or keep in the fridge in a covered container for up to a week.

Use peanut butter with no additives. The ingredients list on the jar should just say “peanuts.”

title: Chewy Oatmeal Chocolate Chip Cookies
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
BAKE TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 8 COOKIES

These easy cookies are essentially protein-rich energy bars disguised as dessert. A pinch of crunchy salt gives them some sophistication, while plenty of dark chocolate and peanut butter add great flavor. This recipe can easily be multiplied to make more.

1 cup oats

2 tablespoons chia seeds, soaked in ¼ cup water for 20 minutes, then drained

1 cup dark chocolate chips

2 tablespoons coconut oil

¼ cup smooth unsalted peanut butter

¼ cup maple syrup

¼ teaspoon vanilla extract

Coarse salt for sprinkling

Preheat your oven to 350°F.

Line a baking sheet with parchment paper or a silicone mat.

Combine all the ingredients except the salt in a bowl and mix well. Form golf-ball-size balls of dough and place them on the baking sheet. Press each ball gently to flatten it into a disc about ½ inch thick.

Sprinkle a little coarse salt on top of each cookie and bake for 30 minutes, turning the pan halfway through.

Use peanut butter with no additives. The ingredients list on the jar should just say “peanuts.”

title: Creamy Chocolate–Coconut Pudding
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 SERVINGS

The surprise in this dessert is avocado, which gives this decadent treat its creamy texture. Don’t forget to finish with a bit of flaky salt—it really puts it over the top.

1 cup ripe avocado, mashed

½ cup coconut milk

2 tablespoons unsweetened cocoa powder

6 medjool dates, pitted

¼ teaspoon vanilla extract

¼ teaspoon flaky salt, like Maldon

Put all the ingredients except the salt in a blender and run it on high until you have a smooth puree. Scrape the sides down at least twice to ensure that all the date pieces have been fully incorporated—you want a silky texture.

Serve with a few flakes of salt on top of each portion.

This is a great make-ahead dish; just put it in an airtight container in the fridge. You can even run it through an ice cream machine if you’d like a frozen version.

title: Watermelon Hydrator
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
PREP TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES 4 (1-CUP) SERVINGS

Forget sports and energy drinks, which are full of additives—this tasty beverage is the ultimate revitalizer. It’s a little sweet, a little sour, and even a little spicy (if you go for a rim). And the sea salt has electrolytes! Multiply the recipe and bring a jug to a party, or just keep a jar handy in the fridge.

FOR THE DRINK

3 cups watermelon, seeded and cut into chunks

1 cup coconut water

1 tablespoon honey

Juice and zest of 1 lime, rind reserved

FOR SERVING

1 teaspoon Tajín

1 lime, cut into slices

Zest of ½ lime

To make the drink, use a blender to blend all the ingredients except the lime zest until smooth.

To coat the glass rims, spread the Tajín on a small plate. Rub the rim of each glass with the inside of the reserved lime rind to get it wet, then invert each glass into the Tajín, turning the glass so the whole rim gets coated.

Put some ice in each glass, then fill with the drink. Garnish with a lime slice and a little zest.

title: Minty Watermelon-Hibiscus Granita
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: FREEZE TIME: 1 HOUR OR MORE MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
FREEZE TIME: 1 HOUR OR MORE MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

Another favorite American ingredient, watermelon, gets its Blue Zones dessert makeover with this easy icy treat, which combines it with bright hibiscus and cooling mint. This is a refreshing delight that works well with a wide variety of fruit.

FOR THE HIBISCUS TEA

1 cup boiling water

2 tablespoons dried hibiscus flowers

FOR THE GRANITA

2 cups seedless watermelon, cut into roughly 1½-inch cubes

1 cup hibiscus tea (see above)

¼ cup honey

¼ cup mint leaves, chopped, plus extra sprigs for garnish

1 tablespoon lime juice, plus zest for garnish

To make the hibiscus tea, slowly pour the boiling water over the hibiscus flowers in a pot or heatproof container. Let the tea steep for 10 minutes, then strain and cool.

To make the granita, put the watermelon, hibiscus tea, and honey in a blender and puree until smooth. Pour the liquid through a strainer into a wide, flat dish, like a square baking pan. Put the pan in the freezer; when it starts to ice over (after 30 minutes or so), use a fork to stir and scrape the mixture into a slush. Then put the pan back in the freezer for another 30 minutes and scrape it again, creating a sort of coarse pink snow. The more times you repeat this process, the finer the ice will become.

Chill your serving bowls at least an hour before serving. This helps keep the ice from melting too quickly.

To serve, spoon some granita into a bowl, add a sprig of mint, grate a little lime zest over the top, and enjoy.

The hibiscus tea is a lovely drink by itself, so feel free to make extra and enjoy it hot or iced.

title: No-Bake Marzipan Cookie Bites
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 12 BALLS
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 12 BALLS

These delicious morsels evoke chocolate-covered marzipan logs, but in a healthy Blue Zones way that benefits from creamy almond butter and raw cacao nibs.

½ cup cooked chickpeas

¼ cup almond butter

¼ cup maple syrup

1 teaspoon coconut oil

¼ teaspoon almond extract

¼ teaspoon vanilla extract

½ cup raw cacao nibs

Put all the ingredients except the cacao nibs in a food processor and blend until smooth.

Use your hands to form balls about 1¼ inches in diameter. Place the cacao nibs in an even layer on a shallow dish and roll each ball in the nibs to coat; roll again between your hands briefly to push the nibs into the dough.

Serve immediately, or keep in the fridge in a covered container for up to a week.

It’s much easier to shape these with wet hands.

title: Banana Ice Cream
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES WITH BLENDER; 20 MINUTES WITH ICE CREAM MAKER MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS
body:
PREP TIME: 10 MINUTES WITH BLENDER; 20 MINUTES WITH ICE CREAM MAKER MAKES 4 TO 6 SERVINGS

This frozen dessert offers all the rich, creamy decadence of traditional ice cream, without the bad-for-you sugar and dairy. Fully Blue Zones–approved, our cold treat is made from bananas and dates. You’ll have to plan ahead to freeze your bananas, but the rest comes easily.

2 bananas, peeled and frozen solid

6 medjool dates, pitted and chopped

½ cup coconut cream, chilled

¼ teaspoon vanilla extract

Combine all the ingredients in a blender and run it until you have a smooth puree.

Serve immediately in chilled bowls, or if you have an ice cream maker, run the mixture through according to the manufacturer’s instructions before serving.

To make a chocolate version, add 1 tablespoon of unsweetened cocoa powder and 1 more date to the recipe.

WORTHWHILE TOPPING COMBOS

Toasted and chopped pistachios

Raw honey

Dusting of ground cardamom

Walnut butter

Dried unsweetened apple, chopped

Dusting of ground cinnamon

Cacao nibs

Toasted walnuts

Maple syrup

Almond butter

Dried unsweetened cherries, chopped

Coconut flakes

title: No-Bake Chocolate Mousse Pie
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
body:
FREEZE TIME: 30 MINUTES MAKES 8 SERVINGS

Adventists have learned to use plant foods like tofu to reinvent classic comfort food dishes, like in this chocolate mousse pie. This four-ingredient recipe will charm even the biggest chocolate lovers.

1¾ cups semisweet chocolate chips

12 ounces silken tofu, patted dry

½ cup vanilla almond milk

Ready-made graham cracker pie crust

Berries or chopped nuts, for topping (optional)

In a microwave-safe bowl, melt the chocolate chips in the microwave in 30-second increments until fully melted.

Combine the melted chocolate, tofu, and almond milk in a blender and pulse until smooth, about 1 minute.

Pour the mixture into the pie crust and smooth the top with a knife. Cover and freeze until set, about 30 minutes.

Serve topped with berries or chopped nuts of your choice (if using).

title: Mango-Tajín Ice Pops
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: FREEZE TIME: SEVERAL HOURS, DEPENDING ON YOUR FREEZER MAKES ABOUT 6 ICE POPS
body:
FREEZE TIME: SEVERAL HOURS, DEPENDING ON YOUR FREEZER MAKES ABOUT 6 ICE POPS

You can infuse your desserts with the Mexican flavor profiles Americans love so much. Tajín is a Mexican spice blend made from chile, lime, and salt. It’s often sprinkled on mangoes and other fresh fruit for a sweet-sour-savory-spicy treat. These easy pops come together in minutes and can be made well ahead of time.

2 cups mango, cut into chunks

2 tablespoons lime juice

2 teaspoons honey

1 teaspoon Tajín seasoning

Put the mango, lime juice, and honey in a blender and run it, scraping the sides down once or twice, until you have a smooth puree. Pour the puree into ice pop molds and freeze for several hours.

To serve, take the pops out of the freezer and let them sit on the counter for about 1 minute so the outermost edge just starts to thaw—this will help the spice stick to it. Pull each pop out of its mold, sprinkle on a little Tajín, and enjoy.

This recipe scales up well, so you can easily double it (or more) for a party.

title: Blueberry Spritz
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
desc: COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 CUP OF SYRUP (ENOUGH FOR 8 SERVINGS)
body:
COOK TIME: 5 MINUTES MAKES ABOUT 1 CUP OF SYRUP (ENOUGH FOR 8 SERVINGS)

Wonderfully refreshing, especially over ice in the summer, this drink doubles down on the antioxidants in blueberries by bringing some red wine to the party. Besides being great for flavoring seltzer, the blueberry syrup is a delicious addition drizzled over yogurt, oatmeal, Banana Ice Cream (see here), and Mango-Tajín Ice Pops (see here).

FOR THE SYRUP

2 cups blueberries

¼ cup red wine

¼ cup honey

1 teaspoon fresh ginger, grated

TO SERVE

Unflavored seltzer water, chilled

Blueberries, for garnish (optional)

Lemon wheels, for garnish (optional)

Mint sprigs, for garnish (optional)

Put all the syrup ingredients in a saucepan over medium-high heat and boil until the blueberries burst and the liquid begins to thicken, about 5 minutes. Pour the syrup through a strainer, pushing on the solids with a spoon or spatula to extract all the liquid.

For each 12-ounce serving, put 2 tablespoons of syrup in a glass, fill the glass with seltzer, and stir gently to dissolve all the syrup. Garnish with a few fresh blueberries, a lemon wheel, or a mint sprig if you’d like.

Don’t throw out the blueberry skins after you strain the syrup! Freeze them and blend them into your next batch of Mango-Tajín Ice Pops (see here). Blueberries and mangoes make a great combination—and finding delicious uses for by-products is pretty tasty, too.

title: Apple-Cinnamon-Raisin Hand Pies
book: The Blue Zones Kitchen One Pot Meals
author: Dan Buettner
